Name this hopping technique (two words: Switch ___).

tasks.title: Defeat double-tagging
tasks.teach: Double-tagging hops a frame from VLAN 1 to another VLAN using two 802.1Q tags. The fix: make the native VLAN a dedicated, unused ID and tag it.
tasks.chal:
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999 Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20

Which VLAN ID did this config pick as the safe, dedicated native? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 999 — a dedicated unused native defeats double-tagging; allow only VLANs 10 and 20 on the trunk.
tasks.example: Fix double-tagging by making the native VLAN a dedicated, unused ID (e.g. 999) and tagging it, and pruning the allowed list.

lab.intro: Check the hardened trunk config.

steps.out:
interface GigabitEthernet0/24
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 999   <-- dedicated, unused
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20

steps2: On the switch: show running-config interface gi0/24
Read the native vlan line
Submit the dedicated native VLAN id used here.

tasks.title: Prove VRF isolation
tasks.teach:
VRFs give each VLAN its own routing table on one device, so one cannot route to another.

🔑 Key point

Isolation — VRF-lite is separate routing tables on a single device, ideal for enterprise segmentation.
tasks.chal:
$ ip vrf exec vrf-user ping -c1 10.10.20.1 connect: Network is unreachable # VLAN 20 doesn't exist in the user VRF $ ip route show vrf vrf-user 10.10.10.0/24 dev enp0s8.10 # only its own network

In one word, what property do the separate VRF tables enforce? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: Each VRF sees only its own routes.
tasks.learn: Isolation — VRF-lite is separate routing tables on a single device, ideal for enterprise segmentation.
tasks.example: Bind each VLAN interface to its own VRF and the kernel keeps a separate routing table per VRF — cross-VLAN routing simply fails.

lab.intro: Prove VLAN 10 cannot route into VLAN 20.

steps.out: connect: Network is unreachable   # VLAN 20 is not in the user VRF -> isolated
10.10.10.0/24 dev enp0s8.10   # only its own network

steps2: Create VRFs and bind VLAN ifaces (Part 4.2 of the handbook)
Run ip vrf exec vrf-user ping 10.10.20.1 → unreachable
In one word, name the property the VRF enforces.

tasks.title: The audit command
tasks.teach: You need to confirm a trunk's native VLAN and its allowed list in one shot.
tasks.chal: Type the Cisco command (case-insensitive) that reveals both. Submit it as the flag.
tasks.learn: show interfaces trunk (or ip -d link on Linux) reveals native + allowed VLANs — most leaks show here.
tasks.example: show interfaces trunk is the single command that exposes most real leaks: native mismatch or an over-broad allowed list.

lab.intro: The task is the audit command itself.

steps.out:
Port    Native vlan  Allowed vlans
Gi0/24  999          10,20   # native + allowed in one view

steps2: Run the one command that shows native + allowed VLANs together
Submit it (lower-case) as the flag.

tasks.title: Why not VLAN 1
tasks.teach: Every switch ships with VLAN 1 active everywhere.
tasks.chal: Why must VLAN 1 never carry data or management traffic? In one word, it is the ___ VLAN. Submit TG{•••••••}.
hints: It is on by default and well known.
tasks.learn: Default — a known target. Move all hosts off it and use dedicated VLANs for data and management.
tasks.example: VLAN 1 is the default on every switch — management, DTP and CDP ride it out of the box. Being well-known and always-on makes it a target; keep all data and management off it.

tasks.title: The segmentation maxim
tasks.teach: A common false comfort about VLANs. Decode it.
tasks.chal:
Decode the note.

Decode this to reveal the flag (use the 🧰 Toolkit → ROT13):

N_IYNA_VF_ABG_N_FRPHEVGL_OBHAQNEL_OL_VGFRYS
hints: Open the Toolkit (top bar), paste the string, and use the ROT13 button.
tasks.learn: Right — VLANs separate only if the trunks and ports are hardened; otherwise it is a false sense of safety.
tasks.example: The note is ROT13 (each letter shifted 13). Decode it in the Toolkit to read why a VLAN alone is not a security boundary.

tasks.title: Scenario: segmented, crossed anyway
tasks.teach: In the handbook incident a 'segmented' network was crossed anyway: the trunk's native VLAN was left at 1, a test host sat on VLAN 1, and access ports were left in dynamic trunking mode — so double-tagging and switch-spoofing both worked.
tasks.chal: Besides native-VLAN 1, what port setting let switch-spoofing succeed? The ports were left in ___ mode. Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Dynamic (auto) trunking. Hard-set access mode + nonegotiate, dedicate the native VLAN, and clear VLAN 1 — every path closes.
tasks.example: Two misconfigurations combined: native VLAN left at 1 (enables double-tagging) and access ports left dynamic (enables switch-spoofing). Fix both and the paths close.

rooms.title: Network Segmentation
rooms.subtitle: Turn one big target into many small, defended zones.
rooms.blurb: Design zones, read firewall rules and drop logs, and see how segmentation stops lateral movement — from the TG lab.

tasks.title: Name the traffic
tasks.teach:
North-south traffic goes in and out of the network; east-west is traffic between internal systems — the path an intruder uses to spread.

🔑 Key point

Lateral movement — segmentation's whole purpose is to cut the east-west paths it needs.
tasks.chal: What is that spreading between internal hosts called? Submit TG{•••••••_••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Lateral movement — segmentation's whole purpose is to cut the east-west paths it needs.
tasks.example: North-south = in/out of the network. East-west = host-to-host inside it — the path an intruder uses to spread from a foothold.

tasks.title: Reach the core
tasks.teach: The flat lab becomes zones: User 10.10.10.0/24, DMZ .20, Server .30, Secure core .40, Management .50.
tasks.chal: The secure core (DC01, backups) is reachable only via one hardened host. What is that host called? Submit TG{••••_••••}.
hints: You 'jump' through it to admin the core.
tasks.learn: Jump host — the single audited chokepoint into the most sensitive zone.
tasks.example: Zones: User 10.10.10.0/24 · DMZ .20 · Server .30 · Secure core .40 · Management .50. The core is reached only through an audited jump host.

lab.intro: Trace which boundaries you cross to reach the core.

steps.out:
1  10.10.30.1   0.4 ms   # server-zone gateway
2  10.10.40.10  0.9 ms   # core reached via the segmentation gateway only

steps2: From a server-zone host: traceroute 10.10.40.10
Note the hop through the gateway — the core sits behind it
What single hardened host is the only admin way in? (two words).

tasks.title: Read the allow rule
tasks.teach:
Segment boundaries are allow-lists — only named flows cross.

🔑 Key point

443 only. Everything else from the user zone to that server is implicitly denied.
tasks.chal:
nft add rule inet seg forward ip saddr 10.10.10.0/24 ip daddr 10.10.30.12 tcp dport 443 accept nft add rule inet seg forward ip saddr 10.10.20.0/24 ip daddr 10.10.30.12 tcp dport 8080 accept

On which port may the user zone reach the app server 10.10.30.12? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 443 only. Everything else from the user zone to that server is implicitly denied.
tasks.example: Each boundary rule is an allow-list: only the named source, destination and port cross; everything else is denied.

lab.intro: Read the gateway ruleset and find the only port the user zone may use to the app server.
steps2: On the gateway: sudo nft list ruleset
Find the rule with source 10.10.10.0/24 to 10.10.30.12
Submit the allowed dport.

tasks.title: Read the drop log
tasks.teach:
A boundary that blocks also records — drop logs are detection gold.

🔑 Key point

MySQL. A user workstation reaching for a DB port is exactly the east-west move segmentation denies.
tasks.chal:
SEG-DROP SRC=10.10.10.21 DST=10.10.30.12 DPT=3306 # user host -> DB SEG-DROP SRC=10.10.10.21 DST=10.10.40.10 DPT=22 # user host -> core SSH SEG-DROP SRC=10.10.10.21 DST=10.10.30.0/24 DPT=445 # sweeping the server zone

Port 3306 was blocked on the first line. Which database service is that? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: MySQL. A user workstation reaching for a DB port is exactly the east-west move segmentation denies.
tasks.example: Every dropped packet is logged with source, destination and port — a blocked attempt is also detection.

lab.intro: Grep the boundary drop log and identify the blocked database port.

steps.out:
SEG-DROP SRC=10.10.10.21 DST=10.10.30.12 DPT=3306   # user host -> DB port
SEG-DROP SRC=10.10.10.21 DST=10.10.40.10 DPT=22
SEG-DROP SRC=10.10.10.21 DST=10.10.30.0/24 DPT=445

steps2: On the gateway: grep SEG-DROP /var/log/kern.log
Port 3306 is the classic database port
Name that database service.

tasks.title: Read the sweep
tasks.teach:
The third drop line shows one host hitting port 445 across the whole server subnet.

🔑 Key point

SMB — the sweep is lateral reconnaissance; the boundary blocked and logged every attempt.
tasks.chal: Which protocol (port 445), heavily abused for lateral movement, is being swept? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: SMB — the sweep is lateral reconnaissance; the boundary blocked and logged every attempt.
tasks.example: One host hitting the same port across a whole subnet is a sweep — reconnaissance for lateral movement.

lab.intro: Spot the port being swept across the server subnet.

steps.out: SEG-DROP SRC=10.10.10.21 DST=10.10.30.0/24 DPT=445   # swept across the whole server zone

steps2: Filter the drop log for the server subnet
One port is hit across many hosts (445)
Name that protocol.

tasks.title: The biggest single win
tasks.teach: If you can make only one segmentation cut, the handbook is clear which gives the most protection for the least effort.
tasks.chal: Separate ___ from servers. Submit the missing word as TG{•••••}.
hints: Workstations are where compromise usually lands.
tasks.learn: Users — separating workstations from servers breaks the most common attack path (workstation → server).
tasks.example: If you make just one cut, separate users from servers: it breaks the most common attack path (a compromised workstation reaching a server) for the least effort.

tasks.title: Write the finding
tasks.teach:
You audit the boundary and find a gap.

🔑 Key point

22 (SSH). Admin access to the core must come only from the jump host — never a user workstation.
tasks.chal:
Finding: From the user segment (10.10.10.0/24), TCP __ to the secure core (10.10.40.10) is reachable. Evidence: ws01$ Test-NetConnection 10.10.40.10 -Port 22 => True

Which port should NOT be reachable from users to the core? Submit TG{••}.
tasks.learn: 22 (SSH). Admin access to the core must come only from the jump host — never a user workstation.
tasks.example: Admin access to the core must come only from the jump host — a user workstation reaching core SSH is a finding.

lab.intro: Test reachability from a user host to the secure core.

steps.out:
ComputerName     : 10.10.40.10
RemotePort       : 22
TcpTestSucceeded : True   <-- user host can reach core SSH (should be False!)

steps2: From WS01: Test-NetConnection 10.10.40.10 -Port 22 (or nc -vz on Kali)
It succeeds — users should never reach core admin ports
Submit the port that should be blocked.

tasks.title: Only the jump host
tasks.teach: The rules are tightened so not the whole mgmt subnet but one host may admin the core:
tasks.chal:
nft add rule inet seg forward ip saddr 10.10.50.10 ip daddr 10.10.40.0/24 tcp dport {22,3389} accept

Granting the minimum access needed and no more is which principle? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Least privilege — scope the allow-rule to the single jump host, not the entire management subnet.
tasks.example: Least privilege at the boundary: scope the admin rule to the single jump host 10.10.50.10, not the whole 10.10.50.0/24 management subnet.

lab.intro: Find which single source may administer the secure core.

steps.out: ip saddr 10.10.50.10 ip daddr 10.10.40.0/24 tcp dport { 22, 3389 } accept  # ONLY the jump host

steps2: On the gateway: sudo nft list ruleset | grep 10.10.40
Only one source IP is allowed to admin the core
Name the principle this applies (two words).

tasks.title: The segmentation maxim
tasks.teach: The one-line truth about what segmentation buys you. Decode it.
tasks.chal:
Decode the note.

Decode this to reveal the flag (use the 🧰 Toolkit → Base64):

U1RPUFNfU09NRVdIRVJFX0ZST01fQkVDT01JTkdfRVZFUllXSEVSRQ==
hints: Open the Toolkit (top bar), paste the string, and use the Base64 button.
tasks.learn: Exactly — it won't stop a foothold, but it stops that foothold from becoming the whole network.
tasks.example: The note is Base64. Decode it in the Toolkit — it states what segmentation actually buys you when a host is compromised.

tasks.title: Scenario: contain the breach
tasks.teach: Segmentation does not stop an attacker getting in somewhere; it stops that somewhere from becoming everywhere. From a compromised user host behind good boundaries, every east-west attempt is dropped and logged.
tasks.chal: In one word, what security outcome does segmentation deliver once a host is compromised? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Containment — the breach is confined to one zone, bought cheaply with boundaries and drop-logging.
tasks.example: Segmentation won’t stop a foothold, but drop-logging shows every blocked east-west attempt — the breach is confined to one zone. That outcome is containment.

rooms.title: MPLS/VPN Security
rooms.subtitle: Labels, VRFs and the trust you must not over-grant.
rooms.blurb: Understand label switching and MPLS/VPN separation, read VRF/RT output, and catch a cross-VPN leak — per RFC 4364/5920.

tasks.title: How MPLS forwards
tasks.teach: Instead of a destination lookup at every hop, MPLS routers switch packets by a short ___ that each router swaps for the next along a Label Switched Path.
tasks.chal: Submit the missing word as TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Label — forwarding by label, not per-hop IP lookup, is what makes MPLS fast and path-controlled.
tasks.example: A normal router looks up the destination IP at every hop. MPLS swaps a short label instead — set up once, switched fast along the LSP.

tasks.title: The trust boundary
tasks.teach: MPLS roles: CE (customer edge), PE (provider edge), P (provider core). Customer separation is created and enforced at one of them, which holds the per-customer VRFs.
tasks.chal: Which role is the trust boundary? Submit TG{••}.
tasks.learn: PE — the Provider Edge holds the VRFs; the P core switches by transport label and knows nothing of customers.
tasks.example: CE = customer edge, PE = provider edge (holds the VRFs), P = provider core (label switching only). Separation lives on the PE.

tasks.title: What keeps customers apart
tasks.teach: MPLS/VPN separation = VRF + RD + RT + MP-BGP. One of those is the policy deciding which VRFs import and export which routes.
tasks.chal: Name it (two words). Submit TG{•••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: Route Target — get the RTs wrong and you leak routes between customers; get them right and the VPNs stay separate.
tasks.example: Route Targets are the import/export policy: VRF CUST_A exports 65000:100 and imports 65000:100. Import 65000:200 as well and you pull in CUST_B’s routes.

lab.intro: Inspect the VRF’s route targets on the PE.

steps.out:
VRF CUST_A; RD 65000:100
  Import VPN route-target communities: 65000:100
  Export VPN route-target communities: 65000:100

steps2: Build the MPLS/VPN lab (Part 4) in FRRouting or Packet Tracer
On PE1: show vrf detail CUST_A
The import/export policy is called the ___ (two words).

tasks.title: MPLS is not encryption
tasks.teach: RFC 4364 says a correctly run MPLS/VPN gives security comparable to a private network — but it separates, it does not encrypt.
tasks.chal: What do you add over MPLS when you need confidentiality on the wire? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: IPsec over MPLS — private transport plus end-to-end confidentiality, the standard answer for regulated data.
tasks.example: MPLS/VPN separates customers but sends traffic in the clear on provider links. For confidentiality (regulated/inter-provider data) run IPsec over MPLS end to end.

tasks.title: Read the VRF output
tasks.teach:
You audit a PE after a change and test reachability between two customers.

🔑 Key point

Route leak — the cross-VPN leak the handbook flags as Critical; the extra import RT (65000:200) is the cause.
tasks.chal:
PE1# show vrf detail CUST_A | include Route-target import RT: 65000:100 65000:200 <-- 200 belongs to CUST_B! CE-A# ping CE-B => reply (should FAIL)

Customer A can now reach Customer B because of a wrong import RT. In two words, what is this failure? Submit TG{•••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Route leak — the cross-VPN leak the handbook flags as Critical; the extra import RT (65000:200) is the cause.
tasks.example: If CE-A can reach CE-B, separation failed. The cause is almost always an extra, wrong import route-target on one VRF.

lab.intro: Confirm the cross-VPN leak after a bad change.

steps.out:
VRF CUST_A; RD 65000:100
  Import route-target communities: 65000:100  65000:200   <-- 200 is CUST_B!
B   10.20.0.0/16 [200/0] via ...   # CUST_B prefix leaked into CUST_A

steps2: In the lab, add a wrong import RT to CUST_A, then show ip route vrf CUST_A
You now see CUST_B’s prefixes
In two words, name this failure.

tasks.title: Never from the customer
tasks.teach:
A core rule of MPLS edge security: the PE must never accept one specific thing from a CE, or a customer could inject into the provider core.

🔑 Key point

Labels — never accept labelled packets from a CE; add uRPF toward the customer to drop spoofed sources.
tasks.chal: What must the PE refuse from a CE? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Labels — never accept labelled packets from a CE; add uRPF toward the customer to drop spoofed sources.
tasks.example: The PE must drop labelled packets arriving from a CE; otherwise a customer could inject into the core’s label space. Pair with uRPF toward the customer.

lab.intro: Confirm the PE rejects labels from the customer edge.

steps.out:
Interface   IP    Tunnel   BGP-LU
Gi0/0 (to P-core)   Yes   No    No   # labels enabled toward core
Gi0/1 (to CE-A)     No    No    No   # NO labels accepted from the customer

steps2: Build the MPLS lab (Part 4) in FRR or Packet Tracer
On PE1: show mpls interface — the CE-facing link must not accept labels
What must the PE never accept from a CE? (one word, plural).

tasks.title: Protect the control plane
tasks.teach: LDP and BGP must be authenticated, and peers should be accepted only from the expected distance — a TTL check that drops any control-plane packet more than one hop away.
tasks.chal: Name that TTL-security mechanism. Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: GTSM — with MD5/TCP-AO passwords it stops forged or distant LDP/BGP peers.
tasks.example: GTSM (TTL security) accepts control-plane packets only from one hop away: neighbor x ttl-security hops 1. With MD5/TCP-AO it blocks forged or distant LDP/BGP peers.

lab.intro: Check whether the BGP session enforces TTL security.

steps.out:
neighbor 10.0.0.2 remote-as 65000
neighbor 10.0.0.2 password <key>
neighbor 10.0.0.2 ttl-security hops 1   # accepts only 1-hop-away peer

steps2: On the PE: show run | include neighbor
The ttl-security hops 1 line is the control you want
Name that mechanism (4 letters).

tasks.title: Why two labels
tasks.teach: A VPN packet carries a label stack: an outer transport label the core uses, and an inner label only the egress PE reads.
tasks.chal: What does that inner (VPN) label tell the egress PE to pick? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: VRF — the inner label selects the customer's VRF, which is why the core can stay customer-agnostic.
tasks.example: A VPN packet carries two labels: an outer transport label the P core uses, and an inner VPN label the egress PE reads to pick the right customer VRF.

tasks.title: The MPLS maxim
tasks.teach: The one sentence that keeps you from over-trusting MPLS. Decode it.
tasks.chal:
Decode the note.

Decode this to reveal the flag (use the 🧰 Toolkit → Base64):

TVBMU19TRVBBUkFURVNfSVRfRE9FU19OT1RfRU5DUllQVA==
hints: Open the Toolkit (top bar), paste the string, and use the Base64 button.
tasks.learn: Right — separation is real but rests on correct RTs and a secure core; it is not encryption.
tasks.example: The note is Base64. Decode it in the Toolkit — it is the one sentence that stops you over-trusting MPLS.

tasks.title: Scenario: the shared-service change
tasks.teach: A provider adds a shared service for many customers. An engineer sets an import RT too broadly; no one diffs the change against intent. Customer A begins seeing Customer B's routes — a Critical cross-VPN leak.
tasks.chal: Which assurance control, applied at change time, would have flagged the wrong import RT? Submit TG{••••••_••••}.
hints: Compare the RT/VRF config against the intended design.
tasks.learn: Config diff (RT/VRF vs intended design) — MPLS security is really continuous assurance that the assumptions still hold.
tasks.example: The leak came from a broad import RT added without review. A config diff of RTs/VRFs against the intended design, run at change time, flags it before it ships.

rooms.title: Firewall Security
rooms.subtitle: Default-deny, rule order, stateful inspection and clean rule bases.
rooms.blurb: Design zones, write a default-deny rule base, read state and logs, and audit for the dangerous rules.

tasks.title: Three kinds of firewall
tasks.teach:
A firewall is a controlled boundary between networks that decides which traffic may pass. They come in three generations, and knowing the difference tells you what each can and cannot protect.

Packet filters are the oldest: they judge each packet in isolation by source/destination IP and port. Fast, but blind to context — they cannot tell a legitimate reply from an unsolicited packet. Stateful firewalls are today's baseline: they track every connection in a state table, so when your host opens a connection outbound, the matching reply is allowed automatically and anything out-of-state is dropped. Next-generation firewalls (NGFW) add application awareness, user identity, intrusion prevention (IPS) and URL/TLS inspection — they can tell that traffic on port 443 is really a file-transfer app trying to hide, and block it by application rather than port.

Why it matters: most real firewalls are stateful or NGFW. A stateless packet filter forces you to write fragile rules for return traffic and misses modern evasion. Pick the generation that matches the threat and the visibility you need.
tasks.chal: Which firewall generation tracks connection state so replies are allowed automatically? Submit TG{••••••••}.
hints: It keeps a state table of connections.
tasks.learn: Stateful — the modern baseline. It allows replies to connections it has seen and drops out-of-state packets.
tasks.example: Stateless: you must write two rules (out and back). Stateful: one rule out, and the reply is tracked and allowed — fewer rules, fewer mistakes.

tasks.title: Default-deny
tasks.teach:
Default-deny is the single most important idea in firewalling: block everything, then explicitly allow only what must pass. The opposite — allow everything and block known-bad — always loses, because you cannot enumerate every bad thing.

In practice the rule base is a list evaluated top-down, first-match-wins, ending in an implicit or explicit deny at the very bottom that also logs. So the structure is: stateful established/related accept first, then your specific allow rules, then log; drop last. Any packet that matches no allow rule falls through to that final deny and is recorded.

Why it matters: with default-deny, a service you forgot to allow simply fails closed (safe) instead of being silently exposed. Without it, every new service is open until someone notices. 'Allow what must, deny the rest' is the whole philosophy on one line.
tasks.chal: What is the principle of blocking all traffic and permitting only what is explicitly needed? Submit TG{•••••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Default-deny — the boundary fails closed. The final rule logs and drops everything not explicitly allowed.
tasks.example: nftables skeleton: chain forward { policy drop; } — the policy itself is deny, so nothing passes until you add accept rules.

lab.intro: Confirm the firewall fails closed by default.

steps.out: chain forward { type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop; }   <- default-deny confirmed

steps2: On the firewall: sudo nft list ruleset
Find the forward chain’s policy
It should read drop — submit the two-word name of this principle.

tasks.title: Rule order & shadowed rules
tasks.teach:
Because rules are read top-down and the first match wins, order is everything. A rule placed below a broader rule that already matches its traffic can never fire — it is shadowed, a silent, dangerous fault because the control you think you have does not apply.

The classic case: an administrator adds a broad LAN → any allow near the top, then later adds a deny LAN → DB below it to protect the database. The deny is shadowed — the broad allow already matched, so the database was never protected. The fix is to move the specific deny above the broad allow (first-match-wins), or better, remove the over-broad rule entirely.

Why it matters: shadowed and over-broad rules are how 'we have a firewall' still ends in a breach. Reading a rule base in order, like the firewall does, is the core review skill.
tasks.chal:
order rule 8 LAN -> any : any ALLOW # broad 14 LAN -> DB-zone : 3306 DENY # intended to block the DB

Rule 14 never applies because rule 8 matches first. What is a rule that can never match called? Submit TG{••••••••}.
hints: A broader rule above hides it.
tasks.learn: Shadowed — rule 8 matches first, so rule 14 is dead. Move the deny above, or remove the broad allow.
tasks.example: Audit with counters: nft list ruleset shows packet counts per rule. A rule stuck at 0 hits is either unused or shadowed.

tasks.title: The allow matrix
tasks.teach:
You do not write firewall rules ad-hoc — you start from an allow matrix: a grid of which zone may reach which, on which service. It forces you to decide every flow deliberately, and it doubles as your test plan afterwards.

Zones are the interfaces/segments: WAN (internet), DMZ (public-facing services), LAN (users), MGMT (admin). The matrix says, for each From→To pair, what is permitted. Everything not in the matrix is denied.
tasks.chal:
From \ To WAN DMZ LAN MGMT WAN - tcp/443→web Deny Deny LAN web/DNS tcp/443→web - Deny MGMT Deny Admin Admin -

On which port may LAN reach the DMZ web host? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 443. The matrix drives the rules and the tests — if a flow is not in it, the firewall denies it.
tasks.example: That cell becomes one rule: ip saddr 10.10.10.0/24 ip daddr 10.10.20.10 tcp dport 443 accept — one rule, one purpose.

tasks.title: Stateful inspection
tasks.teach:
Stateful inspection is what lets you write a single rule for an outbound flow and have the replies work automatically. The firewall records each connection in a state table (conntrack): the first packet is NEW and matched against your rules; once allowed, the connection becomes ESTABLISHED, and its return packets are ESTABLISHED/RELATED and accepted without a separate reverse rule.

That is why the first rule in a good rule base is ct state established,related accept. Out-of-state packets — a reply with no matching request, a crafted ACK — do not match and are dropped. Statefulness is both convenience and security.
tasks.chal: You allow LAN → web and add no reverse rule, yet the page loads. Which connection state lets the replies back in? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Established — tracked replies are accepted automatically; out-of-state packets are dropped.
tasks.example: conntrack -L shows live entries: tcp ESTABLISHED src=10.10.10.21 dst=10.10.20.10 dport=443 — the firewall remembers this flow.

lab.intro: Read the connection state table.

steps.out:
tcp 6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=10.10.10.21 dst=10.10.20.10 sport=50512 dport=443 [ASSURED]
tcp 6 118 SYN_SENT src=10.10.10.21 dst=203.0.113.9 dport=4444   # half-open?

steps2: On the firewall: sudo conntrack -L (or nft list ruleset for state rules)
Find the state that return traffic rides on
Submit that state name.

tasks.title: SNAT vs DNAT
tasks.teach:
NAT rewrites addresses as packets cross the firewall, and it comes in two directions you must not confuse. SNAT (source NAT / masquerade) rewrites the source on the way out, so many private hosts share one public IP. DNAT (destination NAT / port-forward) rewrites the destination on the way in, publishing an internal service to the internet.

Crucially, NAT is not security by itself — a DNAT that forwards 443 to a DMZ host still needs a matching accept filter rule, and you should publish only that one service, nothing else.
tasks.chal: You publish the DMZ web server to the internet by forwarding inbound port 443 to it. Which NAT is that? Submit TG{••••}.
hints: Rewrites the destination on inbound traffic.
tasks.learn: DNAT (port forward). SNAT hides outbound sources; DNAT publishes an inbound service — always paired with a tight allow rule.
tasks.example: iif "wan" tcp dport 443 dnat to 10.10.20.10:443 — plus a filter accept for WAN→10.10.20.10:443. Nothing else is exposed.

tasks.title: Read the firewall log
tasks.teach:
A logging firewall is a sensor, not just a gate. Every deny it records is intelligence: port sweeps, blocked lateral attempts, and — most valuable — suspicious outbound (egress) traffic that signals a compromise.

🔑 Key point

3306 (MySQL). The firewall blocked it and recorded it — and the 60-second egress to an external IP is a beacon worth hunting.
tasks.chal:
DENY in=wan src=203.0.113.9 dst= dports 22,23,3389,445 # port sweep from internet DENY in=lan src=10.10.10.21 dst=10.10.20.10 dpt=3306 x12 # user host probing the DB ALLOW in=lan src=10.10.10.21 dst=185.x.x.x dpt=443 every 60s # regular egress - beacon?

A user workstation is repeatedly probing one blocked port on the DB host. Which port (service) is it after? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: 3306 (MySQL). The firewall blocked it and recorded it — and the 60-second egress to an external IP is a beacon worth hunting.
tasks.example: Egress control matters: default-deny outbound too. The beacon line only stands out because normal outbound is tightly allowed.

lab.intro: Hunt the dangerous lines in the firewall log.

steps.out:
DENY src=203.0.113.9 dports 22,23,3389,445            # external sweep
DENY src=10.10.10.21 dst=10.10.20.10 dpt=3306 (x12)   # internal DB probing

steps2: On the firewall: grep DENY /var/log/firewall.log
Find the internal host repeatedly hitting one DB port
Submit that port number.

tasks.title: Audit: the any-any rule
tasks.teach:
The most dangerous rule in any firewall is the any-any allow — permit any source to any destination on any service. It disables the firewall for that direction while looking like a single harmless line, and it is almost always a 'temporary' fix that nobody removed.

Rule-base hygiene means hunting three faults: any-any / overly broad rules (tighten or remove), shadowed rules (reorder), and unused rules (zero counters — remove). Every rule should be documented with an owner, purpose, ticket and review date; no permanent 'temporary' rules.
tasks.chal: What do we call a rule permitting any source to any destination on any port — effectively disabling the firewall for that flow? Submit TG{•••_•••}.
tasks.learn: Any-any — the firewall in name only. Find them with counters, tighten to least privilege, and give every rule an expiry.
tasks.example: Finding: FW-06 · Over-broad any-any rule permits unrestricted LAN egress · Risk: High. That is exactly the line attackers exfiltrate through.

lab.intro: Audit the inherited rule base for the three classic faults.

steps.cmd: nft -a list chain inet fw forward
steps.out:
ip saddr 10.10.10.0/24 accept    # handle 22  <- ANY destination, ANY port = any-any!
ip saddr 10.10.10.0/24 ip daddr 10.10.30.0/24 drop  # handle 31  (0 packets) <- unused/shadowed

sugg: nft -a list chain inet fw forward

steps2: List with handles & counters: sudo nft -a list chain inet fw forward
Spot the rule with no destination/port restriction
Name that over-broad rule type (two words).

tasks.title: Allow what must
tasks.teach: The whole firewalling philosophy compresses to one line. Decode it.
tasks.chal:
Decode the operator’s note.

Decode this to reveal the flag (use the 🧰 Toolkit → Base64):

QUxMT1dfV0hBVF9NVVNUX0RFTllfVEhFX1JFU1Q=
hints: Open the Toolkit (top bar), paste the string, and use the Base64 button.
tasks.learn: Exactly — default-deny plus least privilege is the entire game.
tasks.example: Everyday: a nightclub guest list that only names who may enter — everyone else is turned away by default (default-deny).

tasks.title: Scenario: the rule nobody removed
tasks.teach:
In the handbook breach, the inbound rules were fine — only the web service was published. The damage came from two internal rules added years earlier and never removed: Rule 22 (LAN → any:any ALLOW), added to 'fix' an app, let the attacker exfiltrate to an external host; and Rule 31 (LAN → DB-zone:any ALLOW), a 'temporary' troubleshooting rule, let a workstation reach the database directly. No zero-day — just broad, unwatched rules.

🔑 Key point

Rule review — regular, documented review removes unused/shadowed/over-broad rules before an attacker finds them.
tasks.chal: Which single recurring practice would have removed rules 22 and 31 long before the breach? Submit TG{••••_••••••}.
hints: Done on a schedule, it catches stale rules.
tasks.learn: Rule review — regular, documented review removes unused/shadowed/over-broad rules before an attacker finds them.
tasks.example: Pair it with change control: every rule carries an owner, purpose, ticket and expiry — so 'temporary' never becomes permanent.

rooms.title: Load Balancer & ADC Security
rooms.subtitle: Distribute, terminate TLS, stay resilient — and harden the device that sees everything.
rooms.blurb: Balance across backends, terminate TLS safely, stop backend bypass, and audit the ADC that holds the keys.

tasks.title: Load balancer vs ADC
tasks.teach:
A load balancer spreads incoming traffic across several backend servers so no single one is overwhelmed and a failure is invisible to users. An ADC (Application Delivery Controller) is a smarter load balancer that also terminates TLS, routes by URL/host/headers, hosts a WAF, rate-limits and caches — it is the full front-end for an application.

The key split is the OSI layer they work at. L4 balancing decides on IP, port and TCP/UDP — fast and simple, connection-level. L7 balancing understands HTTP — it can route /api to one pool and / to another, inspect headers and cookies, and is where TLS, WAF and rate-limiting live. Richer decisions need L7.

Why it matters: because every request passes through it and it often holds the TLS private keys, the ADC is both the place you add protection and a prime target. Securing it well protects every app behind it.
tasks.chal: Which layer of load balancing understands HTTP — URLs, hosts, headers and cookies? Submit TG{••}.
tasks.learn: L7 — application-aware. L4 is fast and connection-level; L7 is where routing, TLS, WAF and rate-limiting happen.
tasks.example: L4: 'send this TCP connection to a backend.' L7: 'POST /login from this cookie → app-pool-A, and run it through the WAF first.'

tasks.title: Balancing algorithms
tasks.teach:
How does the LB choose which backend gets the next request? The common algorithms each suit a situation. Round robin sends each request to the next backend in turn — simple and fair when servers are equal. Least connections favours the backend with the fewest active sessions — better for long-lived connections. Weighted variants send more to bigger servers, and IP hash maps a client consistently to one backend.

Why it matters: the algorithm interacts with health and persistence. Round robin on unequal servers overloads the weak one; the fix is weighting or least-connections.
tasks.chal: Name the simple default that sends each new request to the next backend in turn. Submit TG{•••••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Round robin — fair and simple for equal backends; use weighted or least-connections when servers differ.
tasks.example: HAProxy: balance roundrobin. Change to balance leastconn when sessions are long-lived and uneven.

tasks.title: Meaningful health checks
tasks.teach:
A health check is a probe the LB runs against each backend; if it fails, that backend is pulled out of rotation so users never hit it. The trap is a shallow check — 'is port 443 open?' — which keeps a broken app in rotation because the port answers while the app returns errors.

A meaningful check hits a real endpoint, e.g. GET /health that exercises the app and its database and returns 200 only when truly healthy. Then failover is real: stop a backend and traffic shifts automatically.

🔑 Key point

web2 — its /health returned 503, so the LB stopped sending it traffic. That is real availability, not just 'port open'.
tasks.chal:
$ show stat backend app web1 UP (200 /health) backend app web2 DOWN (health check failed: 503) <- pulled from rotation backend app web3 UP (200 /health)

Which backend has the LB removed from rotation? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: web2 — its /health returned 503, so the LB stopped sending it traffic. That is real availability, not just 'port open'.
tasks.example: HAProxy: option httpchk GET /health — a check that exercises the app, not just the TCP port.

lab.intro: Read the LB stats and find the failed backend.

steps.out:
app,web1,,,UP,200
app,web2,,,DOWN,L7STS/503   <- health check failing
app,web3,,,UP,200

steps2: Query HAProxy stats (socket or the stats page)
Find the backend marked DOWN
Submit its name.

tasks.title: TLS termination modes
tasks.teach:
Where TLS ends decides what the LB can do. There are three modes. Termination: the LB decrypts and talks plaintext to the backend — this enables WAF and inspection, but the backend hop must be protected. Re-encryption (bridging): the LB decrypts, inspects, then re-encrypts to the backend — it protects the backend hop and allows inspection. Passthrough: the LB forwards the encrypted stream untouched — true end-to-end encryption, but the LB cannot inspect or run a WAF.

Why it matters: you cannot run a WAF on traffic you cannot read, and you should not send decrypted traffic over an untrusted hop. The mode is a deliberate trade-off between inspection and confidentiality.
tasks.chal: Which mode decrypts to inspect and re-encrypts so the backend hop stays protected? Submit TG{••_••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Re-encryption (bridging) — inspection plus a protected backend hop. Passthrough gives end-to-end crypto but no inspection.
tasks.example: HAProxy backend: server web1 10.10.30.11:443 check ssl verify required ca-file /etc/ssl/ca.crt — re-encrypts to the backend and verifies its cert.

tasks.title: Terminate TLS securely
tasks.teach: Because the ADC is the one place every client's TLS is negotiated, it is the one place to get TLS right for every app behind it. That means TLS 1.2+ only (disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and SSLv3), strong ciphers, a valid certificate chain, and HSTS — the Strict-Transport-Security header that tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS, defeating downgrade and strip attacks.
tasks.chal:
$ openssl s_client -connect app.tglab.local:443 -tls1 2>&1 | grep -i alert ... sslv3 alert handshake failure # good - legacy TLS 1.0 refused $ curl -sI https://app.tglab.local | grep -i strict Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

Which response header forces browsers to use HTTPS only? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: HSTS — with TLS 1.2+ only and strong ciphers, it gives consistent, downgrade-resistant HTTPS for every app on the ADC.
tasks.example: HAProxy: ssl-min-ver TLSv1.2 and http-response set-header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains".

lab.intro: Verify the ADC presents strong TLS and refuses legacy protocols.

steps.out: 140... sslv3 alert handshake failure:... no protocols available   # TLS 1.0 correctly refused
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

steps2: Try legacy TLS: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1 — it should fail
Check the header: curl -sI https://host | grep -i strict
Name that HTTPS-forcing header (4 letters).

tasks.title: Stop backend bypass
tasks.teach:
All the LB's TLS, WAF and rate-limiting is worthless if attackers can reach the backends directly, bypassing the front door. A backend that answers the internet on its own IP/port is an open side-door around every control.

The fix: backends listen only on an internal interface, and the firewall allows traffic to them only from the LB. Verify by scanning a backend from outside — its app ports should be filtered, with only the LB's published port reachable.
tasks.chal:
kali$ nmap -Pn -p 8081,8082,443 10.10.30.11 8081/tcp filtered 8082/tcp filtered 443/tcp open # only reachable via the LB / as expected

When a backend answers the internet directly, attackers skip the LB's TLS and WAF. What is this failure called (one word)? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Bypass — lock backends to the LB only. Direct-to-backend access defeats every edge control.
tasks.example: Firewall rule: allow saddr <LB-IP> daddr <backend> tcp dport 443 — nothing else may reach the backend.

lab.intro: Scan a backend from outside to prove it is not directly exposed.

steps.out:
8081/tcp filtered
8082/tcp filtered
443/tcp  open     # only the LB-published port answers

steps2: From Kali: nmap -Pn -p 8081,8082,443 <backend>
App ports should be filtered; only the LB path open
If backends answer directly, what is the attack called? (one word)

tasks.title: Rate limiting
tasks.teach: The ADC is the natural place to blunt abuse before it reaches the app: rate limiting caps requests per client/session over time, stopping brute-force logins, credential stuffing, scraping and Layer-7 floods. Combined with connection limits, timeouts and (for big volumetric attacks) upstream scrubbing or a CDN, it absorbs abuse at the edge.
tasks.chal: What control caps how many requests a single client may make in a window, blunting brute force and scraping? Submit TG{••••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Rate limit — per-IP/session caps at the edge stop brute force, stuffing, scraping and L7 DoS before they hit the app.
tasks.example: Set a per-IP cap and tight timeouts on /login; slow, low-and-slow clients get dropped before they exhaust the backend.

tasks.title: Security headers at the edge
tasks.teach: Browsers enforce a set of protections only if the server sends the right headers. Setting them once at the ADC gives every app behind it consistent protection. Key ones: HSTS (HTTPS-only), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (stop MIME sniffing), and X-Frame-Options: DENY (stop your pages being framed — clickjacking).
tasks.chal: Which header stops your site from being embedded in a frame on another site (clickjacking)? Submit TG{•_•••••_•••••••}.
hints: Hyphen/underscore form of the header name.
tasks.learn: X-Frame-Options (DENY) — set at the ADC, every app is protected from clickjacking at once.
tasks.example: HAProxy: http-response set-header X-Frame-Options DENY and X-Content-Type-Options nosniff — one place, all apps.

tasks.title: Centralise TLS
tasks.teach: The ADC's security value in one line. Decode it.
tasks.chal:
Decode the architect’s note.

Decode this to reveal the flag (use the 🧰 Toolkit → Base64):

T05FX1BMQUNFX1RPX0dFVF9UTFNfUklHSFQ=
hints: Open the Toolkit (top bar), paste the string, and use the Base64 button.
tasks.learn: Right — fix TLS and headers once at the edge and every app inherits it.
tasks.example: Everyday: one reception desk handles all ID checks for the building, so each office inside doesn't have to repeat them (central TLS termination).

tasks.title: Scenario: the device that holds the keys
tasks.teach: The ADC terminates TLS, so it holds the private keys and sees plaintext for every app it fronts. In the handbook incident, a compromised, unpatched ADC with its admin exposed to the internet let an attacker steal those keys — making past captured traffic decryptable and every fronted app exposed.
tasks.chal: What must you most urgently protect and rotate on an ADC after any compromise, because it decrypts everything behind it? Submit TG{•••••••_••••}.
hints: It terminates TLS, so it holds these.
tasks.learn: Private keys — protect and rotate them, keep admin off the internet, patch fast, and firewall the backends. The ADC is the keys to the kingdom.
tasks.example: Hardening checklist: patch fast · admin off the internet · MFA/RBAC · modern TLS + HSTS · protect/rotate keys · firewall backends · log to SIEM.

rooms.title: Web Application Firewall
rooms.subtitle: Inspect the HTTP request, block the OWASP Top 10, tune without blind spots.
rooms.blurb: Deploy ModSecurity + the OWASP CRS, read anomaly scores and logs, tune false positives, and virtual-patch.

tasks.title: What a WAF is
tasks.teach:
A network firewall judges connections by IP and port; it has no idea what is inside an HTTP request. A Web Application Firewall (WAF) works at Layer 7: it reads the actual request — the URL, headers, cookies and body — understands web attacks, and blocks malicious payloads while letting real users through.

It exists because port 443 is wide open to the world, applications are imperfect, and bots scan constantly. A WAF buys time: it blocks known exploit patterns at the edge so a vulnerability cannot be trivially exploited before you patch it. It is a safety net, not a substitute for secure code.
tasks.chal: At which OSI layer does a WAF inspect the HTTP request content? Submit TG{•••••_•}.
tasks.learn: Layer 7 — the application layer. A WAF reads URLs, headers, cookies and bodies, where web attacks live.
tasks.example: A firewall sees 'TCP to :443 — allow'. A WAF sees '?id=1' OR '1'='1 in the query — SQL injection, block'.

tasks.title: The OWASP Top 10
tasks.teach:
A WAF's job is framed by the OWASP Top 10 — the most critical web application risks. The headline attacks a WAF defends against: Injection (SQLi, command injection — smuggling code/queries through input), Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) (injecting script into pages), path traversal (reading files outside the web root), and automated abuse (credential stuffing, scraping).

Injection is the classic: user input is treated as code. A login field that accepts ' OR '1'='1 can turn a query into one that always returns true. The WAF blocks the malicious pattern; the real fix is parameterised queries in the app.

🔑 Key point

SQL injection — input treated as query. The WAF blocks the payload; parameterised queries fix the root cause.
tasks.chal: Which attack smuggles database queries or commands in through user input? Submit TG{•••_•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: SQL injection — input treated as query. The WAF blocks the payload; parameterised queries fix the root cause.
tasks.example: ?id=1' OR '1'='1 turns WHERE id=1 into WHERE id=1 OR 1=1 — true for every row. CRS rule 942 catches it.

tasks.title: The OWASP Core Rule Set
tasks.teach:
You do not write WAF rules from scratch. The OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS) is a free, community-maintained set of rules that ModSecurity loads to detect the Top 10. It uses a negative security model (block known-bad patterns) and is organised by attack family — rule IDs in the 942xxx range are SQLi, 941xxx are XSS, 930xxx are path traversal (LFI).

CRS has paranoia levels (1–4): higher levels add stricter rules that catch more attacks but produce more false positives. You start at a sensible default and tune up only with care.
tasks.chal: What is the free, standard ruleset ModSecurity loads to detect the OWASP Top 10? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: CRS — the OWASP Core Rule Set. Rule families: 942=SQLi, 941=XSS, 930=traversal. Paranoia levels trade coverage for false positives.
tasks.example: Enabled via IncludeOptional /etc/modsecurity/crs/rules/*.conf — hundreds of maintained rules you did not have to write.

tasks.title: Anomaly scoring
tasks.teach:
Modern CRS does not block on a single rule match. Instead each matched rule adds to an anomaly score, and the request is blocked only when the total crosses a threshold (default 5 inbound). This reduces false positives: one loose rule matching weakly is not enough to block; several attack indicators together are.

🔑 Key point

403 Forbidden. Scores accumulate across matched rules; crossing the threshold triggers the block.
tasks.chal:
[id 942100] SQL Injection ARGS:id="1' OR '1'='1" score +5 [id 920350] Host header is an IP score +2 Inbound Anomaly Score 12 >= 5 -> 403

Multiple rules pushed the score past the threshold. What HTTP status does the WAF return to block the request? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 403 Forbidden. Scores accumulate across matched rules; crossing the threshold triggers the block.
tasks.example: A single weak match (+2) stays under 5 and passes; a real SQLi (+5) plus another indicator crosses 5 and is blocked — fewer false positives.

tasks.title: Detection vs blocking
tasks.teach: A WAF runs in one of two modes, set by SecRuleEngine. DetectionOnly logs what it would block but lets everything through — essential when you first deploy, so you can see false positives without breaking the site. On actively blocks. The safe rollout is: deploy in DetectionOnly, watch the logs, tune out false positives, then switch to On.
tasks.chal:
$ grep SecRuleEngine /etc/modsecurity/modsecurity.conf SecRuleEngine DetectionOnly # logging, not blocking (yet)

Which SecRuleEngine value logs attacks but does not block, for safe initial tuning? Submit TG{•••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: DetectionOnly — observe and tune first, then flip to On to enforce. Blocking before tuning breaks real traffic.
tasks.example: Go live: sed -i 's/^SecRuleEngine .*/SecRuleEngine On/' modsecurity.conf after the logs are clean of false positives.

lab.intro: Check which mode the WAF is running in.

steps.out: SecRuleEngine DetectionOnly   # logs matches but does not block yet

steps2: On the web server: grep SecRuleEngine /etc/modsecurity/modsecurity.conf
Read the current mode
Submit that value (one word).

tasks.title: Deploy ModSecurity
tasks.teach: The free, production-grade WAF stack is ModSecurity (the engine) plus the OWASP CRS (the rules), running as a module inside Apache or nginx — an embedded deployment. Other models exist (reverse-proxy, inline appliance, cloud WAF), but embedded is the classic lab and small-site setup.
tasks.chal:
$ sudo apt -y install apache2 libapache2-mod-security2 modsecurity-crs $ apachectl -M | grep security2 security2_module (shared) # the WAF engine is loaded

Name the open-source WAF engine that loads the CRS inside Apache/nginx. Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: ModSecurity — the engine; the CRS supplies the rules. Together, a full free WAF in front of your app.
tasks.example: nginx users: libnginx-mod-http-modsecurity, modsecurity on;, and point modsecurity_rules_file at the CRS. Same concepts.

lab.intro: Confirm the WAF module is loaded in the web server.

steps.out: security2_module (shared)   # ModSecurity is active

steps2: Install: apt install libapache2-mod-security2 modsecurity-crs
Verify: apachectl -M | grep security2
Name the engine (one word).

tasks.title: Read the WAF log
tasks.teach:
The ModSecurity audit log is the WAF's intelligence feed: every block records the rule id, the attack type, the matched value and the source IP. The rule id tells you the attack family at a glance — 942xxx = SQL injection, 941xxx = XSS, 930xxx = path traversal.

🔑 Key point

942 = SQL injection. Knowing the families (942 SQLi, 941 XSS, 930 LFI) lets you read a WAF log at a glance.
tasks.chal: [id 942100] SQL Injection ARGS:id="1' OR '1'='1" src=10.10.10.50 BLOCKED [id 941100] XSS ARGS:q="
tasks.learn: 942 = SQL injection. Knowing the families (942 SQLi, 941 XSS, 930 LFI) lets you read a WAF log at a glance.
tasks.example: Review the top-firing rules weekly — they are either real attacks (intelligence) or your next false-positive exclusions.

lab.intro: Fire an attack and read which rule caught it.

steps.out: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
... [id "942100"] [msg "SQL Injection Attack Detected"] ARGS:id ...

steps2: Fire a SQLi payload in a URL parameter (e.g. id=1' OR '1'='1) — expect HTTP 403
Read the audit log: tail /var/log/apache2/modsec_audit.log
Submit the rule-id family (first 3 digits) for SQLi.

tasks.title: Tune false positives
tasks.teach: A WAF that blocks real users gets turned off — so tuning is survival. When a legitimate request trips a rule (say a code-editor field that legitimately contains SQL-like text on /save), you write a narrow exclusion: disable that one rule for that one parameter on that one path — never globally, which would blind the WAF everywhere.
tasks.chal:
SecRule REQUEST_URI "@beginsWith /save" \ "id:10001,phase:1,pass,nolog,ctl:ruleRemoveTargetById=942100;ARGS:content"

What is a narrow rule that stops a specific legitimate request from tripping a specific CRS rule called? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: It excludes one target from one rule.
tasks.learn: Exclusion — scoped to one rule, one parameter, one path. Treat WAF rules as code: reviewed, commented, tested.
tasks.example: The exclusion above removes only rule 942100 only for ARGS:content only on /save — SQLi elsewhere is still blocked.

tasks.title: Virtual patching
tasks.teach: When a vulnerability is announced but you cannot patch the app immediately, a WAF buys time with a virtual patch: a custom rule that blocks the specific exploit at the edge until the real fix ships. It is a stopgap, not a cure, but it closes the window of exposure.
tasks.chal:
SecRule ARGS:fmt "@rx (?i)(\.\./|cmd=|;)" \ "id:10002,phase:2,deny,status:403,log,msg:'TG virtual patch: legacy report exploit'"

What is a custom WAF rule that blocks a known exploit until the app can be properly fixed called (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••_•••••}.
hints: A patch at the WAF, not in the code.
tasks.learn: Virtual patch — block the specific exploit at the edge now; ship the real code fix as soon as you can.
tasks.example: The rule above denies traversal/command patterns in the fmt parameter with a 403 and a clear log message — a targeted shield.

tasks.title: Scenario: stop the credential stuffing
tasks.teach:
Your login endpoint is being hammered: thousands of login attempts from many IPs, reusing passwords leaked elsewhere. The CRS signature rules do not fire — the requests are individually 'valid'. The defence is not a signature but a rate control.

🔑 Key point

Rate limiting (with bot detection) on /login — the answer to credential stuffing, scraping and L7 DoS, which signatures alone cannot stop.
tasks.chal: Which WAF/ADC control stops automated login abuse by capping attempts per client over time? Submit TG{••••_••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Rate limiting (with bot detection) on /login — the answer to credential stuffing, scraping and L7 DoS, which signatures alone cannot stop.
tasks.example: Layer it: rate limit + bot fingerprinting + challenge suspicious clients. Signatures catch payloads; rate control catches abuse of valid requests.

rooms.title: Web Server Hosting
rooms.subtitle: Serve a site safely — the request path, TLS, permissions and hardening.
rooms.blurb: Understand the request path, host on Apache/Nginx, set correct permissions and TLS, and harden the server.

tasks.title: The request path
tasks.teach:
Before you host anything, understand what happens when someone opens your site. The browser takes the address name and asks DNS for the matching IP. It then opens a TCP connection to the server — on port 80 for plain HTTP, or port 443 for HTTPS (encrypted with TLS). It sends an HTTP request (GET /); the web server finds the file under its document root and returns the HTML, which the browser renders.

Why it matters: every hosting decision — which port, which certificate, where files live, who may read them — maps onto a step of this path. Anything public must use 443/TLS so the connection is encrypted and shows the padlock.
tasks.chal: Which port does a public website use for encrypted HTTPS traffic? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 443 — HTTPS over TLS. Port 80 is plain HTTP and should redirect to 443 for anything public.
tasks.example: Path: name → DNS → IP → :443 (TLS) → GET / → document root → HTML back. Each arrow is a thing you configure and secure.

tasks.title: Choosing the web server
tasks.teach:
The common web servers each have a niche. Apache is the flexible, ubiquitous cross-platform server (great with PHP via its module). Nginx is the high-performance choice for static content and as a reverse proxy (runs PHP via PHP-FPM). IIS is Microsoft's server on Windows. XAMPP bundles Apache + PHP + MySQL + phpMyAdmin for quick local development/demos.

Why it matters: pick by workload. A high-traffic static site or a reverse proxy in front of apps leans Nginx; a flexible PHP host leans Apache; a quick PHP+DB demo on your laptop leans XAMPP.
tasks.chal: Which server is known for high-performance static serving and as a reverse proxy? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Nginx — high-performance static + reverse proxy. Apache is the flexible PHP workhorse; XAMPP is the quick dev bundle.
tasks.example: Production Linux site → Apache or Nginx. PHP+DB demo → XAMPP. High-traffic edge/proxy → Nginx.

tasks.title: The document root
tasks.teach: The document root is the folder on disk the web server publishes — a request for /about.html maps to <docroot>/about.html. On Debian/Ubuntu Apache it defaults to /var/www/html. Files outside the document root are not served (unless a misconfiguration or traversal bug exposes them), which is exactly why path-traversal attacks (../../etc/passwd) are dangerous.
tasks.chal: What is the term for the directory a web server publishes to the web? Submit TG{••••••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Document root — e.g. /var/www/html. Keep sensitive files out of it, and block traversal so nothing above it is served.
tasks.example: Apache vhost: DocumentRoot /var/www/nimbus — only files under there are reachable over the web.

tasks.title: TLS certificates
tasks.teach: HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS, and TLS needs a certificate — a file that proves the server's identity and carries the public key used to set up encryption. A browser trusts a certificate signed by a known Certificate Authority (CA); a self-signed cert works in a lab but triggers a warning. The padlock in the address bar means a valid certificate and an encrypted connection.
tasks.chal: What must a server present to turn http:// into a trusted https:// with a padlock? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
hints: Signed by a CA; carries the public key.
tasks.learn: Certificate — a CA-signed TLS certificate gives the padlock. Self-signed works in a lab but warns; use a real CA (e.g. Let's Encrypt) in production.
tasks.example: IIS: Site → Bindings → Add → https, 443, select the certificate. Linux: point Apache/Nginx at the cert + key and listen on 443.

tasks.title: Virtual hosts
tasks.teach: One server, one IP, many sites — that is what virtual hosts do. The web server reads the Host: header of each request and serves the matching site and document root. This lets app.example.com and blog.example.com live on the same machine.
tasks.chal:
# /etc/apache2/sites-available/nimbus.conf ServerName nimbus.local DocumentRoot /var/www/nimbus

What feature serves multiple sites from one server by matching the request's Host header? Submit TG{•••••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Virtual host — one server hosts many sites, each with its own name and document root. Enable with a2ensite on Apache.
tasks.example: sudo a2ensite nimbus && sudo systemctl reload apache2 — the site at nimbus.local goes live.

tasks.title: File permissions
tasks.teach: A web server runs as an unprivileged user (on Debian/Ubuntu Apache that is www-data). Site files should be owned appropriately and readable by that user, but not world-writable — if the web user can write the code it serves, an attacker who exploits the app can modify the site. Correct ownership and least-privilege permissions are foundational hardening.
tasks.chal:
$ sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/nimbus $ ls -l /var/www/nimbus -rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 1240 index.html # owner rw, others read-only

Which user does Apache run as on Debian/Ubuntu, and thus should own the site files? Submit TG{•••-••••}.
tasks.learn: www-data — give it read access, not write, to the site. Never make served files world-writable.
tasks.example: chown -R www-data:www-data sets ownership; files stay 644 and directories 755 — readable, not writable by the web process.

lab.intro: Check who owns the site files.

steps.out:
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 1240 index.html
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data  980 about.html

steps2: On the server: ls -l /var/www/nimbus
Read the owner column
Submit the web-server user (hyphenated).

tasks.title: 403 Forbidden
tasks.teach: A 403 Forbidden means the server understood the request but refuses to serve it. The two usual causes: file/directory permissions the web user cannot read, or directory listing is disabled and there is no index file. (Compare: 404 = not found, 500 = server error, 200 = OK.) Reading status codes is the fastest way to diagnose hosting problems.
tasks.chal:
$ curl -I http://localhost/private/ HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden # permissions, or directory listing blocked

Which HTTP status code means the server refuses to serve the request (permissions or listing blocked)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 403 Forbidden — fix the permissions or add an index file. 404 is not-found, 500 is a server error, 200 is OK.
tasks.example: curl -I shows just the status line and headers — the quickest hosting diagnostic you have.

lab.intro: Read the status code the server returns.

steps.out:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Server: Apache

steps2: Request a protected path: curl -I http://localhost/private/
Read the status line
Submit the 3-digit code for “refused”.

tasks.title: Stop information disclosure
tasks.teach: A default web server leaks helpful-to-attackers details: the exact software and version in the Server header, and full directory listings when there is no index file. Both are information disclosure — they hand an attacker a map and a version to look up exploits for. Hardening means stripping version banners (ServerTokens Prod / server_tokens off) and disabling directory listing (Options -Indexes).
tasks.chal: Leaking your server version and directory contents is an example of which weakness (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••••••_••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Information disclosure — hide the version (ServerTokens Prod), turn off listing (Options -Indexes), and use custom error pages.
tasks.example: Before: Server: Apache/2.4.52 (Ubuntu). After ServerTokens Prod: just Server: Apache — less to fingerprint.

tasks.title: Confirm it's serving
tasks.teach: The simplest operational check: is the site actually up and returning content? curl -I returns the status line, and systemctl is-active confirms the service is running. A healthy static site returns 200 OK.
tasks.chal:
$ systemctl is-active apache2 active $ curl -I http://localhost/ HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Which HTTP status code confirms the page was served successfully? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 200 OK — the service is up and serving. Combine with systemctl is-active for a quick health check.
tasks.example: Make these two commands muscle memory: systemctl is-active <svc> and curl -I http://localhost/.

lab.intro: Verify the web server is up and serving.

steps.out:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: Apache
Content-Type: text/html

steps2: Run curl -I http://localhost/
Read the status line
Submit the 3-digit success code.

tasks.title: Scenario: hardening the host
tasks.teach:
You are putting a public site live. On its own the web server is reachable, patchable, and only as safe as its config. The professional pattern is not to expose the raw server but to layer defences: TLS + HSTS, correct file permissions, no version/listing leaks, regular patching — and a WAF/load balancer in front so web attacks and TLS are handled at a hardened edge.

🔑 Key point

Defense in depth — the web server is one layer; the edge (WAF/LB), TLS, permissions and patching are the others. If one fails, the rest hold.
tasks.chal: Putting a WAF/LB in front and layering TLS, permissions and patching is an application of which principle? Submit TG{•••••••_••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Defense in depth — the web server is one layer; the edge (WAF/LB), TLS, permissions and patching are the others. If one fails, the rest hold.
tasks.example: Edge WAF/LB → TLS/HSTS → hardened server (no banners, no listing, least-privilege files) → patched app. Each layer backs up the next.

rooms.title: Intrusion Detection & Prevention (IDS/IPS)
rooms.subtitle: Detect the attack inside allowed traffic — signatures, tuning and response.
rooms.blurb: Deploy a sensor, read and write Suricata rules, tune out noise, and turn alerts into action.

tasks.title: IDS vs IPS vs firewall
tasks.teach:
A firewall decides whether traffic may pass; it does not look at what that allowed traffic contains. That blind spot is what an IDS/IPS fills. An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) sits passively on a copy of the traffic and alerts when it sees an attack. An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) sits inline in the data path and can alert and block the attack as it happens.

The trade-off is risk. A passive IDS can never break traffic, but it can only shout after the fact. An inline IPS can stop an attack mid-flight, but a bad rule can block legitimate traffic and cause an outage — which is why you start in IDS mode and only go inline after tuning.
tasks.chal: Which one sits inline and can actively block the attack, not just alert? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: IPS — inline, detect and block. IDS is passive, detect and alert. The firewall only allows/denies by header.
tasks.example: Firewall: 'TCP to :443 — allow.' IDS/IPS: 'that allowed :443 session contains a known exploit — alert (IDS) or drop (IPS).'

tasks.title: Detection methods
tasks.teach:
Sensors detect in several complementary ways. Signature-based matches known-bad patterns (a specific exploit string) — precise and low-noise, but blind to anything new. Anomaly-based flags deviations from a learned baseline — it can catch novel attacks, but it is noisier. Reputation / IOC blocks known-bad IPs, domains and hashes from threat intel. Protocol analysis flags traffic that violates how a protocol should behave.

Why it matters: no single method is enough. Signatures catch the known cheaply; anomaly and behavioural methods catch the unknown. Real detection layers them.
tasks.chal: Which method matches known-bad patterns precisely but misses brand-new attacks? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: A rule for a known exploit string.
tasks.learn: Signature-based — precise for the known, blind to the novel. Pair it with anomaly and reputation detection.
tasks.example: Signature: 'alert on the exact SQLi string.' Anomaly: 'this host suddenly talks to 500 others — unlike its baseline.'

tasks.title: How the sensor sees traffic
tasks.teach: A sensor can only detect what it can see, so where and how you feed it traffic is half the battle. Three options: a switch SPAN/port mirror copies traffic to the sensor (passive — but can drop packets under load); a hardware TAP makes a reliable physical copy (passive); or inline, where traffic actually flows through the sensor (required for IPS blocking, but the sensor is now in the data path).
tasks.chal: Which placement is required for an IPS to actually block traffic? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Inline — only a sensor in the data path can drop a packet. SPAN/TAP are passive (IDS): they see a copy but cannot block.
tasks.example: SPAN is cheap but drops under load; a TAP is a reliable copy; inline enables prevention at the cost of being a potential chokepoint.

tasks.title: Anatomy of a signature rule
tasks.teach: Suricata/Snort rules describe traffic to match and what to do about it. The shape is: action proto src dir dst ( options ). The action is alert (IDS) or drop/reject (IPS); the header sets protocol, addresses, ports and direction (->); and the options carry the detection logic plus metadata. Two fields identify the rule itself: sid (unique rule ID) and rev (revision).
tasks.chal:
alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 80 ( \ msg:"TG web attack"; content:"/etc/passwd"; \ classtype:web-application-attack; sid:1000001; rev:1; )

Which field gives a rule its unique identifier? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: sid — the Signature ID uniquely identifies the rule; rev tracks its revision. You use the sid to find, tune or suppress a rule.
tasks.example: $HOME_NET is your inside network — set it correctly or direction-aware rules (->) fire backwards.

tasks.title: Read the alert
tasks.teach:
Every alert names the rule that fired and the connection it fired on. The quickest log is fast.log: it shows the gid:sid:rev (which rule and revision), the msg (what it detected), the classtype/priority, and the 5-tuple (src IP:port → dst IP:port, protocol). Reading these fields tells you what matched and where to look next.

🔑 Key point

9000001 — the sid. From it you can open the rule text and the matching packet/flow to confirm the detection.
tasks.chal:
[**] [1:9000001:1] TG LOCAL cleartext password over HTTP [**] [Classification: Policy Violation] [Priority: 2] 10.10.10.21:50512 -> 10.10.30.12:80 TCP

Which rule (sid) fired for this alert? Submit it as TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: 9000001 — the sid. From it you can open the rule text and the matching packet/flow to confirm the detection.
tasks.example: 5-tuple reading: 10.10.10.21 (a workstation) POSTed a cleartext password to 10.10.30.12:80 — a policy violation worth fixing.

lab.intro: Watch the alerts stream from the sensor.
steps2: On the sensor: sudo tail -f /var/log/suricata/fast.log
Find the cleartext-password alert
Submit its sid (the middle number of 1:sid:rev).

tasks.title: Write a detection rule
tasks.teach: Custom rules are how you detect what matters to your environment. A rule's detection logic lives in keywords: content: matches a byte string in the payload, http.method/http.request_body scope it to parts of an HTTP request, flow: sets direction/state, nocase ignores case. Put your rules in local.rules, reload, and test by generating the traffic.
tasks.chal:
alert http $HOME_NET any -> any any ( \ msg:"TG cleartext password over HTTP"; \ flow:established,to_server; http.method; content:"POST"; \ http.request_body; content:"password="; nocase; sid:9000001; rev:1; )

Which keyword matches a literal byte string (like password=) in the payload? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: content — the core match keyword. Combine with http.* scoping and flow: for precise, low-noise rules.
tasks.example: Test it: curl -d "user=a&password=secret" http://10.10.30.12/login then grep 9000001 fast.log — your alert fires.

lab.intro: Reload your rule and trigger it.
steps2: Add the rule to local.rules; reload: suricatasc -c reload-rules
Generate the traffic (the curl above)
Which keyword matched the password= bytes? Submit it.

tasks.title: Tune out the noise
tasks.teach:
The number-one reason IDS deployments fail is alert fatigue: so many alerts that analysts stop reading them, and the one real alert drowns. Tuning is not optional housekeeping — it is the core of making detection work. You disable rules for tech you don't run, suppress/threshold noisy rules from known-good sources (your own scanner, monitoring), and set an accurate HOME_NET so direction-aware rules behave.

🔑 Key point

False positive — suppress/threshold the known-good triggers so real detections stand out. Fewer, better alerts beats more alerts.
tasks.chal: An alert that fires on benign traffic, wasting analyst time, is a ___? Submit TG{•••••_••••••••}.
hints: Benign traffic alerted as an attack.
tasks.learn: False positive — suppress/threshold the known-good triggers so real detections stand out. Fewer, better alerts beats more alerts.
tasks.example: threshold.config can suppress a noisy sid from your scanner's IP — the rule still protects against everyone else.

tasks.title: Evasion
tasks.teach: Attackers actively try to slip past detection. Encryption (TLS) hides the payload from signatures (counter: metadata/JA3, anomaly). Fragmentation splits the attack across packets so no single one matches (counter: stream reassembly — keep it on). Encoding/obfuscation alters the pattern (counter: normalisation, decode layers). Low-and-slow stays under thresholds (counter: long-window anomaly detection). Living-off-the-land uses legitimate tools (counter: behavioural/host telemetry).
tasks.chal: Splitting an attack across multiple packets to defeat a single-packet signature is called ___? Submit TG{•••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Fragmentation — defeated by stream reassembly, which rebuilds the full payload before matching. Keep reassembly enabled.
tasks.example: Against TLS, you cannot see the payload — so you pivot to metadata: JA3 fingerprints, SNI, and flow patterns (beacon timing).

tasks.title: Ship the metadata
tasks.teach: Modern sensors are valued as much for their rich telemetry as for signatures. Suricata writes structured EVE JSON — not just alerts, but http, dns, tls and flow events. Shipped to a SIEM, this lets you correlate alerts into incidents and hunt in the metadata for what no signature caught: beacons, odd domains, large transfers.
tasks.chal:
$ tail -f /var/log/suricata/eve.json | jq 'select(.event_type=="alert")' { "event_type":"alert", "alert":{"signature":"ET SCAN ...","signature_id":2013028}, ... }

What is the structured JSON log format Suricata ships for correlation and hunting? Submit TG{•••_••••}.
tasks.learn: EVE JSON — alerts plus http/dns/tls/flow metadata. Ship it to a SIEM, correlate, and hunt for what rules missed.
tasks.example: Hunt example: jq 'select(.event_type=="flow")' to find a host beaconing to a new IP every 60s — no signature required.

lab.intro: Query the structured alert feed.

steps.out: {"event_type":"alert","src_ip":"10.10.10.50","alert":{"signature":"ET SCAN Potential SSH Scan","signature_id":2013028}}

steps2: On the sensor, jq the alerts out of eve.json (select event_type == alert)
Note it also carries http/dns/tls/flow events
Name this structured log format (two words).

tasks.title: Scenario: the alert that was read
tasks.teach:
Two companies, same intrusion. Company A ran the IDS untuned — ~40,000 alerts a day to a console nobody owned, no SIEM correlation, no workflow. The real alerts existed, buried; the breach ran for weeks. Company B tuned to ~80 high-fidelity alerts a day that analysts trusted and read, with an owned, rehearsed response workflow — they isolated the host and blocked the C2 within the hour, before exfiltration completed.

🔑 Key point

Alert fatigue — detection without tuning and a response workflow is just logging. Fewer, trustworthy alerts plus an owned workflow is what actually protects.
tasks.chal: What is the single most common cause of IDS failure, which buried Company A's real alerts? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Alert fatigue — detection without tuning and a response workflow is just logging. Fewer, trustworthy alerts plus an owned workflow is what actually protects.
tasks.example: The lesson: 'the alert that was actually read' beats a perfect rule nobody acts on. Tune relentlessly; own the alert-to-action loop.

rooms.title: Network Monitoring
rooms.subtitle: Turn traffic into visibility — flows, metrics, logs and the baseline.
rooms.blurb: Collect metrics/flows/logs/packets, baseline normal, build actionable alerts, and catch attacks in the flows.

tasks.title: The four data sources
tasks.teach:
Monitoring turns raw traffic into visibility, and it draws on four complementary data sources. Metrics (via SNMP) are cheap numeric counters — bandwidth, CPU, interface utilisation — great for capacity and trends. Flows (NetFlow/IPFIX) record who talked to whom, how much, over what port — metadata with no payload, ideal for seeing scans, beacons and exfiltration. Logs (syslog) carry events — logins, drops, errors. Packets (full capture) give the deepest detail — the actual content — but are expensive to keep.

Why it matters: each source answers a different question. You reach for the cheapest source that answers yours, and escalate to packets only when you truly need the content.
tasks.chal: Which source tells you 'who talked to whom, how much, on what port' cheaply, with no payload? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Flows — connection metadata. Perfect for scans, beacons, exfiltration and lateral movement, at a fraction of the cost of full packets.
tasks.example: Capacity question → metrics. 'Who did this host talk to?' → flows. 'What exactly did it send?' → packets. Match the source to the question.

tasks.title: Baseline is everything
tasks.teach:
Monitoring's whole power rests on one idea: you can only recognise unusual if you know what normal looks like. A baseline is that learned picture of normal — typical traffic volumes, which hosts talk to which, when the busy hours are. Deviations from the baseline are what surface outages and attacks before users even notice.

Why it matters: an alert like 'host sent 12 MB outbound' is meaningless without a baseline; against a baseline of 'this host normally sends 50 KB', it screams exfiltration. Trends also tell you when a link or device is about to run out of headroom.
tasks.chal: You can only spot 'unusual' by comparing against a known ___. Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Baseline — the heart of monitoring. Establish it first (a week of normal), then alert on deviations.
tasks.example: Baseline: 'web1 serves ~200 req/min, 9am–6pm.' Alert-worthy deviation: '2,000 req/min at 3am from one IP.'

tasks.title: NetFlow
tasks.teach: NetFlow (and its standard IPFIX) is how network devices export connection records to a collector. Each flow record is the 5-tuple (src/dst IP, src/dst port, protocol) plus bytes, packets and timestamps. It is cheap because it is metadata — no payload — yet it answers most security questions about who and how much. You read it with tools like nfdump.
tasks.chal:
$ nfdump -R /flows -s ip/bytes -n 3 Src IP Addr Flows Bytes 10.10.10.21 842 12.1 M <- one host, huge outbound 10.10.30.11 5120 88.0 M 10.10.10.22 410 2.1 M

Name the flow-record technology routers/switches export to a collector. Submit TG{•••••••}.
hints: Cisco's flow export; IPFIX is the standard.
tasks.learn: NetFlow — 5-tuple + bytes + time, exported to a collector and read with nfdump. The 12.1 MB from a workstation is a flag to investigate.
tasks.example: Flow record: 10.10.10.21:50519 → 185.x.x.x:443, 8 pkts, every 60s — a beacon, visible without ever touching a payload.

lab.intro: Read who the top talkers are from flow records.

steps.out:
Src IP Addr    Flows   Bytes
10.10.10.21    842     12.1 M   <- unusual outbound for a workstation
10.10.30.11    5120    88.0 M

steps2: On the collector: nfdump -R /var/flows -s ip/bytes -n 10
Find the workstation with abnormal outbound volume
Name the flow technology being read.

tasks.title: SNMP metrics
tasks.teach: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is how you poll devices for numeric counters — interface bytes, errors, CPU, memory — identified by OIDs. A collector polls these on a schedule and stores time series; devices can also push SNMP traps on events. Always use SNMPv3, which adds authentication and privacy — v1/v2c send community strings in the clear.
