tasks.learn: STIX — the common data model for intel objects and their relationships. It makes intelligence portable between platforms and partners.
tasks.example: A STIX bundle can say 'indicator 185.23.44.9 indicates malware X used-by actor Y' — relationships a machine can ingest and act on.

tasks.title: TAXII
tasks.teach: If STIX is the language, TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information) is the transport — the protocol for sharing STIX data over HTTPS, via collections you can subscribe to and poll. Together, STIX/TAXII let organisations and sharing communities exchange threat intel automatically: you subscribe to a TAXII feed and new STIX indicators flow straight into your platform.
tasks.chal: Which protocol transports/shares STIX intelligence over the wire? Submit TG{•••••}.
hints: Trusted Automated eXchange of Intel Info.
tasks.learn: TAXII — the delivery mechanism for STIX. Subscribe to a TAXII collection and structured intel arrives automatically, ready to operationalise.
tasks.example: STIX = what the intel says; TAXII = how it travels. A CERT publishes STIX over TAXII; members poll the collection and auto-ingest the latest indicators.

tasks.title: Traffic Light Protocol
tasks.teach: Sharing intelligence safely needs clear handling rules. The TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) marks how widely a piece of intel may be shared: TLP:RED (named recipients only), TLP:AMBER (your org, need-to-know), TLP:GREEN (your community), TLP:CLEAR (public). It is a simple, universal label that prevents sensitive intel leaking beyond its intended audience.
tasks.chal: What simple colour-coded marking controls how widely shared intelligence may be redistributed? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: TLP — RED/AMBER/GREEN/CLEAR. Respect the marking: over-sharing TLP:RED can burn a source or a sensitive investigation.
tasks.example: A CERT shares actor details as TLP:AMBER — use it inside your org on a need-to-know basis, but don't post it publicly or forward it to vendors.

tasks.title: MISP
tasks.teach: MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform) is the leading open-source platform for storing, correlating and sharing threat intelligence within and between communities. Members publish 'events' (indicators, context, relationships), MISP correlates overlapping indicators across events, and it can import/export STIX and feed indicators straight into detection tools. It is how many CERTs and ISACs share intel in practice.
tasks.chal:
MISP event #4821 "Ransomware campaign - Oct 2026" TLP:AMBER attributes: 185.23.44.9 (ip-dst) | evil-c2.top (domain) | 4f2a...e9 (sha256) correlates with 3 other events -> same infrastructure reused

Name the leading open-source threat-intelligence sharing platform. Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: MISP — community intel sharing with automatic correlation and STIX/feed export. The correlation ('this IOC appears in 3 campaigns') is its superpower.
tasks.example: You add an IOC to MISP and it lights up: the same IP appears in three other members' events — instantly you know it's a shared, active campaign.

lab.intro: Query the sharing platform for an indicator's correlations.

steps.out:
Found in 4 events (TLP:AMBER):
 #4821 Ransomware Oct2026  #4790 ...  -> infrastructure reused across campaigns

steps2: Search the indicator in MISP
See which events/campaigns it correlates with
Name this sharing platform.

tasks.title: Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP)
tasks.teach: As feeds multiply, you need somewhere to manage them: a TIP (Threat Intelligence Platform) aggregates intel from many sources (feeds, OSINT, MISP, internal), deduplicates and scores it, enriches indicators, and pushes the useful ones out to your SIEM/SOAR/EDR. It is the central hub that turns a flood of raw feeds into a curated, scored, operational indicator set — so your tools aren't drowned in low-quality IOCs.
tasks.chal: What platform aggregates, scores and pushes threat intel to your security tools (abbr.)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: TIP — the hub between feeds and controls. It dedupes, scores and enriches, so only high-confidence, relevant intel reaches the SIEM/SOAR/EDR.
tasks.example: Without a TIP: 12 feeds dumped raw into the SIEM = noise and false positives. With a TIP: scored, deduped, enriched indicators your tools can trust.

tasks.title: Operationalise: enrich the SOC
tasks.teach: The payoff is feeding intel into the SOC's tools. In the SIEM, indicators enrich alerts and auto-match logs ('this logged IP is known-bad'). In SOAR, playbooks look up and act on intel automatically. In the EDR, IOCs block across the fleet. For the hunt team, actor TTPs become hypotheses. The most common first step is enrichment — adding intel context so every alert arrives already prioritised.
tasks.chal: Adding threat-intel context to alerts and logs in the SIEM (so they arrive prioritised) is called ___? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Enrichment — intel makes each alert self-prioritising ('src is known C2'). From there: SOAR acts, EDR blocks, hunters test TTP hypotheses.
tasks.example: Alert enriched with intel: 'connection to 185.23.44.9 — known ransomware C2 (TLP:AMBER, MISP #4821, high confidence)'. No research needed to prioritise.

tasks.title: Scenario: collection to a blocked attack
tasks.teach: End to end: a PIR drives collection; OSINT and a TAXII feed surface an actor's new C2 domain and IPs; you correlate them in MISP (TLP:AMBER), score them in the TIP, and push them to the SIEM (enrich + alert), EDR (block) and hunt team (TTP hypotheses) — with a human in the loop approving the blocks. Intelligence collected this morning blocks the attack this afternoon. This end-to-end intel-to-action flow has a name.
tasks.chal: What is the end-to-end intel-to-action flow (collect → enrich → act, human-gated) called? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Pipeline — the intel-to-action pipeline, human-gated for the consequential steps, is CTI operations realised: collection this morning becomes a blocked attack this afternoon.
tasks.example: PIR → OSINT/TAXII → MISP (correlate, TLP) → TIP (score) → SIEM/EDR/SOAR (enrich/block) with human approval → the attack is stopped. That's the pipeline.

rooms.title: Virtualization & Hypervisor Security
rooms.subtitle: Protect the boundary, harden the host — isolation, escape and lifecycle.
rooms.blurb: Understand hypervisor types and VM isolation, the escape threat, hardening the management plane, and securing snapshots.

tasks.title: What a hypervisor is
tasks.teach:
Virtualization runs many isolated virtual machines (VMs) on one physical host, each with its own OS, sharing the hardware. The software that makes this possible is the hypervisor (or VMM — Virtual Machine Monitor): it creates and runs the VMs, allocates CPU/memory/IO to each, and — critically — enforces the isolation that keeps one VM from seeing or touching another. The hypervisor is the trusted layer everything rests on.

Why it matters: because every VM depends on the hypervisor for its isolation, the hypervisor is the single most security-critical component. Compromise a VM and you have one tenant; compromise the hypervisor and you have them all.
tasks.chal: What is the software layer that creates, runs and isolates virtual machines? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Hypervisor — the trusted layer that enforces VM isolation. Its compromise affects every VM on the host, so it is the top hardening priority.
tasks.example: ESXi, Hyper-V and KVM are hypervisors. Each VM thinks it has its own machine; the hypervisor keeps that illusion — and the isolation — intact.

tasks.title: Type 1 vs Type 2
tasks.teach: Hypervisors come in two kinds. Type 1 (bare-metal) runs directly on the hardware — ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM — with no host OS beneath it; it is the production standard, with a smaller attack surface. Type 2 (hosted) runs as an application on top of a normal OS — VirtualBox, VMware Workstation — convenient for desktops but with the whole host OS as extra attack surface beneath it.
tasks.chal: Which hypervisor type runs directly on the hardware (bare-metal), like ESXi? Submit TG{••••_•}.
tasks.learn: Type 1 — bare-metal, production-grade, minimal attack surface. Type 2 runs on a host OS (handy for labs/desktops, larger surface).
tasks.example: Datacentre: Type 1 (ESXi) on the bare server. Your laptop: Type 2 (VirtualBox) on top of Windows. Different trust models and attack surfaces.

tasks.title: VM isolation
tasks.teach: The whole security promise of virtualization is isolation: each VM is confined to its own virtual CPU, memory and devices, unable to read another VM's memory or the host's — all enforced by the hypervisor. This is what lets different tenants (or different trust levels) safely share one physical box. Everything else in hypervisor security exists to keep this isolation boundary intact.
tasks.chal: What is the hypervisor-enforced separation that keeps one VM from touching another called? Submit TG{•••••••••}.
hints: Each VM stays in its own box.
tasks.learn: Isolation — the core guarantee. The host/guest boundary enforced by the hypervisor is what makes multi-tenant virtualization safe.
tasks.example: Two customers' VMs on one host never see each other's memory or disk — isolation makes shared hardware as safe (in principle) as separate machines.

tasks.title: VM escape
tasks.teach: The worst-case hypervisor attack is VM escape: a flaw lets code inside a guest VM break out of its isolation and reach the hypervisor or host — and from there, every other VM. It is rare and hard (it requires a hypervisor vulnerability), but catastrophic, because it collapses the entire multi-tenant trust model. Defending against it is why you keep the hypervisor patched and its attack surface minimal.
tasks.chal:
guest VM ──X──> hypervisor / host ──> every other VM ^ breaking the isolation boundary (catastrophic)

What is it called when code breaks out of a guest VM to reach the hypervisor/host (two words)? Submit TG{••_••••••}.
tasks.learn: VM escape — the boundary breach that compromises all tenants. Rare but catastrophic; patch the hypervisor fast and shrink its attack surface.
tasks.example: Historical escapes (e.g. VENOM, via emulated devices) prove it's possible — which is why 'just patch the guest' isn't enough; the hypervisor must be patched too.

tasks.title: Resource control & noisy neighbours
tasks.teach: Isolation is about security; resource control is about one VM not harming others' performance. Without limits, a noisy neighbour — a VM hogging CPU, memory or IO — can starve the others on the host (an availability problem, and a denial-of-service vector). Hypervisors enforce per-VM limits/reservations/shares to prevent this. (Related and subtler: CPU side-channel attacks like Spectre can leak data across VMs via shared hardware.)
tasks.chal: A VM that hogs host resources and degrades the others is called a ___ (two words)? Submit TG{•••••_•••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Noisy neighbour — contained with resource limits/shares. It is an availability (and DoS) concern; side-channel leakage is the subtler cross-VM risk.
tasks.example: Set CPU/memory limits so one runaway VM can't starve the host. Without them, a single busy (or malicious) VM degrades every other tenant.

tasks.title: Harden the management plane
tasks.teach: Attackers rarely need a VM escape if the management plane is weak. The hypervisor's management interface (vCenter/ESXi web UI, Hyper-V manager, the API) is the keys to every VM — so it must be locked down: never exposed to the internet, MFA and RBAC on admin access, on an isolated management network, patched, with lockdown mode enabled on ESXi. A compromised management plane hands over all VMs without touching the isolation boundary at all.
tasks.chal: Which plane — the hypervisor's admin interface/API — must be locked down (isolated, MFA, no internet)? Submit TG{••••••••••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Management plane — vCenter/ESXi/API. Isolate it, MFA + RBAC it, patch it, enable lockdown mode. It's an easier path to all VMs than any escape.
tasks.example: An internet-exposed vCenter with weak creds = game over for every VM it manages — no exotic escape needed. Lock the management plane first.

lab.intro: Check ESXi lockdown mode (management-plane hardening).

steps.out:
Path: /Security/LockdownMode
   Int Value: 0   <- DISABLED (should be enabled to restrict direct host access)

steps2: On ESXi check lockdown mode (host UI or esxcli)
Enable it so management goes only through vCenter
Name the plane you are hardening (two words).

tasks.title: Secure snapshots
tasks.teach: A snapshot captures a VM's exact state (disk + memory) at a point in time — great for rollback, but a security liability if mishandled. A snapshot contains everything the VM had then, including credentials and secrets in memory and old vulnerable states; left lying around or copied off, it is a data-leak and rollback-attack risk (reverting can undo patches or re-enable a disabled account). Manage snapshots deliberately: limit, protect and expire them.
tasks.chal: What point-in-time VM state capture can leak in-memory secrets if left unmanaged? Submit TG{••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Snapshot — convenient but sensitive. It holds memory (and secrets); reverting can undo security fixes. Limit, protect and expire snapshots.
tasks.example: Revert a VM to a month-old snapshot and you may re-open a patched vulnerability or restore a disabled attacker account — rollback has security consequences.

tasks.title: Templates & golden images
tasks.teach: New VMs shouldn't be built by hand each time — you clone them from a template (a hardened, patched base VM). If the template is secure, every VM born from it starts secure; if the template is stale or misconfigured, every clone inherits the weakness. So the template (golden image) is a high-leverage security control: harden once, inherit everywhere — and keep it patched.
tasks.chal: What hardened base VM is cloned to create new, consistently-secure VMs? Submit TG{••••••••}.
hints: The golden image to clone from.
tasks.learn: Template (golden image) — harden and patch once; every clone inherits it. A stale template spreads the same weakness to every new VM.
tasks.example: Patch and CIS-harden the template monthly, and 500 VMs cloned from it start compliant. Neglect it, and you mass-produce vulnerable machines.

tasks.title: Hypervisor attack surface
tasks.teach:
Minimise what the hypervisor exposes. Disable unneeded services and emulated devices (many escapes target emulated hardware), remove unused network adapters, keep the hypervisor patched promptly (a hypervisor CVE can mean escape), separate management/VM/storage traffic, and don't run extra software on the host. Less surface on the layer that enforces all isolation means fewer paths to an escape.

🔑 Key point

Side channel — leaks across the isolation boundary via shared hardware (caches, speculative execution). Mitigated by microcode/patches and scheduling controls.
tasks.chal: Cross-VM data leaks via shared CPU hardware (e.g. Spectre/Meltdown) are what class of attack (two words)? Submit TG{••••_•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Side channel — leaks across the isolation boundary via shared hardware (caches, speculative execution). Mitigated by microcode/patches and scheduling controls.
tasks.example: Spectre/Meltdown showed one VM could, in theory, infer another's data through CPU timing — a reason to patch firmware/microcode, not just the OS.

tasks.title: Scenario: protect the boundary
tasks.teach:
Securing virtualization is layered: harden and patch the hypervisor, lock down the management plane, enforce isolation and resource limits, keep templates patched, control snapshots, and segment management/VM/storage networks. No single control is enough — a weak management plane beats perfect isolation, and an unpatched hypervisor beats a hardened guest. The approach that layers all of these is the same one that secures everything else.

🔑 Key point

Defense in depth — patch the hypervisor, lock the management plane, enforce isolation, harden templates, control snapshots, segment networks. Each backs up the others.
tasks.chal: Layering hypervisor, management-plane, isolation and network controls together is an application of which principle? Submit TG{•••••••_••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Defense in depth — patch the hypervisor, lock the management plane, enforce isolation, harden templates, control snapshots, segment networks. Each backs up the others.
tasks.example: The attacker who can't escape the VM tries the management plane; the one who can't reach that tries a stale snapshot. Layers mean every path is covered.

rooms.title: Container & Orchestration Security
rooms.subtitle: Secure the image, harden the runtime, lock down the cluster.
rooms.blurb: Understand the shared-kernel trade-off, namespaces/cgroups/capabilities, image and supply-chain security, and Kubernetes RBAC.

tasks.title: Containers vs VMs
tasks.teach:
A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS; a container virtualizes the operating system — it packages an app and its libraries but shares the host's kernel with every other container. That makes containers lightweight and fast, but it means the isolation is thinner than a VM's: there's one kernel between all containers and the host, so a kernel vulnerability or a misconfiguration can let a container affect its neighbours or the host.

Why it matters: the shared kernel is the whole security story. VM isolation is a hypervisor boundary; container isolation is kernel features (namespaces, cgroups, capabilities). Thinner boundary = more care needed at runtime.
tasks.chal: Containers share the host's ___ (making their isolation thinner than a VM's). Submit TG{••••••}.
hints: One of these between all containers.
tasks.learn: Kernel — shared by all containers on a host. The thin boundary is why container runtime hardening matters so much more than for VMs.
tasks.example: 10 VMs = 10 kernels (strong isolation). 10 containers = 1 shared kernel (light isolation). A kernel flaw can cross container boundaries; a hypervisor is a sturdier wall.

tasks.title: Namespaces
tasks.teach: Container isolation is built from Linux kernel features, and the first is namespaces — they give each container its own view of the system: its own process tree (PID namespace), network stack, mounts, hostname and users. A container sees only its own processes and network, not the host's or other containers'. Namespaces are what make a container look like its own machine.
tasks.chal: Which Linux feature gives each container its own isolated view of processes, network and mounts? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Namespaces — per-container views of PIDs, network, mounts, etc. They provide the isolation half of containment (cgroups provide the limits).
tasks.example: Inside a container, ps shows only its own PID 1 and children — the PID namespace hides the host's processes entirely.

tasks.title: cgroups
tasks.teach: The second kernel feature is cgroups (control groups) — they limit and account for the resources a container may use: CPU, memory, disk and network IO. Where namespaces isolate what a container sees, cgroups limit what it can consume, preventing one container from starving the host or its neighbours (the container version of the noisy-neighbour problem).
tasks.chal: Which Linux feature limits a container's CPU/memory/IO consumption? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: cgroups — resource limits and accounting. Namespaces isolate the view; cgroups cap the consumption. Set memory/CPU limits on every container.
tasks.example: docker run --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 uses cgroups to cap the container — a runaway process can't eat the whole host.

tasks.title: Capabilities & privilege
tasks.teach: Linux root power is split into fine-grained capabilities (CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, etc.). Containers should run with the fewest capabilities they need — drop all and add back only what's required. The cardinal sin is the --privileged flag: it gives the container all capabilities and broad host access, effectively removing the isolation. A privileged container is close to running as root on the host.
tasks.chal:
$ docker run --privileged ... # DANGEROUS: all caps, host device access # better: $ docker run --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE ...

Which Docker flag gives a container all capabilities and broad host access (and must be avoided)? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: privileged — grants all capabilities + host device access, gutting isolation. Drop all caps and add back only what's needed instead.
tasks.example: A --privileged container can often reach host devices and escape to the host. Almost nothing legitimately needs it; drop caps instead.

tasks.title: Run as non-root
tasks.teach: By default many containers run as root inside the container — and because of the shared kernel, container-root is dangerously close to host-root if anything goes wrong. Running as a non-root user (and ideally rootless containers, where the runtime itself doesn't need root) dramatically reduces the blast radius of a container compromise. 'Don't run as root' is the single highest-value container runtime control.
tasks.chal: To limit blast radius, containers should run as a ___ user, not root. Submit TG{•••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Non-root — set USER in the image and runAsNonRoot in Kubernetes. Combined with dropped caps and no --privileged, a compromise stays contained.
tasks.example: Container-root + a kernel bug = host-root. Non-root + dropped caps + read-only FS = a compromised container that can do very little.

tasks.title: Scan the image
tasks.teach: A container image bundles an OS base plus libraries — any of which can carry known vulnerabilities. Image scanning checks an image against vulnerability databases before you deploy it, flagging CVEs in the packages and base layers. Tools like Trivy, Grype and Clair do this; you scan in CI so a vulnerable image never reaches production. Use minimal base images (distroless/alpine) to shrink what there is to scan and exploit.
tasks.chal:
$ trivy image myapp:1.4 myapp:1.4 (debian 12) Total: 7 (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 3, MEDIUM: 2) openssl 3.0.9 CVE-2023-XXXX CRITICAL -> fix: 3.0.11

What is checking a container image for known vulnerabilities before deploy called? Submit TG{••••••••}.
hints: Find the CVEs in the image.
tasks.learn: Scanning — catch vulnerable packages before production (Trivy/Grype/Clair), in CI. Minimal base images (distroless) reduce what can be vulnerable.
tasks.example: Scan in the pipeline: a CRITICAL CVE in the base image fails the build, so it's fixed before deploy — not discovered in production.

lab.intro: Scan a container image for vulnerabilities.

steps.out:
myapp:1.4 (debian 12)
Total: 7 (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 3)
openssl 3.0.9  CVE-2023-XXXX CRITICAL -> fixed in 3.0.11

steps2: Run trivy image <image> (or Grype)
Review CRITICAL/HIGH CVEs and their fixes
Name this pre-deploy image check.

tasks.title: Supply chain & signing
tasks.teach: You must trust that an image is what it claims to be and came from where you expect — that's supply-chain security. You pull only from trusted registries, sign images (e.g. with cosign/Sigstore) and verify signatures at deploy via admission control, and track contents with an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials). Signing proves provenance and integrity: a tampered or unsigned image is rejected before it runs.
tasks.chal: What proves an image's provenance and integrity so a tampered one is rejected at deploy? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Signing — with admission control verifying signatures, only trusted, untampered images run. Pair with an SBOM and trusted registries.
tasks.example: Admission controller policy: 'only run images signed by our key'. An attacker who sneaks an unsigned/tampered image into the registry can't get it deployed.

tasks.title: Runtime hardening
tasks.teach: Harden the running container so even a compromised app can do little: run non-root, drop all capabilities (add back the minimum), make the root filesystem read-only (so malware can't write a payload or modify the app), apply a seccomp profile (restrict syscalls), and never use --privileged. A read-only filesystem alone stops a huge class of attacks that depend on writing to disk.
tasks.chal: Making a container's filesystem ___ stops an attacker writing payloads or altering the app (two words)? Submit TG{••••_••••}.
tasks.learn: Read-only root filesystem — plus non-root, dropped caps and seccomp. A compromised process can't persist or tamper if it can't write.
tasks.example: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in the pod spec: the web app still serves, but malware can't drop a webshell or rewrite the binary.

tasks.title: Kubernetes & RBAC
tasks.teach: At scale, Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster via its control plane (the API server, etcd, scheduler). The API server is the keys to the cluster, so you secure it with RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) — granting each user/service account only the specific actions it needs on specific resources. Over-broad RBAC (cluster-admin for everything) is the most common Kubernetes weakness; least-privilege RBAC is the foundation of cluster security.
tasks.chal:
$ kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --as=system:serviceaccount:default:web yes <- this service account is cluster-admin! over-privileged, fix the RBAC

Which Kubernetes mechanism grants least-privilege access to the cluster API? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: RBAC — scope every user/service account to the minimum. A web pod with cluster-admin is a disaster waiting to happen; grant only what's needed.
tasks.example: Also apply Pod Security Standards (no privileged pods), NetworkPolicies (default-deny pod traffic) and a secrets manager — RBAC is the start, not the end.

lab.intro: Check a service account for over-broad permissions.

steps.out: yes   <- service account "web" can do everything (cluster-admin) = over-privileged

steps2: Test a service account: kubectl auth can-i ...
If it can do everything, tighten its Role/RoleBinding
Name the K8s least-privilege mechanism.

tasks.title: Scenario: image to locked-down cluster
tasks.teach: End to end: you scan and sign the image, run it non-root with dropped caps and a read-only filesystem, deploy to Kubernetes under least-privilege RBAC, default-deny NetworkPolicies and a secrets manager — and watch running behaviour with a runtime-detection tool that alerts on anomalies (a shell spawned in a container, an unexpected connection). Name that behavioural runtime-security tool.
tasks.chal: Which open-source tool detects anomalous container runtime behaviour (e.g. a shell in a container)? Submit TG{•••••}.
tasks.learn: Falco — runtime threat detection (CNCF). It alerts on suspicious syscalls/behaviour, the detection layer atop scanning, signing, RBAC and runtime hardening.
tasks.example: Falco rule fires: 'a shell was spawned inside the payments container' — a classic post-exploitation signal, caught at runtime even if everything upstream was bypassed.

rooms.title: Data Centre Security
rooms.subtitle: From the fence to the backups — physical, environmental and resilient.
rooms.blurb: Design layered physical access, environmental controls and redundancy; treat availability as a security property.

tasks.title: Availability is security
tasks.teach:
A data centre is the physical facility holding the servers, storage and network everything else runs on — so its security is the foundation under all the digital controls. The guiding idea here is that availability is a security property: the 'A' in the CIA triad. A facility that floods, overheats, loses power or burns is a security failure just as surely as a breach — the data and services become unavailable. Data-centre security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability, physically.

Why it matters: the best firewalls and encryption are worthless if someone walks into the server room, or the cooling fails and everything shuts down. Physical and environmental security underpin everything.
tasks.chal: Which CIA property — kept up by power, cooling and redundancy — does data-centre resilience most directly protect? Submit TG{••••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Availability — the 'A' of CIA. A facility that goes down is a security failure; power, cooling, fire protection and redundancy are security controls.
tasks.example: A ransomware outage and a cooling failure both end the same way: services down. That's why uptime engineering is security, not just operations.

tasks.title: Layered physical access
tasks.teach: Physical security is defence in depth made concrete: a hardened perimeter (fence, gates, CCTV), then layered access inward — reception, badge/biometric doors, and for sensitive areas a mantrap (an interlocking two-door airlock that admits one authorised person at a time). Inside the data hall, racks and cages add another layer. Each boundary requires stronger authorisation than the last, so a single breached door doesn't expose the servers.
tasks.chal: What interlocking two-door airlock admits one authorised person at a time (defeating tailgating)? Submit TG{•••••••}.
tasks.learn: Mantrap — one person, one authorisation, per entry. With perimeter, badges/biometrics, CCTV and cages, it's layered physical defence in depth.
tasks.example: Layers: fence → reception → badge door → biometric → mantrap → locked cage → rack. Breaching one gets you to the next barrier, not the servers.

tasks.title: Tailgating
tasks.teach: The most common physical attack needs no hacking: tailgating (piggybacking) — an unauthorised person simply follows an authorised one through a secured door before it closes, bypassing the access control entirely. It's defeated by mantraps (one person per cycle), anti-passback rules, turnstiles, security awareness ('don't hold the door'), and guards/CCTV. People, not locks, are usually the weak point.
tasks.chal: What is following an authorised person through a secure door without badging called? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
tasks.learn: Tailgating — the human bypass of access control. Mantraps, anti-passback, turnstiles and awareness ('never hold the door') stop it.
tasks.example: An attacker in a delivery uniform carrying boxes asks you to hold the door — polite instinct beats the badge reader. That's tailgating; a mantrap prevents it.

tasks.title: Power: UPS & generators
tasks.teach: Servers need clean, continuous power. A UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) — a battery system — provides instant backup the moment mains power fails, bridging the gap (seconds to minutes) until generators start and take over for longer outages. Dual power feeds and N+1 UPS/generator capacity mean no single power failure takes the facility down. Power is the most common cause of data-centre outages, so it's engineered with redundancy.
tasks.chal: What battery system provides instant backup power the moment mains fails (before generators start)? Submit TG{•••}.
tasks.learn: UPS — instant battery bridge to the generators. With dual feeds and N+1 capacity, no single power fault causes an outage.
tasks.example: Mains drops → UPS carries the load in milliseconds → generator spins up in ~30s and takes over → UPS recharges. Seamless, because power loss = outage = security failure.

tasks.title: Cooling & fire
tasks.teach: Dense racks generate huge heat; without cooling (precision HVAC/CRAC units, hot/cold aisle containment) equipment overheats and shuts down within minutes — so cooling is redundant and monitored. And because electronics and fire are a lethal mix, data centres use fire suppression designed not to destroy equipment: clean-agent gas systems (or pre-action, not wet, sprinklers) that put out fire without soaking the servers, plus very early smoke detection.
tasks.chal: What clean-agent/gas system extinguishes fire without water-damaging the equipment (two words)? Submit TG{••••_•••••••••••}.
hints: Put out fire, spare the servers.
tasks.learn: Fire suppression — clean-agent gas (or pre-action) systems plus early detection. Cooling (redundant HVAC, hot/cold aisles) keeps it from overheating in the first place.
tasks.example: A normal sprinkler would destroy a server room. Clean-agent suppression smothers the fire chemically, leaving the hardware intact and recoverable.

tasks.title: Redundancy, N+1 & Tiers
tasks.teach:
Resilience means no single point of failure. N+1 redundancy provides one spare for every component needed (N units of capacity plus one extra), so any single failure is covered; 2N fully duplicates. The Uptime Institute Tier model (Tier I–IV) rates a facility's redundancy and expected availability, with Tier III/IV offering concurrent maintainability and fault tolerance. Redundancy is how availability is engineered.

🔑 Key point

N+1 — one spare covers any single failure. 2N fully duplicates; the Tier model (I–IV) rates the overall redundancy and availability.

Key term: N+I
tasks.chal: What redundancy level provides one spare for every needed component (N plus one)? Submit TG{•+•}.
tasks.learn: N+1 — one spare covers any single failure. 2N fully duplicates; the Tier model (I–IV) rates the overall redundancy and availability.
tasks.example: N+1 cooling: if you need 4 CRAC units, you install 5. One can fail (or be serviced) with zero impact — concurrent maintainability.

tasks.title: Backups: the 3-2-1 rule
tasks.teach: Storage security includes getting backups right. The 3-2-1 rule: keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with 1 copy offsite. Modern practice adds immutable (WORM) backups that ransomware can't encrypt or delete, and defines RPO (how much data you can afford to lose) and RTO (how fast you must recover). And the golden rule: an untested backup is not a backup — restore-test regularly.
tasks.chal: What backup rule says keep 3 copies, on 2 media, with 1 offsite? Submit TG{•-•-•}.
tasks.learn: 3-2-1 — 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite; add immutable copies against ransomware. Define RPO/RTO, and test restores — an untested backup may not work.
tasks.example: Ransomware encrypts production and the onsite backup — the offsite, immutable copy is what saves you. 3-2-1 plus immutability is modern backup security.

tasks.title: Monitoring the facility
tasks.teach: You monitor a data centre on two levels. Physical/environmental: a DCIM (Data Centre Infrastructure Management) system tracks power, cooling, temperature, humidity and space; CCTV and access logs track who went where. Logical: the usual SIEM watches the systems. Correlating both (an access-log entry to the cage at 3am and a server tampered with) is how physical and cyber monitoring together catch what either alone would miss.
tasks.chal: What system monitors data-centre power, cooling, temperature and space (abbr.)? Submit TG{••••}.
tasks.learn: DCIM — the facility's telemetry (power/cooling/environment/space). Correlate it with CCTV, access logs and the SIEM for full physical + logical visibility.
tasks.example: DCIM alerts 'cold-aisle temperature rising' before a cooling failure becomes an outage — environmental monitoring as an availability control.

lab.intro: Review physical access logs for an out-of-hours entry.

steps.out:
03:14 BADGE rnehra GRANTED CAGE-7   (out of hours)
03:14 MANTRAP cycle OK  CCTV: clip #4471   <- correlate with any server tamper

steps2: Review the door/access logs (and DCIM/CCTV) for the sensitive area
Flag out-of-hours or unexpected entries
Name the facility-monitoring system (4 letters).

tasks.title: Network & storage security
tasks.teach:
Inside the facility, the network and storage need securing too. The data-centre network is segmented — management, production and storage traffic kept on separate networks/VLANs so a breach in one can't reach the others (the same zero-trust, least-privilege thinking as elsewhere, applied to the fabric). Storage (SAN/NAS) holds the crown-jewel data, so it is access-controlled and encrypted at rest, ensuring a stolen or decommissioned disk reveals nothing.

🔑 Key point

Encryption at rest — plus network segmentation (management/production/storage apart) and storage access control. A pulled disk is then just scrap to a thief.
tasks.chal: Protecting SAN/NAS data at rest so a stolen disk is unreadable relies on ___? Submit TG{••••••••••}.
hints: Make the stored data unreadable without a key.
tasks.learn: Encryption at rest — plus network segmentation (management/production/storage apart) and storage access control. A pulled disk is then just scrap to a thief.
tasks.example: Segment the storage network off the production one, and encrypt the SAN. A compromised app server can't reach the storage fabric, and a stolen drive is unreadable.

tasks.title: Scenario: fence to backups
tasks.teach:
Securing a data centre end to end layers every control: a hardened perimeter and mantrap access, CCTV and guards, N+1 power (UPS + generators) and cooling, clean-agent fire suppression, network segmentation, encrypted storage, 3-2-1 immutable backups, DCIM + SIEM monitoring, and a tested DR plan. No single control secures the facility; the approach that layers physical, environmental, network and data controls together is the familiar one.

🔑 Key point

Defense in depth — perimeter → access → environment → network → storage → backups → monitoring, each backing up the next. With availability engineered in, the facility is secure end to end.
tasks.chal: Layering physical, environmental, network and backup controls from the fence to the data is which principle (three words)? Submit TG{•••••••_••_•••••}.
tasks.learn: Defense in depth — perimeter → access → environment → network → storage → backups → monitoring, each backing up the next. With availability engineered in, the facility is secure end to end.
tasks.example: Breach the fence and you meet CCTV; pass reception and you meet the mantrap; reach a rack and you meet the cage and logs. And if all else fails, the offsite immutable backup still stands.
